Students fear hurting the person. Without CPR, a person in cardiac arrest will die; broken ribs are a possible but acceptable risk.
Students think an AED could shock someone who doesn't need it. AEDs analyze the rhythm and only advise a shock when needed; just follow the prompts.

days.guide: Explain the chain of survival; the student draws it and explains why each link matters (for every minute without CPR and defibrillation, survival falls).

questions.q: Why is early CPR so important?
questions.a: It keeps oxygen-rich blood flowing to the brain and heart until a defibrillator and EMS arrive.

questions.q: What's the first link in the out-of-hospital chain?
questions.a: Recognizing cardiac arrest and calling 911 (activating emergency response).

days.guide: Demonstrate hand position and posture; the student does compressions on the manikin/cushion to 'Stayin' Alive' in 30-compression sets, counting aloud.

questions.q: How deep and fast should adult compressions be?
questions.a: At least 2 inches (no more than about 2.4 inches) at 100–120 per minute.

questions.q: Why allow the chest to fully rise between compressions?
questions.a: Full recoil lets the heart refill with blood.

days.guide: Demonstrate head-tilt/chin-lift and rescue breaths with a face shield on the manikin (1 second each, chest visibly rises). Practice 30:2 cycles.

questions.q: How long should each rescue breath last?
questions.a: About 1 second, just enough to make the chest rise.

questions.q: What if you're untrained or unwilling to give breaths?
questions.a: Do hands-only CPR: continuous compressions until help or an AED arrives.

days.guide: Watch the AED trainer video and walk through the steps on paper: turn on, follow prompts, expose and dry chest, place pads, stand clear for analysis, shock if advised, resume CPR immediately.

questions.q: What's the first thing to do when the AED arrives?
questions.a: Turn it on and follow its voice prompts.

questions.q: What should everyone do while the AED analyzes or shocks?
questions.a: Stand clear — no one touches the person.

days.guide: The student demonstrates 2 minutes of CPR from scene check through compressions/breaths; score with the checklist.

questions.q: How many compressions and breaths are in one cycle?
questions.a: 30 compressions and 2 breaths.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills check (2 minutes): Proficient = checks scene, checks responsiveness and breathing (≤10 s), calls/sends someone for 911 and an AED, hand placement on the center of the chest (lower half of sternum), arms straight and shoulders over hands, depth about 2 inches, rate 100–120/min (count about 30 compressions in 15–18 seconds), full recoil, minimal interruptions, 30:2 with breaths if trained (or hands-only). Developing = 1–2 errors corrected with cues. Beginning = 3+ errors. Chain of survival (adult out-of-hospital): recognize cardiac arrest and activate EMS, early high-quality CPR, rapid defibrillation, advanced resuscitation by EMS, post-cardiac-arrest care, and recovery.

weeks.prep: Gather a doll for infant practice, a manikin or firm pillow, and a sturdy chair. Practice choking techniques only on a pillow or chair, never with real thrusts on a person. Review the 2025 American Heart Association guideline update: for infants, compressions with two thumbs (encircling hands) or the heel of one hand; for choking adults and children, alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts is now recommended (the Red Cross also teaches this).
misconceptions: Students do abdominal thrusts on infants. Infants (under 1 year) get back blows and chest thrusts only.
Students give back blows to a person who can cough forcefully. If they can cough or speak, encourage coughing and stay with them; act only if they can't breathe, cough or speak.
Students compress infants too deeply or too shallowly. Infant compressions are about 1.5 inches (4 cm), one-third the chest depth.

days.guide: Demonstrate on a pillow strapped to a chair back: back blows, then abdominal thrusts; then self-rescue by thrusting the abdomen against a chair back.

questions.q: How can you tell someone is truly choking?
questions.a: They can't cough, speak or breathe and often clutch the throat.

questions.q: Where do you place your fist for abdominal thrusts?
questions.a: Just above the navel, below the breastbone, thumb side in.

days.guide: Explain child CPR (age 1 to puberty) differences and practice five 30:2 cycles.

questions.q: How deep are compressions for a child?
questions.a: About 2 inches, about one-third the depth of the chest.

questions.q: If you're alone and didn't see a child collapse, when do you call 911?
questions.a: Give about 2 minutes (5 cycles) of CPR first, then call (unless you have a phone to call on speaker immediately).

days.guide: Practice infant CPR on the doll with the two-thumb encircling technique (or two fingers as older materials show), counting aloud.

questions.q: How deep and fast are infant compressions?
questions.a: About 1.5 inches at 100–120 per minute.

questions.q: How do you give breaths to an infant?
questions.a: Cover the infant's mouth and nose with your mouth and give gentle puffs, each about 1 second, until the chest rises.

days.guide: Practice infant choking relief on the doll: 5 back blows, 5 chest thrusts, supporting the head and keeping it lower than the chest.

questions.q: Why not use abdominal thrusts on infants?
questions.a: They can injure an infant's internal organs; back blows and chest thrusts are used instead.

questions.q: What do you do if the infant becomes unresponsive?
questions.a: Call 911 if not done, begin CPR, and look in the mouth for the object before giving breaths (remove only if seen).

days.guide: The student demonstrates adult, child and infant choking relief and child/infant CPR; score with the checklist.

questions.q: What should you do if a choking adult becomes unresponsive?
questions.a: Lower them to the ground, call 911, and begin CPR starting with compressions; check the mouth for the object before breaths.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills checklist key: Adult/child choking — confirm choking (can't cough/speak/breathe; hands at throat), get consent, call 911 or have someone call, give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades and 5 abdominal thrusts (fist just above the navel, quick inward-upward), repeat until object out or person unresponsive (then begin CPR, checking mouth for object before breaths). Self-rescue — thrust abdomen against a chair back. Infant choking — support head and jaw, face-down on forearm with head lower than chest, 5 back blows, turn over, 5 chest thrusts on the center of the chest just below the nipple line, repeat. Child CPR — 30:2 (single rescuer), one or two hands, about 2 inches (one-third chest depth), 100–120/min. Infant CPR — 30:2, two thumbs (encircling) or heel of one hand per 2025 AHA, or two fingers per older training; about 1.5 inches; 100–120/min. Proficient = all steps correct.

weeks.prep: Gather gloves, gauze, a rolled towel (for packing practice), a commercial tourniquet if available (or a triangular bandage and a stick for improvised practice), a rolled magazine, triangular bandage, and an elastic bandage. Queue the Stop the Bleed overview and an epinephrine auto-injector trainer video. Parental note: some materials show injuries.
misconceptions: Students apply a tourniquet loosely or remove it to check. Tighten until bleeding stops, note the time, and leave it on for EMS to remove.
Students put ice, butter or ointment on burns. Cool with cool running water (not ice) for at least 10 minutes (20 for chemical burns), then cover loosely.
Students wait to see if stroke symptoms go away. Call 911 immediately and note the time symptoms started; treatment is time-critical.

days.guide: Teach Stop the Bleed: direct pressure, wound packing, tourniquet. The student practices pressure and packing on a rolled towel and applies a tourniquet to a family member's arm or a pillow (don't tighten painfully on a person).

questions.q: Where do you place a tourniquet?
questions.a: 2–3 inches above the wound (between the wound and the heart), not over a joint.

questions.q: What should you do after applying a tourniquet?
questions.a: Note the time and leave it in place for EMS.

days.guide: The student learns first aid for thermal, chemical and electrical burns and when to call 911.

questions.q: What's the first aid for a minor thermal burn?
questions.a: Cool it under cool running water for at least 10 minutes, then cover loosely with a sterile dressing.

questions.q: Why must you turn off power before helping someone with an electrical injury?
questions.a: So the rescuer isn't electrocuted; the person may still be in contact with the current.

days.guide: The student splints a 'forearm fracture' with a rolled magazine and triangular bandage sling, then practices RICE on an ankle.

questions.q: How do you check that a splint isn't too tight?
questions.a: Check fingers for warmth, color, sensation and movement before and after splinting.

questions.q: What does RICE stand for?
questions.a: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.

days.guide: The student learns BE-FAST for stroke, signs of heart attack, seizure care, diabetic emergencies and anaphylaxis; watch the auto-injector trainer video.

questions.q: What should you do for someone having a seizure?
questions.a: Protect them from injury (move objects, cushion the head), don't restrain them or put anything in the mouth, time the seizure, roll them onto their side after, and call 911 if it lasts over 5 minutes or it's their first.

questions.q: A diabetic person is confused and sweaty but can swallow. What could help?
questions.a: Give sugar (juice, regular soda, glucose tablets) for suspected low blood sugar; call 911 if they don't improve or can't swallow.

days.guide: Give the 10-scenario quiz. Review.

questions.q: A friend stung by a bee has trouble breathing and swelling lips. What do you do?
questions.a: Call 911 and help them use their epinephrine auto-injector in the outer thigh; keep monitoring and be ready for CPR.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario quiz key (example items): 1) Severe arm bleeding — call 911, gloves, firm direct pressure; if life-threatening and not controlled, tourniquet 2–3 inches above the wound (not on a joint), note time. 2) Deep wound in the thigh/armpit area — pack the wound with gauze and hold pressure. 3) Kitchen burn — cool running water 10+ min, remove rings, cover loosely, call 911 if large, on face/hands/genitals, or deep. 4) Chemical burn — brush off dry chemical, flush with water 20+ minutes, remove contaminated clothing. 5) Electrical burn — turn off power first, call 911 (possible internal injury and heart rhythm problems). 6) Suspected forearm fracture — splint in position found, padding, check circulation beyond the splint. 7) Sprain — RICE: rest, ice (20 min with cloth), compression, elevation. 8) Stroke — BE-FAST: Balance, Eyes, Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911. 9) Heart attack — call 911, help the person rest, aspirin if not allergic and directed; be ready for CPR. 10) Anaphylaxis — call 911, help use epinephrine auto-injector in the outer thigh, second dose after 5–15 min if needed.

weeks.prep: Gather a rope and a plastic bottle with a little water (for the throw). Find the Red Cross or AHA blended First Aid/CPR/AED course options and costs, or schedule an in-person session. Prepare the Unit 6 written test and the skills checklist.
misconceptions: Students think drowning looks like splashing and yelling. Drowning is often quiet: the person is vertical, head low, mouth at water level, unable to wave or call.
Students treat heat stroke like heat exhaustion. Heat stroke (confusion, very high body temperature, may stop sweating) is life-threatening: call 911 and cool aggressively (cold-water immersion).
Students rub frostbitten skin or rewarm a hypothermic person quickly with hot water. Handle gently; don't rub; rewarm gradually.

days.guide: Compare heat exhaustion vs. heat stroke and frostbite vs. hypothermia; the student makes a quick-reference card.

questions.q: Name two signs that separate heat stroke from heat exhaustion.
questions.a: Confusion or altered mental state, and very high body temperature (about 104 °F+) with hot skin; sweating may have stopped.

questions.q: What's the first aid for heat stroke?
questions.a: Call 911 and cool the person immediately, ideally by cold-water immersion or ice packs and wet cloths with fanning.

days.guide: The student learns drowning signs and practices reach-throw-don't-go, throwing the rope and bottle to a target 15 feet away.

questions.q: What does drowning usually look like?
questions.a: Quiet: vertical in the water, head back, mouth at the surface, unable to wave or call for help.

questions.q: Why 'don't go' into the water?
questions.a: A panicking swimmer can pull the rescuer under; untrained rescuers often drown themselves.

days.guide: Run three mock scenarios with family, rotating rescuer and patient roles; debrief each.

questions.q: In the bleeding-cyclist scenario, what comes before treating the wound?
questions.a: Check the scene (traffic), put on gloves, call 911.

days.guide: The student completes an online/blended module or schedules an in-person skills session for a recognized certification.

questions.q: Why does a certification require an in-person skills check?
questions.a: Instructors must verify correct depth, rate and technique that can't be judged online.

days.guide: Give the written Unit 6 test and a timed CPR/AED skills demonstration.

questions.q: How quickly should AED pads be applied after it arrives?
questions.a: As soon as possible, with minimal interruption to compressions.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test key (written, sample): 1) Check–Call–Care. 2) Adult compressions — 2 inches, 100–120/min, 30:2. 3) Infant compressions — 1.5 inches. 4) AED steps — on, pads, analyze, shock if advised, resume CPR. 5) Infant choking — 5 back blows, 5 chest thrusts. 6) Tourniquet placement — 2–3 inches above wound, not on a joint. 7) Burn — cool water 10+ min. 8) BE-FAST. 9) Heat exhaustion — heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, dizziness, nausea: move to cool place, fluids, loosen clothing. Heat stroke — confusion, hot skin, body temp ~104 °F or higher: call 911, cool rapidly. 10) Hypothermia — shivering (may stop), confusion, core temperature below 95 °F: get to warmth, remove wet clothes, warm blankets, warm sweet drinks if alert. 11) Frostbite — numb, white/gray waxy skin: warm gently, don't rub. 12) Water rescue — Reach or Throw, Don't Go. Skills test: timed 2-minute CPR with AED (pads placed within 90 seconds of arrival) scored with the Week 20 checklist.

weeks.prep: Read KidsHealth (for teens) articles on anxiety and depression. Parental note: these weeks discuss mental illness and, next week, suicide. Check in privately with your teen about how they are doing; if you have concerns about their safety, call or text 988 or contact a mental health professional.
misconceptions: Students think mental health means having or not having an illness. Mental health is a continuum; everyone moves along it (thriving, coping, struggling, in crisis).
Students think depression is just sadness or weakness. It is a medical condition affecting mood, thinking, sleep and energy that lasts at least two weeks and is treatable.
Students think therapy is only for severe problems. Therapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy, helps many people with everyday stress as well as illness.

days.guide: Draw the continuum. The student places everyday examples (stressed before a test, can't sleep for weeks, feeling great after a hike) and explains the difference between normal stress and a problem that needs help.

questions.q: When does sadness become a concern worth getting help for?
questions.a: When it lasts two weeks or more, or interferes with school, relationships, sleep, eating or daily life.

days.guide: The student researches anxiety disorders and depression on KidsHealth and charts symptoms, causes and treatments.

questions.q: Name two evidence-based treatments for depression.
questions.a: Psychotherapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy and medication such as SSRIs, often combined, plus healthy habits.

questions.q: What can cause depression?
questions.a: A mix of genetics, brain chemistry, stressful life events, medical conditions and other factors; it is not a personal failing.

days.guide: The student reads a reliable article and explains how sleep, exercise and social connection affect mood.

questions.q: How does regular exercise help mood?
questions.a: It releases endorphins and other brain chemicals, reduces stress hormones, and improves sleep and self-esteem.

days.guide: The student analyzes two media examples (news or film) for stigmatizing portrayals and rewrites one message using respectful, person-first language.

questions.q: Rewrite 'He's a schizo' respectfully.
questions.a: 'He has schizophrenia' (or 'he's living with schizophrenia').

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review.

questions.q: What's one thing you can do if a friend seems depressed?
questions.a: Listen without judgment, encourage them to talk to a trusted adult or professional, and tell an adult if you are worried about their safety.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Mental health continuum — thriving → reacting/coping → struggling → crisis/ill. 2) Signs of depression lasting 2+ weeks — persistent sadness or irritability, loss of interest, sleep or appetite changes, low energy, trouble concentrating, feelings of worthlessness, thoughts of death. 3) Anxiety disorder — excessive worry or fear that's hard to control and interferes with life (e.g., generalized anxiety, panic, social anxiety). 4) Treatments — therapy (e.g., CBT), medication (e.g., SSRIs prescribed by a doctor), lifestyle (sleep, exercise, social connection). 5) Teens need 8–10 hours of sleep. 6) Exercise reduces symptoms of depression and anxiety. 7) Stigma — negative stereotypes that discourage people from seeking help. 8) Where to get help — trusted adult, doctor, school counselor, therapist, 988.

weeks.prep: Get a journal. Find a guided progressive muscle relaxation and a 10-minute mindfulness audio (e.g., from a reputable health system or UCLA Mindful). Prepare five blaming statements for Day 3.
misconceptions: Students think all stress is bad. Short-term stress can motivate; chronic, unmanaged stress harms health.
Students confuse assertive with aggressive. Assertive communication states your needs respectfully ('I feel… when… I need…'); aggressive blames or attacks.
Students think coping means avoiding the problem. Healthy coping includes problem-solving, relaxation and seeking support, not avoidance or substance use.

days.guide: The student tracks stressors and body responses (headache, tight shoulders, racing heart) for three days and looks for patterns.

questions.q: Name three physical signs of stress.
questions.a: Faster heart rate, muscle tension, headaches, stomachaches, trouble sleeping.

days.guide: Practice box breathing (inhale 4, hold 4, exhale 4, hold 4), progressive muscle relaxation and a 10-minute mindfulness exercise; the student rates each.

questions.q: Why does slow breathing calm the body?
questions.a: It activates the parasympathetic ('rest and digest') nervous system, slowing heart rate and lowering stress hormones.

days.guide: The student rewrites five blaming statements as I-statements and role-plays two with you.

questions.q: Rewrite: 'You never let me use the car!'
questions.a: 'I feel frustrated when I can't use the car for practice because I need driving hours. Can we plan a schedule?'

days.guide: Teach a five-step model: calm down, each person states the problem with I-statements, listen and paraphrase, brainstorm solutions, agree on one and follow up. Role-play a sibling disagreement.

questions.q: Why paraphrase the other person's view?
questions.a: It shows you listened and checks understanding, which lowers defensiveness.

days.guide: The student writes the personal wellness plan. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: What should you do if coping strategies aren't helping?
questions.a: Talk to a trusted adult, doctor or counselor; call or text 988 if in crisis.

weeks.assessment_key: Wellness plan rubric (4 levels): 4 = Names personal stressors and body signals from the log; three specific coping strategies tested this week with when/how to use each; two named trusted adults with contact info; daily habits with measurable targets (8–10 hrs sleep, 60 min activity, screen limits, time with friends); a plan for when coping isn't enough (talk to parent, counselor, 988). 3 = complete but vague. 2 = missing support people or habits. 1 = minimal.

weeks.prep: Parental preview required: read the 988 Lifeline site (988lifeline.org) and a reliable warning-signs page (e.g., American Foundation for Suicide Prevention or NIMH). Check in privately with your teen. If you're ever worried about your teen's immediate safety, call 911 or 988. Keep discussions factual and caring; it is safe and helpful to talk about suicide directly.
misconceptions: Students think asking about suicide puts the idea in someone's head. Research shows asking directly does not increase risk and can open the door to help.
Students think they should keep a friend's suicidal thoughts secret. Safety comes before secrecy; always tell a trusted adult.
Students think people who talk about suicide won't do it. Talk of suicide is a warning sign and must be taken seriously.

days.guide: The student learns warning signs and risk and protective factors from a reliable source and makes a chart.

questions.q: Name three warning signs of suicide.
questions.a: Talking about wanting to die or being a burden, withdrawing from others, giving away possessions, increased substance use, saying goodbye, extreme mood changes.

questions.q: Name two protective factors.
questions.a: Strong connections with family and friends, access to mental health care, problem-solving skills, limited access to lethal means.

days.guide: Model: 'I've noticed you seem really down. Are you thinking about suicide?' Practice listening without judgment in scripted role-plays.

questions.q: What should you do after a friend says yes, they're thinking about suicide?
questions.a: Stay calm, thank them for telling you, listen, don't leave them alone if in danger, and connect them with a trusted adult or 988 right away.

days.guide: The student learns how 988 works (call, text, chat) and lists school, county and online resources.

questions.q: How can someone reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline?
questions.a: Call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org; free, confidential and available 24/7.

days.guide: The student completes a sample safety plan template (not necessarily about themselves) and names who they would tell if a friend were at risk.

questions.q: Why is reducing access to lethal means part of a safety plan?
questions.a: Suicidal crises are often brief; making methods harder to reach gives time for the crisis to pass and saves lives.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test. Review, and remind the student of trusted adults and 988.

questions.q: If a friend asks you to promise not to tell anyone they're suicidal, what do you do?
questions.a: Don't promise; tell a trusted adult right away because their safety matters more than secrecy.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test key (sample): 1) Warning signs — talking about wanting to die or being a burden, looking for ways to end one's life, withdrawing, giving away possessions, extreme mood swings, increased substance use, saying goodbye, sudden calm after depression. 2) Risk factors — depression or other mental illness, previous attempt, substance use, access to lethal means, family history, bullying, loss. 3) Protective factors — connection to family/friends/school, access to care, coping skills, reasons for living, restricted access to lethal means. 4) What to say — 'Are you thinking about suicide?' 5) Next steps — listen, stay with them, remove access to means if safe, tell a trusted adult, call/text 988 or 911 if in immediate danger. 6) 988 — call, text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org; 24/7, free, confidential. 7) Coping strategies and I-statements from Unit 7. 8) Depression vs. normal sadness — 2+ weeks, affects functioning. 9) Stigma prevents help-seeking. 10) Safety plan parts — warning signs, coping strategies, people/places for distraction, people to ask for help, professionals/crisis lines, making the environment safe.

weeks.prep: Read NIDA for Teens articles on alcohol, nicotine and vaping. Find two vape or e-cigarette ads (search older ad archives such as Stanford Research into the Impact of Tobacco Advertising). Parental note: discuss your family's expectations about substances.
misconceptions: Students think vapes are just water vapor. E-cigarette aerosol contains nicotine, ultrafine particles, flavoring chemicals and metals such as nickel and lead.
Students think beer or wine is safer than liquor. A standard drink of each (12 oz beer, 5 oz wine, 1.5 oz liquor) contains about the same alcohol (about 0.6 oz).
Students think it's best to let a very drunk friend 'sleep it off'. Signs of alcohol poisoning require calling 911; BAC can keep rising after drinking stops.

days.guide: The student learns alcohol's effects, BAC factors and the signs of alcohol poisoning.

questions.q: Name three signs of alcohol poisoning.
questions.a: Can't be awakened, vomiting while passed out, slow or irregular breathing, blue/pale skin, seizures, low body temperature.

questions.q: What should you do?
questions.a: Call 911, turn them on their side to prevent choking, stay with them; California's medical amnesty law gives some protection to people under 21 who call for help.

days.guide: The student reads NIDA articles on nicotine and vaping and analyzes a vape ad for techniques that target teens (flavors, colors, influencers, freedom/rebellion themes).

questions.q: Why do flavors matter in vape marketing?
questions.a: Sweet and fruity flavors appeal to young people and mask harshness, making it easier to start.

days.guide: The student explains, with a simple brain diagram, why the adolescent brain is more vulnerable to addiction.

questions.q: Why is the teen brain more vulnerable to addiction?
questions.a: The reward system is very sensitive while the prefrontal cortex (judgment, impulse control) is still developing until the mid-20s; substances can rewire developing circuits.

days.guide: The student lists peer, family, media and advertising influences and rates their strength for themselves.

questions.q: Give an example of a protective influence.
questions.a: Friends who don't use, clear family expectations, sports or activities, accurate information.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review.

questions.q: What's the legal age to buy tobacco or vape products in California?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Alcohol is a depressant that slows the central nervous system. 2) BAC factors — amount and speed of drinking, body size, sex, food in stomach, medications. 3) Alcohol poisoning signs — confusion, vomiting, seizures, slow or irregular breathing, blue or pale skin, low body temperature, can't be woken: call 911, keep them on their side, don't leave them. 4) Nicotine is highly addictive and harms the developing brain (attention, learning, impulse control). 5) One JUUL-type pod may contain about as much nicotine as a pack of cigarettes. 6) Vape aerosol contains nicotine, heavy metals, ultrafine particles and flavoring chemicals. 7) The prefrontal cortex matures into the mid-20s, so teens are more vulnerable to addiction. 8) Legal age for tobacco/vapes and alcohol in California — 21. 9) Standard drink — 12 oz beer, 5 oz wine, 1.5 oz distilled spirits. 10) Influences — peers, family, media and advertising.

weeks.prep: Read NIDA resources on cannabis, prescription drugs, opioids and fentanyl. Queue a naloxone (Narcan) nasal spray training video. Parental note: discuss safe storage and disposal of medications at home; consider keeping naloxone at home.
misconceptions: Students think cannabis is harmless because it's legal for adults. For teens, regular use is linked to problems with memory, attention and learning, and higher risk of psychosis in some; it impairs driving.
Students think pills from a friend or social media are pharmaceutical. Counterfeit pills often contain fentanyl, and a tiny amount (about 2 mg) can be lethal.
Students think naloxone is dangerous to give if unsure. It's safe; it has no effect on someone who hasn't taken opioids, so give it when an overdose is suspected.

days.guide: The student researches short- and long-term effects of cannabis, including on driving.

questions.q: Is it legal to drive after using cannabis in California?
questions.a: No — driving impaired by cannabis is a DUI.

questions.q: Name one effect of regular teen cannabis use.
questions.a: Problems with memory, attention and learning; increased risk of addiction and, for some, psychosis.

days.guide: The student learns risks of prescription misuse and safe disposal.

questions.q: How should you dispose of unused medications?
questions.a: Take them to a pharmacy or police take-back kiosk, or use a take-back event; don't share them.

days.guide: The student learns why counterfeit pills are dangerous and the signs of opioid overdose.

questions.q: Why can't you tell if a pill contains fentanyl by looking?
questions.a: Counterfeit pills are made to look identical to real medications; fentanyl is invisible and tasteless.

questions.q: Name three signs of opioid overdose.
questions.a: Unresponsive, slow or stopped breathing, pinpoint pupils, blue/gray lips, gurgling sounds.

days.guide: Watch the naloxone video and practice the steps with a trainer device or by pantomime.

questions.q: Describe the steps for giving nasal naloxone.
questions.a: Call 911, lay the person on their back, insert the nozzle in one nostril and press the plunger, give rescue breaths if trained, then place them in the recovery position; give a second dose after 2–3 minutes if no response.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review.

questions.q: Will naloxone harm someone who isn't having an opioid overdose?
questions.a: No; it has no effect if no opioids are present.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Short-term cannabis effects — impaired memory, attention, coordination, reaction time; anxiety; altered judgment. 2) Long-term teen use — lower memory/learning, risk of cannabis use disorder, link to psychosis in vulnerable people. 3) Misusing prescription stimulants — heart problems, anxiety, addiction. 4) Safe disposal — pharmacy or police take-back bins or take-back days; never share prescriptions. 5) Fentanyl — synthetic opioid ~50× stronger than heroin; ~2 mg can be lethal; found in counterfeit pills. 6) Overdose signs — unresponsive, slow or stopped breathing, pinpoint pupils, blue or gray lips/fingertips, gurgling or snoring sounds, limp body. 7) Response — call 911, give naloxone (one spray in one nostril), rescue breaths/CPR if trained, recovery position, second dose in 2–3 minutes if no response, stay with the person. 8) Naloxone access — available without a prescription (OTC nasal spray; California pharmacies also furnish it). 9) California's Good Samaritan overdose law gives some protection from drug possession charges to people who seek help. 10) Fentanyl test strips can detect fentanyl but don't make drug use safe.

weeks.prep: Prepare five refusal scenario cards (party with alcohol, friend offering a vape, older teen offering a pill, ride with an impaired driver, pressure to try cannabis edible). Find a local youth helpline and county prevention/treatment services (SAMHSA's findtreatment.gov or the national helpline 1-800-662-4357). Build the Unit 8 test.
misconceptions: Students think refusing requires a long speech. Short, firm refusals work best: 'No thanks,' a reason, an alternative, or leaving.
Students think everyone their age uses. Most teens don't use substances; overestimating peer use increases pressure.
Students think getting help means getting in trouble. Many services are confidential; minors 12+ in California can consent to some outpatient drug and alcohol counseling.

days.guide: Teach refusal strategies; the student practices all five scenario cards with you, using a different strategy each time.

questions.q: A friend offers you a vape at a party. Give a refusal.
questions.a: 'No thanks, I'm not into that. Want to go get food?' — then walk away if they keep pushing.

days.guide: The student analyzes an alcohol or cannabis ad for target audience and persuasive techniques.

questions.q: What's the 'bandwagon' technique?
questions.a: Suggesting everyone is doing it, so you should too.

days.guide: The student locates local treatment and prevention services and a confidential youth helpline, with phone numbers.

questions.q: Where could a teen get confidential help for substance use?
questions.a: A school counselor, doctor, county behavioral health services, or SAMHSA's National Helpline (1-800-662-4357).

days.guide: The student creates a poster or 60-second video with accurate facts and sources encouraging peers to stay substance-free.

questions.q: Why use positive social norms in a campaign?
questions.a: Telling teens that most peers don't use is more effective than scare tactics alone.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test. Review.

questions.q: Name the four refusal steps from this week.
questions.a: Say no firmly, give a reason, suggest an alternative, leave.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test key (sample): 1) Alcohol is a depressant. 2) Alcohol poisoning — call 911, recovery position. 3) Nicotine addiction risk is higher in teens. 4) Vape aerosol contents — nicotine, metals, particles, flavor chemicals. 5) Teen brain — prefrontal cortex develops into mid-20s. 6) Cannabis impairs memory and driving. 7) Fentanyl — tiny amounts lethal; counterfeit pills. 8) Overdose signs and naloxone steps. 9) Refusal strategies — say no firmly, give a reason, suggest an alternative, walk away (also: use humor, blame parents, stick with friends who don't use). 10) Media techniques — glamour, bandwagon, humor, attractive models, implied fun/sexiness, targeting through flavors or social media. 11) Confidential help — SAMHSA national helpline 1-800-662-4357, school counselor, doctor. Advocacy product rubric: accurate facts with sources, clear audience, positive message, call to action.

weeks.prep: Gather three packaged-food labels, open MyPlate.gov (MyPlate Plan for the student's age, sex and activity), and plan a grocery budget for the meal plan. Parental note: Day 4 covers eating disorders; avoid weight-focused comments and watch for warning signs.
misconceptions: Students compare nutrients without checking serving size. Compare per serving and note servings per container.
Students think all fat or all carbohydrates are bad. Active teens need carbohydrates for energy, protein for repair, and healthy fats; focus on whole foods and limiting added sugar and sodium.
Students think eating disorders only affect thin girls. They affect all genders, sizes and backgrounds; they are serious illnesses, not choices.

days.guide: The student compares three labels for serving size, calories, added sugars, sodium and fiber, using %DV (5% low, 20% high).

questions.q: A cereal has 12 g added sugars per serving (24% DV) and the bowl you eat is 2 servings. How much added sugar is that?
questions.a: 24 g, about 48% of the daily value.

days.guide: The student logs three days of meals and compares to MyPlate recommendations.

questions.q: Which food groups do teens most often under-eat?
questions.a: Vegetables, fruits and dairy (calcium) are commonly low.

days.guide: Plan pre- and post-activity snacks and hydration for a sports day.

questions.q: What's a good pre-activity snack 1–2 hours before exercise?
questions.a: Easily digested carbohydrates with a little protein, such as a banana with peanut butter or yogurt with fruit.

questions.q: How can you check hydration?
questions.a: Pale yellow urine; drink water before, during and after activity.

days.guide: The student learns warning signs of eating disorders and where to get help.

questions.q: Name three warning signs of an eating disorder.
questions.a: Preoccupation with weight or food, skipping meals or rigid rules, secret eating, compensatory exercise or vomiting, rapid weight change, withdrawal from social eating.

questions.q: Where can someone get help?
questions.a: A parent or trusted adult, doctor, school counselor, or the ANAD helpline or similar national organizations.

days.guide: The student creates a one-day balanced meal plan within a budget and cooks one meal.

questions.q: Why include protein after exercise?
questions.a: It provides amino acids to repair and build muscle.

weeks.assessment_key: Meal plan rubric: 4 = One-day plan covers all MyPlate groups in appropriate amounts for an active teen (roughly 2,200–3,200 calories depending on age, sex and activity), includes breakfast, lunch, dinner and snacks, limits added sugar (<10% of calories) and sodium (<2,300 mg), includes hydration; cost calculated within the set budget; one meal cooked with a photo and reflection. 3 = balanced but missing cost or a group. 2 = unbalanced or incomplete. 1 = minimal. Note key facts: percent Daily Value of 5% or less is low, 20% or more is high.

weeks.prep: Gather five supplement or skin-care ads, two health products to compare (e.g., two sunscreens or toothpastes) with prices and sizes, and the CRAAP test checklist. Know California's confidential services for minors to explain on Day 3.
misconceptions: Students assume supplements are FDA-approved for safety and effectiveness. Supplements do not need FDA approval before sale; claims like 'supports immunity' are not proof.
Students believe a website with a professional look is reliable. Use the CRAAP test (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose).
Students compare price per package instead of cost per use. Divide price by number of uses or ounces.

days.guide: The student analyzes five ads for health claims and evidence and identifies vague language.

questions.q: What does the FDA disclaimer 'This statement has not been evaluated by the FDA' mean?
questions.a: The claim has not been reviewed or proven; the product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent disease.

days.guide: The student evaluates three health websites with the CRAAP test.

questions.q: Which is more reliable: a .gov health agency page or a supplement company's blog? Why?
questions.a: The .gov page — expert authority, evidence-based, and no profit motive in selling the product.

days.guide: Explain how to make an appointment, read an insurance card (member ID, group number, copay, phone number), and which services California minors can consent to confidentially (e.g., outpatient mental health counseling at 12+, sexual and reproductive health care, drug and alcohol counseling at 12+).

questions.q: What information on an insurance card do you need when making an appointment?
questions.a: The member ID number, group number, insurer name and phone number.

questions.q: Can a 15-year-old in California get confidential reproductive health care?
questions.a: Yes — minors can consent to many sexual and reproductive health services, and providers must keep them confidential.

days.guide: The student compares cost per use and active ingredients of two products.

questions.q: Sunscreen A costs $9 for 3 oz; B costs $14 for 6 oz. Which is cheaper per ounce?
questions.a: A: $3.00/oz; B: $2.33/oz — B is cheaper per ounce.

days.guide: The student writes a consumer guide on choosing a safe product or app.

questions.q: What should you check in a health app's privacy policy?
questions.a: What data it collects, whether it shares or sells data, and whether you can delete your data.

weeks.assessment_key: Consumer guide rubric: 4 = Chooses a product type or health app, explains active ingredients or features to look for (e.g., sunscreen: broad spectrum, SPF 30+, water resistance; toothpaste: fluoride, ADA Seal), how to evaluate claims and sources (CRAAP), cost-per-use comparison with math shown, privacy considerations for apps, and cites reliable sources. 3 = complete with weaker evidence. 2 = mostly opinion. 1 = minimal.

weeks.prep: Open AirNow.gov and your local water supplier's Consumer Confidence Report (annual water quality report). Find your county's cooling center info. Prepare a home audit checklist (smoke alarms on every level and in bedrooms, CO alarms, mold, chemical storage). Build the Unit 9 test.
misconceptions: Students think a cloth mask protects from wildfire smoke. Only a well-fitted N95 or KN95 filters fine particles; staying indoors with filtered air is best.
Students think detected contaminants mean water is unsafe. Water is considered safe if contaminants are below the legal maximum contaminant level (MCL).
Students think CO is detectable by smell. Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless; only a CO alarm detects it.

days.guide: The student checks AirNow for the city and makes a chart of AQI levels and actions, especially during wildfire smoke.

questions.q: The AQI is 165 from wildfire smoke. What should a teen athlete do?
questions.a: It's Unhealthy (red): move practice indoors or reschedule, avoid prolonged outdoor exertion, keep windows closed.

days.guide: The student reads the local water quality report and explains one contaminant (e.g., nitrate, arsenic, lead) — its source, health effect and MCL.

questions.q: What does 'MCL' mean in a water report?
questions.a: Maximum Contaminant Level — the highest level legally allowed in drinking water.

days.guide: The student learns extreme heat risks and finds community cooling centers.

questions.q: Who is most at risk during extreme heat?
questions.a: Older adults, infants and young children, people with chronic illnesses, outdoor workers and athletes, people without air conditioning.

days.guide: The student does the home environmental audit and tests smoke/CO alarms with a parent.

questions.q: Why should you never mix bleach and ammonia cleaners?
questions.a: They react to form toxic chloramine gas.

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test. Review.

questions.q: Name the AQI color for 'Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups'.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test key (sample): 1) %DV 20% or more is high. 2) Added sugar limit — less than 10% of daily calories. 3) Sodium — under 2,300 mg/day. 4) Eating disorder warning signs. 5) Supplements are not FDA-approved before sale. 6) CRAAP test. 7) Cost per use calculation. 8) AQI categories — 0–50 Good (green), 51–100 Moderate (yellow), 101–150 Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups (orange), 151–200 Unhealthy (red), 201–300 Very Unhealthy (purple), 301+ Hazardous (maroon). 9) Smoke actions — stay indoors, close windows, HEPA filter, N95 if outside, limit exertion. 10) Heat illness prevention — hydrate, shade, cooling centers, check on elderly neighbors. 11) CO alarms required in California homes with fuel-burning appliances or attached garages. 12) Store chemicals in original containers, never mix bleach and ammonia.

weeks.prep: Parental preview required. Print a relationship continuum (healthy–unhealthy–abusive; loveisrespect.org has one). Read California's affirmative consent definition and loveisrespect.org resources. Discuss your family's values alongside the facts.
misconceptions: Students think jealousy and constant texting show love. Monitoring, controlling and isolating are warning signs of an unhealthy relationship.

Students think silence or not resisting means consent. Consent must be affirmative, conscious and voluntary; it can be withdrawn anytime and can't be given if someone is intoxicated, asleep or pressured.
Students think sexting between teens is legal if both agree. Creating, sending or possessing sexual images of a minor can violate child pornography laws, even when minors share their own images.

days.guide: The student sorts behavior cards along the continuum and explains placements.

questions.q: Where does 'checks your phone without asking' fall?
questions.a: Unhealthy (controlling); it may move toward abusive if combined with other control.

days.guide: The student learns affirmative consent and practices stating and respecting boundaries in scenarios.

questions.q: Is consent given if a person says yes to one thing but not another?
questions.a: No — consent to one activity does not mean consent to others; it must be given for each activity and can be withdrawn at any time.

days.guide: Discuss online safety, sexting laws and digital dating abuse.

questions.q: Someone pressures you to send a nude photo. What are the risks?
questions.a: It can be shared without consent and can never be fully deleted; for minors, creating or sending such images can violate laws.

days.guide: The student learns signs of dating violence and resources such as Love Is Respect.

questions.q: How can a teen contact Love Is Respect?
questions.a: Text LOVEIS to 22522, call 1-866-331-9474, or chat at loveisrespect.org.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review.

questions.q: What makes consent 'affirmative'?
questions.a: It is an active, clear and voluntary 'yes' — not silence or lack of resistance.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Healthy signs — respect, trust, honesty, equality, good communication, independence. 2) Unhealthy/abusive signs — controlling, jealousy, isolating from friends, checking phone, name-calling, threats, physical harm, pressuring for sex. 3) Affirmative consent — clear, conscious, voluntary agreement; ongoing; can be withdrawn; not possible when incapacitated. 4) Boundaries — personal limits; stating them clearly is healthy. 5) Digital abuse — monitoring, demanding passwords, threatening to share images, constant texting. 6) Sexting laws — sharing sexual images of minors is illegal and can be prosecuted; images can't be taken back. 7) Resources — Love Is Respect (text LOVEIS to 22522 or call 1-866-331-9474), trusted adult, counselor, 911 in danger.

weeks.prep: Parental preview required. Read California Healthy Youth Act (CHYA) information from the California Department of Education and the parent-facing materials. CHYA requires instruction to be medically accurate and include abstinence and all FDA-approved methods of preventing pregnancy and STIs. Choose a time to discuss family values. Look up confidential teen clinics in your county (county public health, Planned Parenthood, or teensource.org).
misconceptions: Students believe myths (e.g., you can't get pregnant the first time, or STIs always cause symptoms). Many STIs have no symptoms; testing is the only way to know.
Students think birth control pills prevent STIs. Only condoms (used correctly every time) reduce STI risk; abstinence is the only 100% effective method.
Students think they need parental permission for testing or contraception in California. Minors can consent to these services confidentially.

days.guide: Review medically accurate information from CHYA-aligned sources on preventing pregnancy and STIs.

questions.q: Do birth control pills protect against STIs?
questions.a: No; only condoms reduce STI risk (abstinence eliminates it).

days.guide: The student locates confidential sexual and reproductive health services in the county.

questions.q: Can a 15-year-old in California get STI testing without parental consent?
questions.a: Yes, minors 12 and older can consent to STI testing and treatment confidentially.

days.guide: The student applies a decision-making model to a relationship scenario.

questions.q: List the steps of a decision-making model.
questions.a: Identify the decision, list options, weigh consequences and values, decide, act, evaluate.

days.guide: Practice opening a conversation with a parent or trusted adult about a health question.

questions.q: How could you start a conversation about a sensitive health question?
questions.a: 'Can I ask you something kind of awkward? I want accurate information about…'

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review.

questions.q: Why should sexually active people get tested even without symptoms?
questions.a: Many STIs have no symptoms but can still cause harm and be spread.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Abstinence is the only 100% effective way to prevent pregnancy and STIs. 2) Condoms reduce risk of pregnancy and many STIs when used correctly every time. 3) Hormonal methods and IUDs prevent pregnancy but not STIs. 4) Many STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhea, HPV, HIV) can have no symptoms; get tested. 5) HPV vaccine prevents cancers caused by HPV. 6) PrEP can prevent HIV. 7) Emergency contraception is available without a prescription. 8) Minors in California can consent to confidential sexual and reproductive health services. 9) Decision-making model — define the decision, list options, consider consequences and values, decide, evaluate. 10) Trusted adults — parent, doctor, school nurse, counselor.

weeks.prep: Gather DMV practice tests, the manikin/pillow, scenario cards from Units 5–6, flashcards from Units 7–9, and a practice final built from all unit keys.
misconceptions: Students re-study what they know well. Use practice-exam results to target weak areas.
Students forget compression rate and depth. Rehearse with music.
Students mix up overlapping numbers (15 ft hydrant, 100 ft signal, 200 ft bike lane/center lane). Make a 'numbers' card.

days.guide: The student takes a DMV practice knowledge test and reviews misses.

questions.q: What's the speed limit in a residential district unless posted?
questions.a: 25 mph.

days.guide: Run first aid scenario cards and 2 minutes of CPR practice.

questions.q: A child is choking and can't cough. What do you do?
questions.a: Call (or have someone call) 911 and give 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or the child becomes unresponsive.

days.guide: Review mental health, substances, nutrition and relationships with flashcards.

questions.q: What are three signs of opioid overdose?
questions.a: Unresponsive, slow or stopped breathing, pinpoint pupils (also blue lips).

days.guide: Give the practice final exam.

questions.q: (After the practice exam) Which unit had the most misses?
questions.a: Answers vary; plan Day 5 study around it.

days.guide: The student studies weak areas from the practice exam using flashcards and handbook pages.

questions.q: What does BE-FAST stand for?
questions.a: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time to call 911.

weeks.assessment_key: Practice final key: cumulative items from Units 1–9; 90%+ shows readiness. Key numbers: permit 15½; 50 hrs/10 night; provisional 11 p.m.–5 a.m., passengers under 20; signal 100 ft; freeway 5 sec; hydrant 15 ft; 3-second rule; BAC 0.08/0.01; CPR 100–120/min, 2 in adult, 1.5 in infant, 30:2; 988; AQI categories; sodium < 2,300 mg.

weeks.prep: Print the written final (cumulative from all unit keys), set up the manikin and an AED trainer or picture cards for the skills final, and print a personal health plan template.
misconceptions: Students write vague health goals ('be healthier'). Use SMART goals: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound.
Students think the permit is automatic after the course. They must still apply, test and plan supervised practice.
Students skip reflection. Ask for specific choices they will make differently.

days.guide: Give the written final exam.

questions.q: (After the exam) Name one topic you want to review more.
questions.a: Answers vary.

days.guide: The student demonstrates CPR/AED and one first aid skill; score with checklists.

questions.q: Where do AED pads go on an adult?
questions.a: One on the upper right chest below the collarbone, the other on the lower left side of the chest below the armpit (follow the pictures on the pads).

days.guide: The student writes a personal health plan with SMART goals in three areas.

questions.q: Turn 'sleep more' into a SMART goal.
questions.a: 'I will be in bed with my phone outside my room by 10:15 p.m. on school nights for the next 4 weeks, tracking it on a calendar.'

days.guide: Review the permit checklist and set a date for the application and DMV appointment with the parent.

questions.q: What must happen before the DMV issues a permit?
questions.a: Completed application, documents, fee, vision test, passing the knowledge test, and parent signature (plus driver ed completion/enrollment).

days.guide: The student writes a reflection on how the course will change their choices.

questions.q: Name one specific choice you'll make differently after this course.
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., 'I'll keep my phone in the glove box while driving' or 'I'll call 911 and use naloxone if I see an overdose.'

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam key: cumulative; use unit keys. Skills final: CPR/AED checklist (Week 20) plus one first aid skill (bleeding control, splinting, or choking) — proficient when all steps are performed correctly. Personal health plan rubric: 4 = three SMART goals in different areas (e.g., physical activity, mental health, nutrition, safety/driving), action steps, supports and barriers, a way to track progress. Reflection: specific changes with examples.

HSS.overview: Modern World History meets about 60 minutes a day around primary sources: source each document (author, date, audience, purpose), read closely, then discuss and write. Expect a quiz or written product most Fridays and a DBQ each unit; use the rubrics in the keys. Several units (imperial atrocities, WWI, the Armenian Genocide, the Holocaust, Hiroshima) contain disturbing material — preview sources and leave time to talk.

weeks.prep: Set up a history notebook (sections for notes, sources, vocabulary). Print excerpts of Pericles' Funeral Oration (from Thucydides), Plato's Allegory of the Cave, and Aristotle's Politics (Book III classification). Find a modern news photograph for sourcing practice.
misconceptions: Thinking Athenian democracy included everyone. Only adult male citizens voted — women, enslaved people and foreigners (metics) were excluded.
Equating 'republic' and 'democracy.' Rome was a republic: citizens elected representatives; Athens practiced direct democracy.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) Direct democracy → citizens vote on laws themselves (Athens). 2) Who could participate in Athenian democracy? → Adult male citizens only. 3) In the Allegory of the Cave, the shadows represent → appearances/ignorance; leaving the cave represents → education/philosophy and seeing truth. 4) Aristotle's good forms and corrupt forms → monarchy/tyranny, aristocracy/oligarchy, polity/democracy (mob rule). 5) Roman checks → two consuls who could veto each other, a Senate, tribunes who could veto on behalf of plebeians. 6) Twelve Tables → Rome's first written laws (c. 450 BCE), posted publicly. Constructed response rubric (4-point): clear claim naming one idea (e.g., Roman republicanism/checks and balances, Greek citizen participation, written law); two specific connections to U.S. government (Senate, veto, elected representatives, written Constitution); explanation of influence.

days.guide: Teach the SOURCING routine with a modern photograph: Who made it? When? For what audience? Why? The student sets up the notebook and sources the photo, then predicts how the source's perspective might shape what it shows.

questions.q: What four questions make up 'sourcing' a document?
questions.a: Who created it (author), when, for what audience, and for what purpose.

questions.q: Why does sourcing matter?
questions.a: A source's author, date and purpose shape what it includes and leaves out, so historians weigh reliability and perspective.

days.guide: Source the Funeral Oration first: given by Pericles in 431 BCE to honor Athenian war dead, recorded by Thucydides. The student reads the excerpt and lists what Athenians valued about democracy, then notes who was excluded.

questions.q: According to Pericles, why is Athens called a democracy?
questions.a: Power is in the hands of the many, not a few; everyone is equal before the law, and advancement depends on merit, not class.

questions.q: What was the purpose and audience of the speech?
questions.a: To honor the war dead and inspire Athenians to keep fighting in the Peloponnesian War — so it praises Athens and may idealize it.

days.guide: Read the Allegory of the Cave aloud and sketch it. Then read Aristotle's classification and have the student fill a 3×2 chart of rule by one/few/many in good and corrupt forms.

questions.q: What does Plato's allegory suggest about who should rule?
questions.a: Those who have escaped ignorance and seen the truth — philosophers — should rule (philosopher-kings), not the uninformed majority.

questions.q: What is the corrupt form of rule by the few in Aristotle's scheme?
questions.a: Oligarchy (the good form is aristocracy).

days.guide: Read a short overview of the Roman Republic, the Twelve Tables and Cicero's idea of natural law. The student diagrams consuls, Senate, assemblies and tribunes with arrows showing who checks whom.

questions.q: How did the Roman Republic prevent one person from gaining too much power?
questions.a: Two consuls served one-year terms and could veto each other; the Senate advised and controlled funds; tribunes could veto actions harmful to plebeians.

questions.q: Why were the Twelve Tables important?
questions.a: They put laws in writing and posted them publicly, so laws applied to all and could not be changed at a judge's whim.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key (about 20 minutes). Then the student writes a constructed-response paragraph: which Greek or Roman idea most shapes U.S. government today? Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Name one Roman institution that resembles part of the U.S. government.
questions.a: The Senate (U.S. Senate), or the veto power (presidential veto), or elected representatives (republic).

weeks.prep: Print excerpts: Exodus 20 (Ten Commandments), a prophetic passage such as 2 Samuel 12 (Nathan confronts King David), Matthew 5–7 (Sermon on the Mount), Japan's 1947 Constitution (Articles 9, 14, 20, 21) and Germany's Basic Law Article 1. Note to parent: these religious texts are studied as historical sources of ideas, per CA standard 10.1.1.
misconceptions: Thinking ancient ideas transferred directly into the Constitution. Ideas passed through centuries of medieval and Enlightenment thought.
Assuming every constitution modeled on the U.S. is identical. Japan's Article 9 renouncing war has no U.S. equivalent.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 essay rubric (4-point): Thesis — explains how at least two ancient traditions shaped the U.S. Constitution and spread globally; Evidence — specific ideas (Greek citizen participation, Roman republic and checks, rule of law in the Twelve Tables, the Hebrew idea that law binds even kings, Christian ideas of individual worth and conscience) and a global example (Japan 1947 Articles 14 and 21; Germany's Basic Law Article 1 'Human dignity shall be inviolable'); Analysis — explains the link rather than listing; Writing — organized, cited.

days.guide: Read Exodus 20 and the story of Nathan rebuking King David. Discuss how a covenant creates law that binds rulers as well as subjects; the student writes two sentences connecting this to 'rule of law.'

questions.q: What idea about rulers appears when the prophet Nathan condemns King David?
questions.a: Even a king is subject to a higher moral law and can be held accountable.

days.guide: Read selections from the Sermon on the Mount (the Beatitudes, the Golden Rule, 'love your enemies'). The student identifies ideas of individual worth and conscience and explains how they could support ideas of equality.

questions.q: What is the Golden Rule as stated in Matthew 7:12?
questions.a: Do to others what you would have them do to you.

questions.q: How could the idea that every person has worth to God influence political thought?
questions.a: It supports the belief that all individuals deserve dignity and equal treatment, which later fed ideas of natural rights.

days.guide: Draw a Venn diagram: Greco-Roman (reason, citizenship, natural law, civic duty) and Judeo-Christian (moral law from God, individual worth, conscience); the overlap includes law above rulers and duty to community. The student fills it with at least four items per section.

questions.q: Name one idea both traditions share.
questions.a: Law should be above any individual ruler (rule of law), or that there is a higher law (natural/divine) that human law should follow.

days.guide: Compare Japan's 1947 constitution (written under U.S. occupation) with the U.S. Bill of Rights in a two-column chart. The student finds at least three parallels and one difference. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which article of Japan's constitution parallels the First Amendment?
questions.a: Article 21 (freedom of assembly, association, speech, press) and Article 20 (freedom of religion).

questions.q: What is unique about Article 9?
questions.a: Japan renounces war as a sovereign right and the threat or use of force to settle international disputes.

days.guide: The student outlines, then writes a one-page essay on how ancient ideas shaped the U.S. Constitution and its global spread. Score with the rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What does Germany's Basic Law Article 1 say, and why after WWII?
questions.a: 'Human dignity shall be inviolable' — written in 1949 in reaction to Nazi crimes against human dignity.

weeks.prep: Excerpts of Magna Carta (1215; clauses 12, 39, 40) and the English Bill of Rights (1689) from the Avalon Project or British Library; Locke's Second Treatise (chapters on the state of nature and dissolution of government); Hobbes's Leviathan ch. 13; Montesquieu's Spirit of Laws (Book XI ch. 6); Rousseau's Social Contract (Book I).
misconceptions: Treating Hobbes and Locke as agreeing because both use a social contract. Hobbes wants an absolute sovereign; Locke wants limited government and a right to revolution.
Thinking Magna Carta created democracy. It protected barons' rights and limited the king, a first step toward rule of law.
weeks.assessment_key: Dialogue rubric (accuracy of ideas): 4 = each philosopher's view stated accurately in his own terms — Hobbes (life in the state of nature 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'; people give power to an absolute sovereign for security), Locke (natural rights of life, liberty and property; government by consent; right to overthrow a government that violates rights), Montesquieu (separation of legislative, executive and judicial powers to prevent tyranny), Rousseau ('Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains'; legitimacy comes from the general will of the people); philosophers respond to one another; 3 = mostly accurate; 2 = one or more views confused; 1 = superficial.

days.guide: Read a short overview of the Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment. The student builds a timeline: Copernicus (1543), Galileo, Newton's Principia (1687), Hobbes (1651), Locke (1689–90), Montesquieu (1748), Voltaire, Rousseau (1762), and explains how applying reason to nature led to applying reason to government.

questions.q: How did the Scientific Revolution lead to the Enlightenment?
questions.a: Thinkers saw that reason and observation could discover natural laws, so they applied reason to society and government, looking for natural rights and better institutions.

days.guide: Read key clauses together. The student lists rights protected by each document and who they protected. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What does Magna Carta clause 39 guarantee?
questions.a: No free man may be imprisoned, stripped of rights or property, or punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land.

questions.q: Name two limits the English Bill of Rights (1689) placed on the monarch.
questions.a: The king could not suspend laws, levy taxes, or keep a standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent; elections must be free; no excessive bail or cruel and unusual punishment.

days.guide: Read Hobbes chapter 13 and Locke's state-of-nature passages. The student charts each thinker's view of human nature, purpose of government, and what happens if government fails. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How does Hobbes describe life without government?
questions.a: 'Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — a war of all against all.

questions.q: According to Locke, what may people do if government violates their natural rights?
questions.a: They may alter or overthrow it and form a new government.

days.guide: Read excerpts of Montesquieu and Rousseau. The student summarizes each main idea in one sentence and connects it to a U.S. institution. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What is Montesquieu's main idea and its U.S. reflection?
questions.a: Separating legislative, executive and judicial powers prevents tyranny — reflected in the three branches and checks and balances.

questions.q: What does Rousseau mean by the 'general will'?
questions.a: Legitimate government follows the collective will of the people for the common good, not any individual's private interest.

days.guide: The student writes a one- to two-page dialogue among Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu and Rousseau at a dinner party debating 'What makes government legitimate?' Score with the rubric for accuracy. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which philosopher would most strongly reject a right to revolution?
questions.a: Hobbes — he argued subjects should obey the sovereign to avoid chaos.

weeks.prep: Declaration of Independence (archives.gov), a summary of the Haitian Revolution and an excerpt of the 1801 Haitian (Saint-Domingue) Constitution, Bolívar's Jamaica Letter (1815) excerpt. Chart template for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking the American Revolution created full equality. Enslaved people, women and Native Americans were excluded.
Overlooking Haiti: it was the only successful revolution led by enslaved people and the first independent Black republic (1804).
weeks.assessment_key: Comparison chart (expected content): American (1775–1783) — leaders: colonial elites (Washington, Jefferson); causes: taxation without representation, Enlightenment rights; result: independent republic, federal written Constitution, slavery persists. Haitian (1791–1804) — leaders: Toussaint Louverture, Jean-Jacques Dessalines; causes: brutal slavery, French Revolution ideals; result: slavery abolished, independence 1804, first Black republic. Latin American (1810–1820s) — leaders: Creoles like Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín; causes: Creole exclusion from power, Napoleon's invasion of Spain, Enlightenment ideas; result: independent republics often dominated by elites and caudillos. Score 4 = every cell accurate; 3 = 1–2 errors; 2 = several gaps; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Read the preamble and the opening of the grievances aloud. The student highlights phrases that echo Locke and writes the Lockean idea beside each. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which phrase echoes Locke's natural rights?
questions.a: 'Unalienable Rights, that among these are Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness' (Locke: life, liberty, property).

questions.q: Which phrase echoes Locke's idea of consent and revolution?
questions.a: Governments derive 'their just powers from the consent of the governed,' and the people may 'alter or to abolish' a destructive government.

days.guide: Discuss what made the American Revolution distinctive: a written constitution, federalism dividing power between national and state governments, and a Bill of Rights. The student writes a paragraph on one distinctive feature and its influence abroad.

questions.q: What is federalism?
questions.a: A system dividing power between a national government and state governments.

days.guide: Read about the Haitian Revolution (1791 uprising, Toussaint Louverture, independence in 1804). Analyze the 1801 constitution excerpt: what did it abolish, and what power did it give Toussaint? Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did the 1801 constitution declare about slavery?
questions.a: Slavery was abolished forever — there could be no slaves in the territory.

questions.q: Why was the Haitian Revolution so significant?
questions.a: It was the only successful slave revolt to create a nation — the first independent Black republic — and it alarmed slaveholding societies throughout the Americas.

days.guide: Source the Jamaica Letter (Bolívar, 1815, written in exile to a British audience). The student identifies Enlightenment ideas and Creole grievances. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What grievance does Bolívar raise for Creoles?
questions.a: Spain excluded American-born Creoles from high offices and trade, treating them as subordinates despite their wealth and education.

questions.q: Why might Bolívar write to a British reader?
questions.a: To win British sympathy and support for Spanish American independence.

days.guide: The student completes the comparison chart for the three revolutions (leaders, causes, ideas, results, who was included/excluded). Score with the assessment key. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which event in Europe helped trigger Latin American independence movements?
questions.a: Napoleon's invasion of Spain (1808), which weakened Spanish control over its colonies.

weeks.prep: The 1789 cartoon of a Third Estate peasant carrying a clergyman and nobleman; Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789); Olympe de Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman (1791) excerpt; Robespierre's 'On the Principles of Political Morality' (February 1794) excerpt; map of Napoleon's empire (1812). Prepare a 5–6 document DBQ set from these sources.
misconceptions: Seeing the Revolution as one event. It moved through phases: moderate (1789–91), radical/Terror (1792–94), Directory (1795–99), Napoleon (1799–1815).
Viewing Napoleon only as a conqueror. He also spread legal equality (Napoleonic Code) while limiting liberty.
weeks.assessment_key: DBQ rubric (4-point per row): Thesis — directly answers the question with a defensible claim; Evidence — uses at least 4 documents accurately plus outside knowledge; Sourcing — explains author, purpose, audience or context for at least 2 documents; Analysis — groups documents and explains how they support the claim; Writing — organized, clear. 17–20 = proficient. Strong thesis example: 'The Revolution partly achieved its goals: it ended feudal privilege and spread the idea of rights through the Declaration and Napoleonic Code, but the Terror and Napoleon's dictatorship betrayed liberty, and women were excluded, as de Gouges protested.'

days.guide: Analyze the cartoon with the student: who is carrying whom, and what does it say? Then list causes of the Revolution: unequal estates and taxes, royal debt (including from aiding the American Revolution), bread prices, and Enlightenment ideas.

questions.q: What does the cartoon of the peasant carrying the clergy and noble mean?
questions.a: The Third Estate bore the burden of taxes and labor while the privileged First and Second Estates paid little.

questions.q: Name two economic causes of the French Revolution.
questions.a: Royal debt from wars (including the American Revolution) and rising bread prices after poor harvests, with an unfair tax system.

days.guide: Read selected articles of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and de Gouges's response side by side. The student charts how de Gouges rewrites each article. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What does Article 1 of the Declaration of the Rights of Man state?
questions.a: Men are born and remain free and equal in rights.

questions.q: What was de Gouges's main argument?
questions.a: Women are born free and equal to men in rights; if a woman can mount the scaffold (be executed), she must also have the right to mount the speaker's rostrum.

days.guide: Read Robespierre's speech excerpt and source it (February 1794, to the National Convention, during war and the Terror). The student evaluates his justification of terror. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How does Robespierre connect virtue and terror?
questions.a: He says virtue without terror is powerless and terror without virtue is fatal; terror is 'prompt, severe, inflexible justice' that flows from virtue.

questions.q: About how many people were officially executed during the Terror?
questions.a: About 17,000 official executions (with many more deaths in prison and in civil war).

days.guide: The student makes a T-chart of Napoleon's achievements (Napoleonic Code, Concordat, Bank of France, merit-based careers, public schools) and abuses (dictatorship, censorship, wars, restoring slavery in the colonies in 1802). Map his empire at its 1812 height, then explain the Congress of Vienna's goals.

questions.q: What were the goals of the Congress of Vienna (1814–1815)?
questions.a: Restore a balance of power, return legitimate monarchs, and contain France to prevent future revolutions and wars (led by Metternich).

questions.q: What did the Napoleonic Code establish?
questions.a: Equality of male citizens before the law, religious toleration, and protection of property — but it limited women's rights.

days.guide: Give the DBQ: Did the French Revolution achieve its goals? Allow 10 minutes to read documents and plan, 40 minutes to write. Score with the DBQ rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What were the Revolution's stated goals?
questions.a: 'Liberty, equality, fraternity' — ending privilege, securing rights, and creating government by the people.

weeks.prep: Maps of British coalfields, rivers and ports; images of the spinning jenny, water frame, Watt steam engine and early railways (e.g., Stephenson's Rocket). A textile mill case study (e.g., Arkwright's Cromford Mill).
misconceptions: Thinking the Industrial Revolution began with factories. It began with agricultural changes that freed labor and grew the population.
Crediting James Watt with inventing the steam engine. Newcomen built an earlier engine (1712); Watt greatly improved its efficiency (patent 1769).
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) Enclosure → fencing common lands into private farms, pushing small farmers to cities. 2) Crop rotation → alternating crops (e.g., turnips, clover) to restore soil instead of leaving fields fallow. 3) Five factors favoring Britain → coal and iron, rivers and ports, colonies/markets, capital and banks, stable government and navy (also labor supply). 4) Spinning jenny → Hargreaves, spun many threads at once. 5) Water frame → Arkwright, water-powered spinning, led to factories. 6) Watt → improved steam engine efficiency. 7) First major passenger railway → Liverpool–Manchester (1830).

days.guide: Explain enclosure and new methods (Jethro Tull's seed drill, crop rotation with turnips and clover). The student draws a cause-effect chain from these changes to population growth and a workforce for factories.

questions.q: How did enclosure contribute to industrialization?
questions.a: It made farming more efficient but pushed many small farmers off the land, creating a labor force that moved to cities and factories.

questions.q: Why did crop rotation increase food supply?
questions.a: Planting crops like turnips and clover restored soil nutrients, so fields didn't need to lie fallow and fed more livestock.

days.guide: The student maps Britain's coal and iron deposits, navigable rivers and major ports, then lists five factors favoring early industrialization. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Why were rivers important to early industry?
questions.a: They provided water power for mills and cheap transport for heavy goods like coal.

days.guide: The student builds an illustrated chart: invention, inventor, date, what it did, and its effect (flying shuttle 1733, spinning jenny c. 1764, water frame 1769, Watt's improved steam engine 1769/1776, power loom 1785, Stephenson's railways 1825–1830).

questions.q: Why was the steam engine so important?
questions.a: It provided reliable power anywhere, not just near rivers, driving factories, locomotives and steamships.

days.guide: Define land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship. Apply them to a textile mill case study: the student identifies each factor in Arkwright's mill. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: In a textile mill, give an example of capital and of entrepreneurship.
questions.a: Capital: the building and machines (and money to buy them). Entrepreneurship: the owner (e.g., Richard Arkwright) organizing resources and taking the risk.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key. Review answers, and have the student explain any missed item using their chart. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What were the 'factors of production' Britain had in abundance?
questions.a: Land with natural resources (coal, iron), labor (displaced farmers), capital (banks and investors), and entrepreneurs.

weeks.prep: Sadler Committee testimony (1832; e.g., Elizabeth Bentley), Engels, The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845) excerpt on Manchester, Dickens, Hard Times Book I ch. 5 ('The Key-note,' Coketown) from Gutenberg. Parent note: testimony describes beatings and injuries of children.
misconceptions: Assuming reforms happened quickly. Change was gradual: 1833 Factory Act, 1842 Mines Act, 1847 Ten Hours Act.
Thinking only men worked in factories. Women and children were a large part of the textile workforce.
