misconceptions: Forgetting to add eye height in the clinometer lab. The trig calculation gives height above eye level.

Reading the clinometer angle directly when the string shows the complement. Depending on construction, the angle of elevation may be 90° minus the reading; test with a level line (should read 0° elevation).
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Opposite 5, adjacent 12 → angle tan⁻¹(5/12) ≈ 22.6°. 2) Solve right triangle with legs 7 and 10 → hypotenuse ≈ 12.21, angles ≈ 35.0° and 55.0°. 3) Angle of elevation 35° from 50 ft away, eye height 5 ft → 50 tan 35° + 5 ≈ 40.0 ft. 4) ADA ramp (1:12) rising 30 in → 360 in = 30 ft run; angle ≈ 4.76°. 5) A ship sails 40 km at bearing that makes 30° east of north; distance east → 40 sin 30° = 20 km. Lab report rubric: 4 = diagram with angle, distance, eye height; correct tan calculation; final height with units; 2+ error sources; 3 = minor slips; 2 = eye height omitted or wrong ratio; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Introduce sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ as 'what angle has this ratio?' Model completely solving a right triangle (all sides and angles).

questions.q: Legs 7 and 10. Find the angle opposite the 7.
Hypotenuse 10, one leg 6. Find the angle opposite the 6.

days.guide: Build the clinometer: tape a straw along the protractor's straight edge, hang the weighted string from the center hole. Test: sighting a level line should give 0° elevation. Make a conversion note if the string reads 90°.

questions.q: Your clinometer string reads 60° on the protractor (measured from the straw's side). What is the angle of elevation?
questions.a: 90° − 60° = 30° (for a design where level reads 90°).

days.guide: Outside, the student measures distance to the base, sights the top, records the angle and eye height, and repeats 3 times to average. Compute height = d·tan θ + eye height and write the lab report.

questions.q: Standing 40 ft from a tree with angle of elevation 32° and eye height 5 ft, how tall is the tree?

days.guide: Work ADA ramp problems (1 in rise per 12 in run maximum) and navigation problems using sketches.

questions.q: A porch is 24 inches high. What minimum ramp length (horizontal run) meets ADA?
A plane descends at 3° and is 1,500 ft high. How far horizontally until touchdown?
questions.a: 1500/tan 3° ≈ 28,600 ft (about 5.4 miles).

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Which inverse function do you use if you know the opposite and hypotenuse?
questions.a: Inverse sine, sin⁻¹(opposite/hypotenuse).

weeks.prep: Scientific calculator in degree mode; Unit 6 test from the assessment key. Review the formulas: Area = ½ab sin C; a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C; c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
misconceptions: Using the Law of Sines for SAS or SSS (it needs an angle-opposite-side pair). Choose Law of Cosines for SAS and SSS.
Missing the second solution in the SSA ambiguous case. If sin B gives angle B, also check 180° − B.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test with answers: 1) sin 52° ≈ 0.788. 2) Right triangle angle 25°, hypotenuse 30 → opposite ≈ 12.68. 3) Angle of elevation for a 6 ft rise over 20 ft → tan⁻¹(0.3) ≈ 16.7°. 4) Area with a = 8, b = 10, C = 30° → 20. 5) A = 40°, B = 60°, a = 10 → b ≈ 13.47. 6) a = 7, b = 8, C = 60° → c = √57 ≈ 7.55. 7) Sides 5, 7, 8 → angle opposite 7 = 60°. 8) SSA: a = 6, b = 8, A = 30° → sin B = 0.667, B ≈ 41.8° or 138.2° (two triangles). Mastery 80%.

days.guide: Draw an oblique triangle, drop the altitude from B to side b; h = a sin C, so Area = ½ab sin C. The student applies it to several triangles.

questions.q: Find the area of a triangle with sides 8 and 10 and included angle 30°.
Sides 12 and 15 with included 110°. Area?

days.guide: Derive the Law of Sines from two expressions for the same altitude. Solve AAS/ASA problems, then show SSA can give 0, 1, or 2 triangles.

questions.q: a = 6, b = 8, A = 30°. How many triangles?
questions.a: sin B = 8 sin 30°/6 ≈ 0.667 → B ≈ 41.8° or 138.2°; both work (138.2 + 30 < 180), so two triangles.

days.guide: Derive the Law of Cosines by placing C at the origin and using the distance formula (or the altitude). Note it becomes the Pythagorean theorem when C = 90°.

questions.q: a = 7, b = 8, C = 60°. Find c.
Sides 5, 7, 8. Find the angle opposite 7.

days.guide: Give mixed surveying/navigation word problems; the student sketches, identifies given parts (SAS, SSS, ASA, AAS, SSA) and chooses the law.

questions.q: Two hikers leave camp; one walks 3 km, the other 5 km, with 70° between their paths. How far apart are they?

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test from the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: What does the Law of Cosines reduce to when the angle is 90°?
questions.a: The Pythagorean theorem, since cos 90° = 0.

weeks.prep: Compass, string, several circular objects (cans, plates), ruler, calculator.
misconceptions: Confusing arc measure (degrees) with arc length (distance). Arc measure equals the central angle; arc length depends on the radius.
Naming a major arc with two letters. Major arcs and semicircles need three letters (e.g., arc ACB).
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Identify chord, secant, tangent, radius on a diagram (visual check). 2) Central angle 70° → minor arc 70°, major arc 290°. 3) Arcs AB = 80°, BC = 45° adjacent → arc ABC = 125°. 4) Radius 10, chord 6 units from center → chord length 16. 5) Two chords in the same circle are congruent; one's arc is 100° → the other's arc is 100°. 6) Why are all circles similar? → any circle can be translated to share a center with another and dilated by k = r₂/r₁.

days.guide: Take two circles with different centers and radii. Show the translation that moves center to center, then the dilation with k = r₂/r₁. The student writes the argument.

questions.q: Circle A has center (1, 2), radius 3; circle B has center (−4, 0), radius 6. Describe a similarity mapping A to B.
questions.a: Translate by ⟨−5, −2⟩, then dilate about (−4, 0) by scale factor 2.

days.guide: Label diagrams with chord, diameter, radius, secant, tangent, point of tangency, central angle, minor/major arc, semicircle. Quiz with flash diagrams.

questions.q: What is the difference between a chord and a secant?
questions.a: A chord is a segment with both endpoints on the circle; a secant is a line that intersects the circle at two points.

days.guide: Teach: minor arc = central angle; major arc = 360° − minor; arc addition. The student solves problems including algebraic central angles.

questions.q: Central angles of a circle are 2x, 3x, and 4x (filling the whole circle). Find each.

days.guide: Prove congruent chords have congruent central angles (SSS with radii) and that a radius perpendicular to a chord bisects it (HL). Solve chord-distance problems.

questions.q: A circle has radius 10, and a chord is 6 units from the center. How long is the chord?
questions.a: Half-chord = √(100 − 36) = 8, so chord = 16.

questions.q: A chord of length 24 is 5 units from the center. Find the radius.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: A diameter is perpendicular to a chord. What does it do to the chord and its arc?
questions.a: It bisects the chord and its arc.

weeks.prep: GeoGebra, compass, straightedge.
misconceptions: Using the full arc as the inscribed angle measure. Inscribed angle = half the intercepted arc; central angle = the arc.
Forgetting that a tangent meets the radius at 90°, which creates right triangles for the Pythagorean theorem.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Inscribed angle intercepts a 100° arc → 50°. 2) Inscribed angle 34° → arc 68°. 3) An inscribed angle intercepts a semicircle → 90°. 4) Quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, ∠A = 75°, ∠B = 110° → ∠C = 105°, ∠D = 70°. 5) External point P is 13 from center, radius 5 → tangent length 12. 6) Two tangents from P have lengths 2x + 3 and 5x − 9 → x = 4, length 11. Construction check: incircle (bisect two angles, perpendicular from incenter to a side for radius) and circumcircle (perpendicular bisectors of two sides, radius to a vertex), scored 3/2/1 as in Week 2.

days.guide: In GeoGebra, place an inscribed angle and a central angle on the same arc; drag and record. Then prove the case where one side of the inscribed angle is a diameter (isosceles triangle + exterior angle theorem).

questions.q: An inscribed angle intercepts an arc of 140°. What is its measure?
Why is an angle inscribed in a semicircle a right angle?
questions.a: It intercepts a 180° arc, and half of 180° is 90°.

days.guide: Show opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral intercept arcs that together make 360°, so the angles sum to 180°.

questions.q: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed; m∠A = (2x)°, m∠C = (x + 30)°. Find x.

days.guide: Prove the radius-tangent relationship (shortest distance argument) and the two-tangent theorem (HL on two right triangles). Practice problems.

questions.q: Point P is 13 units from the center of a circle of radius 5. Find the length of a tangent from P.
Two tangent segments from P are 3x + 1 and 7. Find x.

days.guide: Construct the incircle (angle bisectors) and circumcircle (perpendicular bisectors). For a tangent from an external point P: bisect OP to get M, draw a circle centered M through O; where it meets the circle are the tangent points.

questions.q: Why does the tangent construction (circle on diameter OP) work?
questions.a: The tangent point T lies on a circle with diameter OP, so ∠OTP is inscribed in a semicircle and equals 90°, making PT ⊥ OT.

days.guide: Give the quiz and construction check in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: A central angle and an inscribed angle intercept the same 80° arc. Give each measure.
questions.a: Central 80°; inscribed 40°.

weeks.prep: Paper plates, string, ruler, scissors, calculator. Leave answers in terms of π and as decimals.
misconceptions: Using diameter instead of radius in A = πr². Circle the radius in every problem first.
Mixing degree and radian mode on calculators when converting. Use the factor π/180 explicitly.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Arc length, r = 6, 60° → 2π ≈ 6.28. 2) Arc length r = 10, 3π/4 radians → 7.5π ≈ 23.56. 3) Convert 45° → π/4; 150° → 5π/6; 2 radians → ≈ 114.6°. 4) Sector area r = 10, 72° → 20π ≈ 62.83. 5) 14-inch pizza cut into 8 slices → area per slice 49π/8 ≈ 19.24 in². 6) Sprinkler radius 15 ft rotating through 120° → 75π ≈ 235.6 ft². 7) Segment area: r = 6, 90° → 9π − 18 ≈ 10.27.

days.guide: Have the student cut a plate into 16 sectors and arrange them alternately into a near-parallelogram: base ≈ half the circumference (πr), height ≈ r, so area ≈ πr². Measure circumference with string to check C/d ≈ π.

questions.q: Explain why the rearranged sectors approach a rectangle with area πr².
questions.a: The base is half the circumference (πr) and the height is the radius r, so area = πr·r = πr².

days.guide: Arc length = (θ/360)·2πr. The student solves forward and backward problems.

questions.q: Find the arc length of a 60° arc in a circle of radius 6.
An arc of length 5π has a central angle of 90°. Find the radius.

days.guide: Wrap a string the length of the radius around the plate's edge and mark the angle: that is 1 radian (about 57.3°). Teach conversions with π radians = 180°.

questions.q: Convert 150° to radians.
Convert 3π/2 radians to degrees.

days.guide: Sector area = (θ/360)·πr². Segment area = sector − triangle. Solve pizza and sprinkler problems.

questions.q: A sprinkler sprays 15 ft and turns through 120°. What area does it water?
Find the segment area for a 90° sector of radius 6.
questions.a: Sector 9π minus triangle 18 → 9π − 18 ≈ 10.27.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: In radians, what is the arc length formula?
questions.a: s = rθ, with θ in radians.

weeks.prep: Desmos, graph paper. Prepare the Unit 7 test (assessment key).
misconceptions: Sign errors with the center: (x + 3)² means h = −3. Rewrite as (x − (−3))².
Forgetting to add the same constants to both sides when completing the square.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test with answers: 1) Inscribed angle on a 110° arc → 55°. 2) Tangent from a point 10 from center of radius 6 → 8. 3) Arc length r = 9, 40° → 2π ≈ 6.28. 4) Sector area r = 4, 135° → 6π ≈ 18.85. 5) Equation of circle center (2, −3), radius 5 → (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 25. 6) x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 → (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25; center (3, −2), r = 5. 7) Is (6, 2) on that circle? → 9 + 16 = 25, yes. 8) Parabola focus (0, 2), directrix y = −2 → x² = 8y. 9) Convert 225° to radians → 5π/4.

days.guide: Take a point (x, y) on a circle with center (h, k) and radius r; the distance formula squared gives the equation. Practice writing equations and reading center/radius.

questions.q: Write the equation of the circle with center (2, −3) and radius 5.
Give the center and radius of (x + 1)² + (y − 4)² = 49.
questions.a: Center (−1, 4), radius 7.

days.guide: Model completing the square for both x and y terms, adding (b/2)² to both sides. The student converts several equations and checks in Desmos.

questions.q: Find the center and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0.
Find the center and radius of x² + y² + 8x − 9 = 0.
questions.a: (x + 4)² + y² = 25: center (−4, 0), radius 5.

days.guide: Substitute the point into the equation, or compute its distance from the center. The student proves or disproves points on circles, including one with radius √ form.

questions.q: Does (1, √3) lie on the circle centered at the origin with radius 2?
questions.a: 1 + 3 = 4 = 2², so yes.

days.guide: Define a parabola as all points equidistant from a focus and a directrix. Set distance to focus equal to distance to directrix and simplify; graph in Desmos.

questions.q: Find the equation of the parabola with focus (0, 2) and directrix y = −2.
questions.a: x² + (y − 2)² = (y + 2)² → x² = 8y, or y = x²/8.

questions.q: Where is the vertex of that parabola?
questions.a: At (0, 0), halfway between focus and directrix.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test from the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: What does r² represent in the circle equation?
questions.a: The square of the radius — the squared distance from every point on the circle to the center.

weeks.prep: Graph paper, tape measure, calculator. For Day 4, choose a room and look up the price per square foot of a flooring option (e.g., laminate around $2–$5/ft²).
misconceptions: Using the slant side instead of the height in parallelogram/triangle area. Height is perpendicular to the base.
Forgetting to subtract cut-outs (or double-counting overlaps) in composite figures.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Trapezoid bases 8 and 12, height 5 → 50. 2) Parallelogram base 9, height 4 → 36. 3) Regular hexagon side 6 → apothem 3√3, area 54√3 ≈ 93.5. 4) Square with a semicircle on one side (side 10) → 100 + 12.5π ≈ 139.3. 5) Rectangle 12 × 8 with a circle of radius 2 removed → 96 − 4π ≈ 83.4. Floor plan rubric: 4 = accurate scaled drawing with measurements, correct area including any irregular parts, waste allowance (~10%), cost with units; 3 = minor calculation error; 2 = missing waste or units, or drawing not to scale; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Review derivations: parallelogram = rectangle rearranged; triangle = half a parallelogram; trapezoid = half a parallelogram made of two copies. The student derives each with sketches.

questions.q: Find the area of a trapezoid with bases 8 and 12 and height 5.
A triangle has base 14 and area 63. Find the height.

days.guide: Show area = ½·apothem·perimeter by splitting into n isosceles triangles; find the apothem with trig (a = s / (2 tan(180°/n))).

questions.q: Find the area of a regular hexagon with side 6.
questions.a: Apothem 3√3; perimeter 36; area = ½·3√3·36 = 54√3 ≈ 93.5.

questions.q: Find the area of a regular pentagon with side 10.

days.guide: Split composite shapes into known pieces, adding or subtracting. The student finds areas of 6 figures with circle parts.

questions.q: A 12 × 8 rectangle has a circular hole of radius 2. Find the remaining area.

days.guide: The student measures a room, sketches it to scale, computes area, adds 10% for waste, and prices flooring.

questions.q: A 12 ft × 15 ft room uses flooring at $3.50/ft² with 10% waste. What is the cost?

days.guide: Give the quiz and score the floor plan with the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: What is an apothem?
questions.a: The perpendicular segment from the center of a regular polygon to the midpoint of a side.

weeks.prep: Clay or play dough, dental floss, paper cutouts (rectangle, right triangle, semicircle), tape, pencil, calculator.
misconceptions: Believing a cube's cross sections can only be squares. Slicing at angles gives rectangles, triangles, pentagons and hexagons.
Forgetting the two bases when computing surface area of a prism or cylinder.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Possible cross sections of a cube → square, rectangle, triangle, pentagon, hexagon (and trapezoid/parallelogram). 2) Cylinder cross sections → circle (parallel to base), rectangle (perpendicular through axis), ellipse (slanted). 3) Rotating a rectangle about one side → cylinder; right triangle about a leg → cone; semicircle about its diameter → sphere. 4) SA of a 2 × 3 × 4 prism → 52. 5) SA of a cylinder r = 3, h = 10 → 78π ≈ 245.0. 6) SA of a square pyramid with base 6 and slant height 5 → 36 + 60 = 96. Lab sketches: full credit for labeled sketches of at least 3 cross sections per solid.

days.guide: Sort solids (prism, pyramid, cylinder, cone, sphere) and count faces, edges, vertices. The student sketches a net for a cube, triangular prism, cylinder and square pyramid.

questions.q: How many faces, edges and vertices does a triangular prism have?
questions.a: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices (F + V − E = 2).

questions.q: What shapes make the net of a cylinder?
questions.a: Two circles and a rectangle.

days.guide: Mold clay cube, cylinder and cone; slice with floss at different angles and sketch each cross section.

questions.q: What cross sections can you get from a cone?
questions.a: Circle (parallel to base), triangle (through the apex vertically), ellipse, and parabola/hyperbola-shaped curves for other angles.

days.guide: Tape paper shapes to a pencil and spin; the student predicts then names each solid of revolution.

questions.q: What solid forms when a right triangle rotates about one leg?
questions.a: A cone.

days.guide: Compute surface area from nets: sum the areas of all faces. Practice prisms, cylinders (2πr² + 2πrh) and pyramids (base + ½·perimeter·slant height).

questions.q: Find the surface area of a cylinder with r = 3 and h = 10.
Find the surface area of a 2 × 3 × 4 rectangular prism.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key and collect lab sketches. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Can a cube have a hexagonal cross section?
questions.a: Yes — a slice through the midpoints of six edges gives a regular hexagon.

weeks.prep: A stack of coins, a paper cone and cylinder with the same base and height (make from cardstock), rice, calculator.
misconceptions: Forgetting the 1/3 for pyramids and cones. Show the rice demo: three cones fill one cylinder.
Using slant height instead of height in cone/pyramid volume.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Cylinder r = 4, h = 10 → 160π ≈ 502.7. 2) Cone r = 4, h = 10 → 160π/3 ≈ 167.6. 3) Square pyramid base 6, height 10 → 120. 4) Sphere r = 3 → 36π ≈ 113.1. 5) Rectangular prism 5 × 4 × 3 → 60. 6) Oblique cylinder r = 2, height 7 → 28π ≈ 88.0 (same as right, by Cavalieri). 7) Ice cream cone r = 3, h = 10 topped with a hemisphere r = 3 → 30π + 18π = 48π ≈ 150.8.

days.guide: Stack coins straight, then push the stack slanted. The student explains why the volume stays the same: every cross section has the same area at each height (Cavalieri's principle).

questions.q: Why does a slanted stack of coins have the same volume as a straight stack?
questions.a: Each layer has the same area at each height, so by Cavalieri's principle the volumes are equal.

days.guide: Volume = base area × height for prisms and cylinders (right or oblique, using perpendicular height).

questions.q: Find the volume of a cylinder with r = 4 and h = 10.
A triangular prism has a base triangle with legs 3 and 4 and length 10. Volume?

days.guide: Fill the paper cone with rice and pour into the cylinder; it takes three cones. Generalize V = ⅓Bh.

questions.q: Find the volume of a cone with radius 3 and height 8.
Find the volume of a square pyramid with base edge 6 and height 10.

days.guide: Introduce V = (4/3)πr³ and composite solids (cone + hemisphere, cylinder + hemispheres).

questions.q: Find the volume of a sphere with radius 3.
A basketball has diameter 9.4 in. Find its volume.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: If a sphere's radius doubles, what happens to its volume?
questions.a: It multiplies by 2³ = 8.

weeks.prep: Kitchen scale (grams), measuring cup, household objects (a rock, a metal spoon, a wood block), calculator. Look up a few CA county populations and areas (census.gov or Wikipedia). Prepare the Unit 8 test.
misconceptions: Inverting the density ratio. Density = mass/volume (or people/area): 'per' means divide by the unit after 'per'.
Mixing units (mL vs cm³ — they are equal; L vs cm³ — 1 L = 1000 cm³).
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test with answers: 1) 5,000 people in 20 km² → 250 people/km². 2) Object with mass 270 g and volume 100 cm³ → 2.7 g/cm³. 3) Volume of a cylinder r = 5, h = 12 → 300π ≈ 942.5. 4) Sphere r = 6 → 288π ≈ 904.8. 5) Composite area: 10 × 6 rectangle with a semicircle of diameter 6 on one end → 60 + 4.5π ≈ 74.1. 6) Cross section of a cylinder sliced parallel to the base → circle. 7) A 355 mL can with r = 3.84 cm → h ≈ 7.67 cm. Design project rubric: 4 = volume equation set to 355 cm³, SA expressed in r, minimum found (table, graph or h = 2r) at r ≈ 3.84 cm, h ≈ 7.67 cm, SA ≈ 278 cm², labeled drawing and comparison to a real can; 3 = correct minimum with minor gaps; 2 = only trial values without conclusion; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Explain density as 'amount per unit.' Compute population density of a few CA counties and a BTU-per-cubic-foot heating problem (e.g., a room needs about 5 BTU per ft³ — use the given value from the problem).

questions.q: Los Angeles County has about 9.7 million people in about 4,060 square miles. Population density?
questions.a: ≈ 2,390 people per square mile.

questions.q: A room 12 × 15 × 8 ft needs 5 BTU per cubic foot. How many BTU?

days.guide: Weigh each object, find volume by water displacement in the measuring cup (1 mL = 1 cm³), and compute density. Compare to known values (water 1 g/cm³, aluminum 2.7).

questions.q: A rock has mass 150 g and raises the water level 60 mL. What is its density?
Will an object with density 0.8 g/cm³ float in water?
questions.a: Yes — it is less dense than water (1 g/cm³).

days.guide: Set up V = πr²h = 355 cm³, write h = 355/(πr²), and SA = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr² + 710/r. The student builds a table or uses Desmos to find the minimum.

questions.q: For a 355 mL can, what radius minimizes surface area?
questions.a: About 3.84 cm (height ≈ 7.67 cm, where h = 2r), SA ≈ 278 cm².

questions.q: Why don't real soda cans use this shape?
questions.a: Real cans (r ≈ 3.3 cm, h ≈ 12.2 cm) are taller for grip, stacking, thicker top/bottom metal, and fitting machines and cupholders.

days.guide: The student writes up the design with a labeled drawing, the table/graph, and the final dimensions and comparison.

questions.q: What should a design write-up include?
questions.a: The problem, equations, method (table/graph), final dimensions with units, a drawing, and a comparison to a real can.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test from the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Why is a cylinder with h = 2r the most efficient?
questions.a: For a fixed volume, that shape gives the smallest surface area (it is closest to a sphere-like proportion for a cylinder).

weeks.prep: Two dice, coins, a standard 52-card deck. Remind yourself: a deck has 4 suits × 13 ranks; 12 face cards.
misconceptions: Counting a sum like 7 as one outcome instead of 6 ordered pairs. Use the 6 × 6 table.
Adding probabilities of overlapping events without subtracting the overlap.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Sample space for flipping 3 coins → 8 outcomes (HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT). 2) P(sum of 7 with two dice) → 6/36 = 1/6. 3) P(sum of 8) → 5/36. 4) P(heart or king) → 16/52 = 4/13. 5) P(not a face card) → 40/52 = 10/13. 6) In a Venn diagram, A ∩ B means → outcomes in both A and B; A ∪ B → in A or B or both; Aᶜ → not in A.

days.guide: Make a tree for 3 coin flips and a 6 × 6 table for two dice. The student counts outcomes for several events.

questions.q: How many outcomes for rolling two dice? How many give a sum of 7?
P(at least one head in 2 coin flips)?

days.guide: Draw Venn diagrams for events from one die roll (A = even, B = greater than 3). Name union, intersection and complement.

questions.q: Roll a die: A = even {2, 4, 6}, B = greater than 3 {4, 5, 6}. Find A ∩ B and A ∪ B.

days.guide: Derive the addition rule from the Venn diagram (overlap counted twice). The student solves card and die problems.

questions.q: P(heart or king) from a standard deck?
P(even or greater than 3) on one die?

days.guide: Roll two dice 100 times and tally sums. Compare experimental frequencies to the theoretical (e.g., P(7) = 1/6 ≈ 16.7%).

questions.q: Why might the experimental results differ from theoretical probability?
questions.a: Random variation; with more trials the experimental frequencies tend to get closer (Law of Large Numbers).

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Are 'rolling an even number' and 'rolling a 5' mutually exclusive?
questions.a: Yes — they cannot both happen, so P(even or 5) = 3/6 + 1/6 = 2/3.

weeks.prep: Deck of cards, coins. Prepare a simple medical-testing example (numbers in the guide).
misconceptions: Confusing P(A|B) and P(B|A). Say it in words: 'probability of A given that B happened' and identify which group you restrict to.
Treating draws without replacement as independent.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) P(heads and rolling a 6) → 1/12. 2) Are 'draw a heart' and 'draw a king' independent? → P(heart and king) = 1/52 = (1/4)(1/13), yes. 3) P(king | face card) → 4/12 = 1/3. 4) P(two aces without replacement) → 4/52 · 3/51 = 1/221. 5) P(two aces with replacement) → 1/169. 6) A test is 99% accurate for a disease that 1% have; among 10,000 people, 99 true positives and 99 false positives → P(disease | positive) = 50%.

days.guide: Define independence: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B). Test with coin/die and with card events.

questions.q: P(heads on a coin and a 6 on a die)?
Are 'draw a red card' and 'draw a face card' independent?
questions.a: P(red and face) = 6/52 = 3/26; P(red)·P(face) = 1/2·12/52 = 6/52. Equal, so yes.

days.guide: Model P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) as restricting the sample space to B. Use the card deck.

questions.q: P(king | face card)?
questions.a: There are 12 face cards and 4 are kings: 4/12 = 1/3.

questions.q: P(heart | red card)?

days.guide: Work through: disease rate 1%, test catches 99% of sick people and wrongly flags 1% of healthy people. Of 10,000 people: 100 sick (99 test positive), 9,900 healthy (99 test positive). P(sick | positive) = 99/198 = 50%. Discuss weather forecasts similarly.

questions.q: In the example, why is P(sick | positive) only 50% even though the test is 99% accurate?
questions.a: The disease is rare, so false positives from the large healthy group equal the true positives.

days.guide: Draw cards without replacement and compute multi-step probabilities, adjusting counts after each draw.

questions.q: P(drawing two hearts in a row without replacement)?
P(drawing a king then a queen without replacement)?

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: If P(A|B) = P(A), what can you conclude?
questions.a: A and B are independent.

weeks.prep: Spreadsheet software; plan two yes/no survey questions with the student (e.g., 'Do you have a pet?' and 'Do you live in a house?'). Arrange to survey 20 people (family, friends, co-op).
misconceptions: Dividing by the grand total when a conditional probability needs the row or column total.
Concluding cause and effect from an association in a two-way table.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz uses this table (100 students): Sports & Music 12, Sports & No music 28, No sports & Music 18, No sports & No music 42. Answers: 1) P(music) → 30/100 = 0.30. 2) P(sports and music) → 0.12. 3) P(music | sports) → 12/40 = 0.30. 4) P(sports | music) → 12/30 = 0.40. 5) Are sports and music independent? → yes, P(music | sports) = P(music) = 0.30. 6) Marginal relative frequency of sports → 0.40. Report rubric: 4 = clean table with totals, joint/marginal/conditional values, a correct independence test, a conclusion with limitations (small sample, not random); 3 = minor errors; 2 = table only with little analysis; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Build the sample table from the assessment key with row and column totals. The student computes joint (cell/grand total) and marginal (total/grand total) relative frequencies.

questions.q: Using the sports/music table, what is the joint relative frequency of 'no sports and no music'?
What is the marginal relative frequency of music?

days.guide: The student surveys 20 people and organizes the results in a two-way table in a spreadsheet with totals.

questions.q: Why should both questions be yes/no or categorical?
questions.a: Two-way tables organize categorical data; each person falls into exactly one cell.

days.guide: Compute conditional probabilities by row and column, then compare P(A|B) to P(A) to test independence.

questions.q: From the sample table, P(sports | music)?
Is P(sports | music) equal to P(sports)? What does that mean?
questions.a: Yes, both 0.40, so playing sports and liking music are independent in this data.

days.guide: The student writes a one-page report: question, table, key probabilities, independence conclusion, and limitations.

questions.q: Name a limitation of a 20-person survey of friends and family.
questions.a: Small, non-random sample; results may not represent a larger population.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key and score the report. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: What does a conditional relative frequency compare?
questions.a: The count in a cell to the total of its row (or column), i.e., the frequency within one group.

weeks.prep: Calculator with nPr/nCr (or use the formulas). Prepare the Unit 9 test from the assessment key.
misconceptions: Using permutations when order doesn't matter (committees, lottery picks).
Forgetting to update counts in multi-stage problems without replacement.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test with answers: 1) P(two red marbles without replacement from 5 red, 3 blue) → 5/8 · 4/7 = 5/14. 2) 4-digit PIN with repetition → 10,000; without repetition → 5,040. 3) Gold/silver/bronze among 8 runners → 8P3 = 336. 4) Choose 3 toppings from 10 → 10C3 = 120. 5) Lottery choose 6 of 49 → 1/13,983,816. 6) P(A or B), P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A and B) = 0.2 → 0.7. 7) Game: roll a die; win $5 on a 6, lose $1 otherwise → expected value 0, fair. 8) P(king | face card) → 1/3.

days.guide: Teach P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B|A) with tree diagrams for multi-stage problems.

questions.q: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue marbles. P(two reds without replacement)?
P(first red then blue without replacement)?

days.guide: Introduce the counting principle and nPr = n!/(n − r)! for arrangements where order matters.

questions.q: How many ways can 8 runners finish 1st, 2nd and 3rd?
How many 4-digit PINs with no repeated digits?

days.guide: Show nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!) divides out the orderings. Compute lottery odds.

questions.q: How many ways to choose 2 people from 5 for a committee?
Probability of winning a 6-of-49 lottery with one ticket?

days.guide: Compute expected value to decide fairness. Discuss product-testing decisions (e.g., sampling items to estimate defect rates).

questions.q: A game costs $1; roll a die and win $5 (plus your dollar back) on a 6. Is it fair?
questions.a: Expected value = (1/6)(5) + (5/6)(−1) = 0, so it is fair.

questions.q: Two players pick who goes first by flipping two coins: A wins if they match, B if they differ. Fair?
questions.a: Yes: P(match) = 2/4 = P(differ).

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test from the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: When do you use combinations instead of permutations?
questions.a: When order does not matter (selections, groups).

weeks.prep: Assemble a cumulative review packet (one page per strand) and a practice final mirroring the final exam structure. Calculator, compass, protractor.
misconceptions: Relying on memory for formulas without knowing when they apply. Have the student build a one-page formula sheet with a sample problem for each.
Skipping diagrams on word problems. Require a labeled sketch.
weeks.assessment_key: Practice final (sample items with answers): 1) Reflect (2, −7) over the y-axis → (−2, −7). 2) Rhombus diagonals 6 and 8 → side 5. 3) △ABC ~ △DEF, k = 3, perimeter of △ABC 12 → △DEF perimeter 36. 4) Right triangle angle 30°, hypotenuse 18 → opposite 9. 5) Inscribed angle 40° → arc 80°. 6) Circle x² + y² − 10y = 0 → center (0, 5), r = 5. 7) Cone r = 6, h = 4 → 48π ≈ 150.8. 8) P(sum 9 with 2 dice) → 4/36 = 1/9. 9) 6C2 → 15. 10) Proof: base angles of an isosceles triangle are congruent. Grade: 90/80/70 cutoffs; use results to plan Week 36 review.

days.guide: Mixed review of transformations, congruence and proof. The student works problems and one proof; check after each set.

questions.q: Rotate (4, 1) 90° counterclockwise about the origin.

days.guide: Mixed review of similarity and trigonometry: give 8–10 problems (similar-triangle proportions, special right triangles, SOH-CAH-TOA, Law of Sines/Cosines). The student works one set of five, you check, then they do the next set; any miss sends them back to their notes for that problem type.

questions.q: A 30-60-90 triangle has hypotenuse 12. Find both legs.
In right △ABC, angle A = 28°, adjacent side 15. Find the opposite side.

days.guide: Mixed review of circles and coordinate geometry: arcs and inscribed angles, tangents, arc length and sectors, circle equations by completing the square, and slope/distance proofs. The student works in sets of five with a check after each set and adds any formula they forgot to their one-page formula sheet.

questions.q: Find the center and radius of x² + y² + 4x − 2y − 4 = 0.
questions.a: (x + 2)² + (y − 1)² = 9: center (−2, 1), radius 3.

days.guide: Mixed review of area, volume and probability: composite areas, surface area and volume of solids, the addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability and counting. The student works in sets of five; for each miss, they write the correct formula and redo a similar problem.

questions.q: Find the volume of a sphere with diameter 10.
P(drawing a red card or an ace)?

days.guide: Give the full practice final in the assessment key under timed conditions; grade it together. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Which three topics had the most errors?
questions.a: Answers vary; the student lists them to guide Week 36 targeted review.

weeks.prep: Prepare the two-part final exam (assessment key). Have the student's error log from the practice final.
misconceptions: Cramming new methods the day before the exam. Focus on the error log topics.
Not checking answers for reasonableness (e.g., a leg longer than the hypotenuse).
weeks.assessment_key: Final exam (sample items with answers). Part 1: 1) Distance (−3, 4) to (3, −4) → 10. 2) Reflect (1, 5) over y = −x → (−5, −1). 3) Interior angle sum of a 9-gon → 1260°. 4) Proof: SAS congruence with a shared side. 5) Dilate (6, −3) by ⅓ → (2, −1). 6) Side splitter: 6/9 = 8/x → x = 12. Part 2: 7) sin⁻¹(0.5) → 30°. 8) Law of Cosines a = 5, b = 6, C = 50° → c ≈ 4.74. 9) Tangent from point 17 from center, radius 8 → 15. 10) Arc length r = 12, 150° → 10π ≈ 31.4. 11) Cylinder r = 3, h = 7 → 63π ≈ 197.9. 12) P(two kings without replacement) → 1/221. 13) 7P2 → 42. Grade cutoffs 90/80/70. Reflection rubric (Day 5): 3 = explains a specific proof's logic accurately and names a career with a concrete geometry use; 2 = general; 1 = minimal.

days.guide: The student reworks the problem types missed on the practice final, explaining each aloud.

questions.q: What is the most common mistake you made on the practice final, and how will you prevent it?
questions.a: Answers vary; a good answer names a specific error (e.g., degree/radian mode) and a check (e.g., test sin 30 = 0.5).

days.guide: Give Part 1 of the final (transformations through similarity) — about 60 minutes.

questions.q: (After) Dilate (6, −3) by ⅓ about the origin.

days.guide: Give Part 2 (trig, circles, volume, probability) — about 60 minutes.

questions.q: (After) Find the length of a tangent from a point 17 units from the center of a circle with radius 8.

days.guide: Return the exam; the student corrects every error and writes the reason for each.

questions.q: Why write a reason for each correction rather than just the right answer?
questions.a: Explaining the error builds understanding and helps avoid repeating it.

days.guide: The student writes a one-page reflection on a favorite proof and a career that uses geometry (architect, surveyor, game designer, nurse calculating dosages in volumes, etc.).

questions.q: Give one specific way a surveyor uses geometry.
questions.a: Using the Law of Sines/Cosines or trig to find distances and property boundaries that can't be measured directly.

PE.overview: PE 10 runs about 45 minutes a day of real activity, organized in units: fitness testing and planning, outdoor education, self-defense, net sports, strength and recovery, invasion games, dance, gymnastics and team sports, ending with a lifetime fitness plan. Begin every session with a dynamic warm-up and end with a cool-down, model or video each skill, then practice with a checklist and log results. Emphasize safety (spotting, controlled partner work, hydration, Ten Essentials), personal progress against the student's own baseline, and the 60-minutes-a-day habit.

weeks.prep: Measure and mark a 20-meter course with cones (or a measured 1-mile route/track). Download the FITNESSGRAM PACER audio (free from the Cooper Institute/FitnessGram or on YouTube) and cadence audio for curl-ups and push-ups. Get a measuring tape, a yardstick for the sit-and-reach (or a box), a ruler, a bathroom scale and a log sheet. Print the FITNESSGRAM Healthy Fitness Zone (HFZ) chart for the student's age and sex. Check for any health conditions that limit testing.
misconceptions: Students sprint the first PACER laps and burn out. Pace with the beeps; the test gets faster each minute.
Students bounce during sit-and-reach. Reach slowly and hold the farthest point for one second; bouncing can cause injury and inflates scores.
Students think BMI measures fitness. BMI is a rough screen of weight relative to height; it doesn't distinguish muscle from fat or measure fitness.

days.guide: Teach a 10-move dynamic warm-up (jog, high knees, butt kicks, walking lunges, leg swings, arm circles, inchworms, skips, lateral shuffles, carioca) and safety expectations (hydration, footwear, stop if chest pain/dizziness, buddy or adult nearby at parks).

questions.q: Why use dynamic stretches before exercise instead of long static holds?
questions.a: Dynamic movements raise heart rate, muscle temperature and range of motion to prepare for activity; long static holds are better after exercise.

questions.q: Name two warning signs to stop exercising immediately.
questions.a: Chest pain, dizziness or fainting, severe shortness of breath, or sharp joint pain.

days.guide: After warming up, the student completes the 20-m PACER (or 1-mile run) while you count laps or time it.

questions.q: When does the PACER end?
questions.a: The second time the student fails to reach the line before the beep.

questions.q: What fitness component does the PACER measure?
questions.a: Aerobic capacity (cardiorespiratory endurance).

days.guide: Demonstrate correct curl-up form (knees bent ~140°, fingertips slide along a measuring strip) and 90° push-up form (body straight, elbows to 90°). The student tests to cadence while you count.

questions.q: What's the cadence for curl-ups and push-ups?
questions.a: One repetition every 3 seconds.

questions.q: What counts as a push-up form error?
questions.a: Not lowering to a 90° elbow angle, sagging or piking hips, not fully extending arms, or stopping to rest.

days.guide: Administer the back-saver sit-and-reach (each side) and trunk lift; measure height and weight and calculate BMI.

questions.q: Why is the trunk lift capped at 12 inches?
questions.a: Lifting higher can strain the lower back; the test measures healthy extension, not maximum.

questions.q: Calculate BMI for 130 lb and 5 ft 6 in.

days.guide: The student compares each result to the HFZ chart and writes a strengths/needs summary with one priority to work on.

questions.q: If your PACER score is below the HFZ, what type of training should you add?
questions.a: Regular aerobic exercise (running, cycling, swimming) at moderate to vigorous intensity, 3–5 days per week.

weeks.assessment_key: Baseline log: full credit when every test is recorded with units and date, compared with the HFZ chart, and labeled 'Needs Improvement', 'Healthy Fitness Zone' or above. Protocol checks: PACER — 20 m laps to the beep, test ends at the second missed beep; 1-mile — time in minutes:seconds; curl-ups — cadence of 1 every 3 seconds, maximum 75, ends at second form error; 90° push-ups — 1 every 3 seconds, elbows to 90°, ends at second form correction; back-saver sit-and-reach — one leg bent, record each side to the nearest half inch, maximum 12 inches; trunk lift — face down, lift upper body slowly and hold, measure chin height, maximum 12 inches (HFZ 9–12 in); BMI = weight (lb) × 703 ÷ height (in)². Example: 130 lb, 66 in → 130 × 703 ÷ 4356 = 21.0.

weeks.prep: Get a stopwatch or heart-rate app. Have the student take resting heart rate on three mornings before getting out of bed. Print an RPE (Borg 6–20 or 0–10) scale. Plan a safe interval-run route.
misconceptions: Students count pulse for 10 seconds and forget to multiply. Count 15 seconds and multiply by 4 (or 30 × 2).
Students take their pulse with their thumb. The thumb has its own pulse; use index and middle fingers on the wrist (radial) or neck (carotid, gently).
Students think harder is always better. FITT intensity should match the goal; easy days support recovery.

days.guide: The student averages three morning resting HRs and calculates max and target zones using Karvonen.

questions.q: Age 15, resting HR 65 bpm: what is the 60–80% target zone?
How do you find your pulse?
questions.a: Two fingers on the radial artery (thumb side of the wrist), count 15 seconds and multiply by 4.

days.guide: The student does a 20-minute interval run (e.g., 2 min jog / 1 min fast × 6, plus warm-up and cool-down), taking HR after each interval.

questions.q: What happened to your heart rate during recovery jogs?
questions.a: It dropped (recovery), though not all the way to resting; faster recovery indicates better fitness.

days.guide: Teach FITT; the student applies it to three sample plans and identifies which FITT variable changes in each.

questions.q: A runner increases from 20 to 30 minutes per run. Which FITT variable changed?
questions.a: Time.

questions.q: Give a FITT plan for building aerobic fitness.
questions.a: F: 4 days/week; I: 60–80% HRR or RPE 13–15; T: 30 minutes; Type: running or cycling.

days.guide: Lead a 30-minute bodyweight circuit (squats, push-ups, lunges, planks, jumping jacks, mountain climbers; 40 s work/20 s rest) and record RPE after each round.

questions.q: What RPE (6–20 scale) corresponds to moderate intensity?
questions.a: About 12–14 ('somewhat hard').

days.guide: Give the heart-rate/FITT quiz and review the HR log.

questions.q: Why does resting heart rate often drop as fitness improves?
questions.a: The heart muscle becomes stronger and pumps more blood per beat (higher stroke volume), so fewer beats are needed.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Estimated max HR — 220 − age (205 for a 15-year-old). 2) Karvonen target HR = (HRR × intensity) + resting HR, where HRR = max HR − resting HR. 3) Example: age 15, RHR 65 → HRR 140; 60% = 149 bpm; 80% = 177 bpm. 4) FITT = Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type. 5) Teens need 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, with vigorous, muscle- and bone-strengthening activity on at least 3 days each. 6) RPE — perceived exertion; moderate ≈ 12–14 on Borg 6–20 (5–6 on 0–10). 7) Lower resting heart rate generally indicates better cardiovascular fitness. HR log full credit: three resting readings and average, plus post-interval readings.

weeks.prep: Print the baseline FITNESSGRAM log and a 4-week plan template. Have the fitness log ready. Find a 20-minute yoga/stretching video for Day 4.
misconceptions: Students write goals they can't measure ('get fit'). SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
Students increase everything at once. Progressive overload means small, gradual increases (about 10% per week in volume).
Students count only formal workouts toward 60 minutes. Walking, biking to errands and active chores count.

days.guide: Model one SMART goal; the student writes three from baseline results.

questions.q: Rewrite 'get stronger' as a SMART goal.
questions.a: 'Increase 90° push-ups from 12 to 18 by December 15 by doing push-up workouts 3 days per week.'

days.guide: The student drafts a 4-week plan with cardio, strength and flexibility days, applying FITT and progression.

questions.q: Why not do intense strength training on the same muscles two days in a row?
questions.a: Muscles need about 48 hours to recover and adapt.

days.guide: The student completes the first 40-minute planned workout and logs it (warm-up, main set, cool-down, RPE).

questions.q: What should a cool-down include?
questions.a: Light activity to gradually lower heart rate, then static stretching.

days.guide: Lead a 20-minute static stretching and yoga routine (hold stretches 15–30 seconds, no bouncing).

questions.q: How long should you hold a static stretch?
questions.a: About 15–30 seconds (up to 60), without bouncing, to the point of mild tension.

days.guide: The student totals the week's activity minutes against the 60-minutes-per-day guideline and adjusts the plan.

questions.q: What three types of activity should teens include weekly?
questions.a: Aerobic activity daily, muscle-strengthening on at least 3 days, and bone-strengthening on at least 3 days.

weeks.assessment_key: Plan rubric: 4 = Three SMART goals tied to baseline needs (e.g., 'Increase PACER from 32 to 40 laps by Week 18 by running 3×/week'); a 4-week plan that includes cardio (3–5 days), strength (2–3 non-consecutive days), flexibility (most days), rest/recovery, warm-up and cool-down, and progression each week; activity log with daily minutes. 3 = plan complete, progression unclear. 2 = missing a component. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather a daypack, water bottles, and the Ten Essentials (navigation, headlamp, sun protection, first aid, knife/tool, fire starter, emergency shelter, extra food, extra water, extra clothes). Choose a local 3–5 mile trail using a trail map app (AllTrails, CalTopo, or park maps). Check weather and trail conditions.
misconceptions: Students think a phone is all the navigation they need. Batteries die and signal drops; carry a paper map and know your route.
Students estimate hiking time by distance alone. Add time for elevation: Naismith's rule — about 1 hour per 3 miles plus 1 hour per 2,000 feet of gain.
Students think biodegradable food scraps are fine to leave. Orange peels and apple cores take a long time to break down and attract wildlife; pack it out.

days.guide: The student packs the Ten Essentials and explains each item's purpose.

questions.q: Why carry extra clothing on a sunny day hike?
questions.a: Weather can change, temperatures drop, and an injury or delay could mean being out after dark; layers prevent hypothermia.

days.guide: The student plans a hike with a map app, calculating distance, elevation gain and estimated time.

questions.q: Estimate time for a 4-mile hike with 1,000 feet of gain using Naismith's rule.
questions.a: 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33 h + 1,000 ÷ 2,000 = 0.5 h → about 1 hour 50 minutes (plus breaks).

days.guide: The student does a 45-minute brisk walk with a loaded daypack, checking heart rate three times.

questions.q: Why train with a loaded pack?
questions.a: To condition legs, core and shoulders for the actual load and check pack fit.

days.guide: The student learns the seven LNT principles and applies them to scenarios.

questions.q: You find an arrowhead on a trail. What should you do?
questions.a: Leave it where it is (Leave what you find); it may also be illegal to remove artifacts from public lands.

days.guide: Complete a 3–5 mile family hike; the student logs time, distance and heart rate.

questions.q: What's a turnaround time and why set one?
questions.a: A preset time to head back regardless of progress, so you return before dark or before weather or fatigue become dangerous.

weeks.assessment_key: Hike log and plan: full credit for route map, distance, elevation gain, time estimate (Naismith), turnaround time, weather check, Ten Essentials checklist, who was told the plan, and log of time, distance and heart rate at 3+ points. Leave No Trace principles: 1) Plan ahead and prepare. 2) Travel and camp on durable surfaces. 3) Dispose of waste properly. 4) Leave what you find. 5) Minimize campfire impacts. 6) Respect wildlife. 7) Be considerate of other visitors.

weeks.prep: Get a baseplate orienteering compass and print a topographic map of a local park (USGS or CalTopo). Look up local magnetic declination (about 11–14° east in most of California; check NOAA's calculator). Set up 8 controls (flags or cones with letters) in a park and make a control map/answer card.
misconceptions: Students hold the compass near metal or phones. Metal and electronics deflect the needle; hold it level and away from them.
Students read close contour lines as flat. Close lines mean steep terrain; widely spaced lines mean gentle slopes.

Students forget declination. True north and magnetic north differ; in California, magnetic north is east of true north, so adjust map bearings accordingly (or use a compass with adjustable declination).

days.guide: Teach compass parts (baseplate, direction-of-travel arrow, rotating bezel, orienting arrow, magnetic needle). The student takes bearings to five objects in the yard.

questions.q: How do you take a bearing to an object?
questions.a: Point the direction-of-travel arrow at the object, rotate the bezel until the orienting arrow lines up under the red north needle ('red in the shed'), then read the degrees at the index line.

days.guide: The student reads contour lines and map symbols on a topo map and identifies hills, valleys and steep slopes.

questions.q: What do V-shaped contour lines pointing uphill indicate?
questions.a: A valley or stream drainage (the V points upstream).

questions.q: If the contour interval is 40 feet and you cross 5 lines, how much elevation do you gain?
questions.a: 200 feet.

days.guide: The student walks 100 m three times counting every left-foot step and averages the pace count.

questions.q: If your pace count is 64 per 100 m, how many paces for 250 m?
questions.a: 160 paces.

days.guide: Run the 8-control park course at a jog; the student navigates with map and compass and records control codes.

questions.q: What should you do if you realize you're lost?
questions.a: Stop, think, observe, plan (STOP): return to the last known point or use landmarks and the map to relocate.

days.guide: The student reflects on navigation errors and teamwork.

questions.q: Name one common navigation error and its fix.
questions.a: Not checking the map often enough — stop at each feature and confirm your position before moving on.

weeks.assessment_key: Orienteering course: score time and accuracy — 8 of 8 controls with correct codes = full accuracy; subtract time penalties (e.g., 5 minutes) per missed or wrong control. Proficient: all controls found, bearings within ±5°, pace counts within 10% of actual distance.

weeks.prep: Find a local climbing gym (many have intro sessions) or a sturdy low playground structure for traverses. Get a slackline or use a curb or 2x4 on the ground as a balance beam. Verify waivers and staff instruction at gyms.
misconceptions: Students climb with their arms. Good climbers push with their legs and keep arms straight to save energy.
Students think spotting means catching the climber. A spotter guides the climber's fall to protect the head and neck and land feet-first on the pad.
Students climb higher than a safe height without a rope. Keep bouldering low (feet no higher than about 3 feet on home structures) and over padding.

days.guide: Lead a grip and core workout: dead hangs (3 × max), planks (3 × 30–60 s), farmer carries (3 × 30 m).

questions.q: Why does grip strength matter in climbing?
questions.a: Holding onto holds depends on finger and forearm strength; fatigue there ends the climb.

days.guide: Watch a footwork video; the student practices three points of contact and precise foot placements on low structures.

questions.q: What does 'three points of contact' mean?
questions.a: Always keeping two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand, on the structure while moving one limb.

days.guide: At a gym or low structure, the student boulders/traverses with a trained spotter.

questions.q: How should you land if you fall while bouldering?
questions.a: Feet first with knees bent, then roll back onto the pad; don't put arms out to catch yourself.

days.guide: Practice slackline or balance-beam challenges (walk forward, backward, turn, single-leg hold).

questions.q: What helps balance on a slackline?
questions.a: Eyes on a fixed point ahead, soft knees, arms up and out, and small adjustments from the hips.

days.guide: The student writes about managing fear and risk while climbing.

questions.q: What's the difference between perceived risk and actual risk?
questions.a: Perceived risk is how dangerous something feels; actual risk is the real chance of harm. Safety gear and spotting lower actual risk even when it feels scary.

weeks.assessment_key: Skill checklist: proficient = maintains three points of contact, quiet precise footwork on edges, arms straight when resting, hips close to the wall, controlled down-climb or safe fall landing (bent knees, roll back), correct spotting stance (hands up, near the hips/torso), completes a traverse of at least 15 feet, and 30+ seconds on a slackline or balance beam. Developing = 1–2 cues needed. Beginning = 3+.

weeks.prep: Arrange a bike ride (helmet, lights, tire check) or a paddle (life jacket required, calm water, adult present). Choose a family hike for the student to lead. Prepare a risk-plan template and the quiz.
misconceptions: Students skip the risk plan for 'easy' outings. Most outdoor emergencies come from small problems (dehydration, heat, getting lost).
Students think wearing a life jacket is optional for good swimmers. Most drowning victims in boating accidents weren't wearing one.
Students lead hikes at their own pace. A leader sets the pace for the slowest member and keeps the group together.

days.guide: The student writes a risk-management plan: weather, water, route, turnaround time, emergency contacts, hazards and responses.

questions.q: What's the internationally recognized distress signal with a whistle?
questions.a: Three blasts, repeated.

days.guide: Ride 60 minutes by bike or paddle with proper safety gear.

questions.q: Which side of the road should cyclists ride on?
questions.a: The right side, with traffic.

days.guide: The student leads a family hike with map and compass, giving a briefing and keeping the group together.

questions.q: What should a hike leader do at a trail junction?
questions.a: Stop, regroup, count people, confirm direction on the map.

days.guide: The student researches three California state parks and outdoor clubs nearby, with activities and costs.

questions.q: Name one benefit of joining an outdoor club.
questions.a: Experienced leaders, group safety, skill instruction and social motivation.

days.guide: Give the outdoor safety and navigation quiz.

questions.q: What does LNT principle 'Respect wildlife' require?
questions.a: Observe from a distance, never feed animals, store food securely.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Ten Essentials list. 2) Naismith's rule. 3) Seven LNT principles. 4) Contour lines close together = steep. 5) Declination in California ≈ 11–14° east. 6) If lost — STOP (stop, think, observe, plan) and stay put if searchers know your plan. 7) Signals for help — three of anything (whistle blasts). 8) Heat illness prevention — water, shade, timing. 9) Bike safety — helmet, ride with traffic, lights at night. 10) Life jacket for paddling. Leadership checklist: plan shared with someone at home, pre-hike briefing, pace for the group, regular navigation checks, headcount at junctions, LNT followed.

weeks.prep: Preview videos on situational awareness and de-escalation (choose age-appropriate sources). Clear a practice space. Parental note: self-defense units focus on awareness, avoidance and escape; keep all partner drills slow and controlled.
misconceptions: Students think self-defense is mostly fighting. Most personal safety is awareness, avoidance and confident communication; physical techniques are a last resort to escape.
Students think being polite means staying in an uncomfortable situation. Clear, firm boundaries are appropriate and safe.
Students mirror an angry person's tone. De-escalation means calm voice, space, open hands and listening.

days.guide: Teach the color codes and practice scanning in a store or park (exits, people, items out of place).

questions.q: Which awareness color should you be in when walking in public?
questions.a: Yellow — relaxed but alert.

days.guide: Role-play assertive verbal boundaries with posture, voice and eye contact.

questions.q: Model an assertive boundary to someone standing too close.
questions.a: Hands up, firm voice: 'Back up. You're too close.'

days.guide: Practice de-escalation techniques in scenarios (angry customer, upset friend).

questions.q: Name three de-escalation techniques.
questions.a: Stay calm and speak softly, give space, listen and acknowledge feelings, avoid threatening body language, offer choices.

days.guide: Practice defensive stance and footwork drills (advance, retreat, pivot) for 20 minutes.

questions.q: Why keep hands up and open in a defensive stance?
questions.a: It protects the face and looks non-aggressive while ready to block.

days.guide: Give the scenario quiz.

questions.q: What is the goal of self-defense?
questions.a: To get away safely and get help — not to win a fight.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario quiz key (sample): 1) Cooper color codes — White: unaware; Yellow: relaxed alert (default in public); Orange: specific potential threat noticed; Red: action (escape/defend). 2) Someone follows you in a parking lot — move toward people and light, keep keys/phone ready, don't go to your car if they're near it, call for help. 3) A stranger asks you to help with something in their car — decline and keep distance. 4) Verbal boundary — firm voice, eye contact, hand up: 'Stop. Back away.' 5) De-escalation — calm tone, give space, listen, acknowledge feelings, offer options, leave. 6) Defensive stance — feet shoulder-width, staggered, knees bent, hands up open in front of the face. 7) Best outcome — escape and get help, then report.

weeks.prep: Use an exercise mat (or a grassy area) and pool noodles. Partner drills must be slow and controlled. Have a phone to record skill videos.
misconceptions: Students reach a hand back to break a fall. Arms straight back can break a wrist; tuck the chin and slap the mat with arms at about 45° to spread force.
Students block with stiff, extended arms. Blocks use bent arms close to the body, with the forearm meeting the strike.
Students strike with a closed fist. Palm-heel strikes reduce hand injuries and use the strong heel of the hand.

days.guide: Practice back and side breakfalls on a mat from sitting, then squatting.

questions.q: Why tuck your chin during a backward fall?
questions.a: To keep the back of your head from hitting the ground.

days.guide: Partner holds a pool noodle and slowly swings high and low; student practices high and low blocks.

questions.q: What part of the arm meets the strike in a block?
questions.a: The forearm, with the arm bent.

days.guide: Practice palm-heel and knee strikes on a pillow or pad.

questions.q: Why use a palm-heel strike instead of a fist?
questions.a: It protects the small bones of the hand while delivering force.

days.guide: Lead a conditioning circuit: 3 × 2-minute shadowboxing rounds with sprawls, burpees and planks between.

questions.q: What fitness component does shadowboxing train most?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance (also coordination and muscular endurance).

days.guide: Record the student demonstrating falls and blocks; review with the checklist.

questions.q: What's the safe way to practice strikes with a partner?
questions.a: Slow speed, light contact on pads only, and a clear stop signal.

weeks.assessment_key: Skill video checklist: back breakfall (chin tucked, rounded back, arms slap at ~45°), side breakfall (both sides), high block and low block with each arm, palm-heel strike and knee strike with correct alignment and balance, return to stance after each. Proficient = all elements correct.

weeks.prep: Mat, a cooperative partner (parent), and slow, controlled practice. Agree on a tap-out/stop word.
misconceptions: Students pull straight back against a wrist grab. Rotate the wrist toward the attacker's thumb, the weakest point of the grip.
Students rely on strength. Leverage and body position (base) let a smaller person escape a larger one.
Students rush escapes. Practice slowly for correct mechanics; speed comes later.

days.guide: Explain levers (force, fulcrum, load) and base (wide, low stance). Demonstrate how lowering center of gravity makes you harder to lift.

questions.q: How does lowering your center of gravity help in an escape?
questions.a: It widens your base and makes you more stable and harder to lift or push.

days.guide: Practice wrist-grab releases toward the thumb, both sides, slowly.

questions.q: Why release toward the thumb?
questions.a: The gap between thumb and fingers is the weakest part of the grip.

days.guide: Practice front and rear bear-hug escapes slowly with a partner.

questions.q: What's the first move in a rear bear-hug escape?
questions.a: Drop your weight (lower base) to make it harder to be lifted.

days.guide: Practice the shrimp (hip escape) and bridge-and-roll from the ground.

questions.q: What's the goal of the shrimp movement?
questions.a: To create space between you and the person on top so you can recover your guard or get up.

days.guide: The student demonstrates four escapes; score with the checklist.

questions.q: After escaping, what should you do?
questions.a: Run to safety and call for help.

weeks.assessment_key: Skill checklist (four escapes): wrist release toward the thumb (same-side and cross grab); front bear-hug escape (drop weight, create space, strike/knee pad, escape); rear bear-hug escape (drop base, step to the side, elbow/back step, turn out); ground escape — bridge-and-roll (trap arm and foot, bridge hips up and roll) or shrimp (hip escape) to create space and stand up. Proficient = correct mechanics on both sides and moving to escape afterward.

weeks.prep: Mat, partner, timer. Prepare the written test and a personal safety plan template.
misconceptions: Students think one technique works for everything. Combine voice, movement, blocks and escape, and adapt.
Students ignore phone safety. Share location with trusted people, lock screen, emergency SOS features.
Students forget to rest during HIIT. Work and rest intervals are both part of the design.

days.guide: Lead a 30-minute drill session reviewing all skills.

questions.q: List the order of response in a threatening situation.
questions.a: Awareness/avoidance → verbal boundary → defend if needed → escape → get help.

days.guide: Run controlled scenario drills combining voice, block and escape.

questions.q: Why use a loud voice in a confrontation?
questions.a: It can startle an attacker, draw attention and help you breathe and act.

days.guide: Lead a HIIT workout (e.g., 30 s work/30 s rest × 12).

questions.q: What does HIIT stand for?
questions.a: High-Intensity Interval Training.

days.guide: The student writes a personal safety plan (routes, phone settings, contacts).

questions.q: Name one phone setting that improves personal safety.
questions.a: Location sharing with a parent, Emergency SOS, or medical ID.

days.guide: Give the skills assessment and written test.

questions.q: Why should you report incidents?
questions.a: So adults or police can help, prevent harm to others and keep records.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills test: scenario drills combining voice command, defensive stance, block and an escape, ending with moving away (proficient = all elements smooth and controlled). Written test key: 1) Color codes. 2) Boundary-setting phrase. 3) De-escalation techniques. 4) Breakfall technique. 5) Release toward the thumb. 6) Lower base in bear hugs. 7) Shrimp/bridge-and-roll purpose. 8) Goal — escape and get help. 9) Personal safety plan elements — routes, trusted contacts, phone location sharing and emergency SOS, meeting places. 10) Report incidents to a trusted adult/police.

weeks.prep: Get pickleball paddles and outdoor balls; find a court (many parks have them) or chalk a court on a driveway (20 × 44 ft, with a 7-ft non-volley zone on each side of the net; a portable net or rope at 34 inches in the middle). Read the USA Pickleball rules summary.
misconceptions: Students volley while standing in the kitchen. You may not volley (hit before the bounce) while touching the non-volley zone, including the line, or by momentum after the shot.
Students volley the return of serve or the third shot. The two-bounce rule: the serve and the return must each bounce before being hit.
Students think either team can score on any rally. In traditional scoring only the serving team scores.

days.guide: Teach the rules and scoring; walk the court and call sample scores.

questions.q: What is the two-bounce rule?
questions.a: The serve must bounce before the receiver returns it, and the return must bounce before the serving team hits it; after that, volleys are allowed.

questions.q: Why does a doubles game start at 0-0-2?
questions.a: Only one player on the first serving team serves at the start, so the game begins as if that team were on its second server.

days.guide: Practice the underhand serve and deep return, 50 each, aiming at targets.

questions.q: Why aim the return deep?
questions.a: It keeps the serving team back at the baseline, giving you time to move to the kitchen line.

days.guide: Practice cross-court dink rallies from the kitchen line.

questions.q: What is a dink?
questions.a: A soft shot from near the kitchen line that arcs over the net and lands in the opponent's kitchen.

days.guide: Practice punch volleys at the kitchen line with a short, firm motion.

questions.q: Can your foot touch the kitchen line when you volley?
questions.a: No — that's a fault.

days.guide: Play doubles games and self-assess on the skill checklist.

questions.q: Who can score points in traditional pickleball scoring?
questions.a: Only the serving team.

weeks.assessment_key: Skill checklist: underhand serve (paddle moving upward, contact below the waist, ball lands in the diagonal service court) 7/10; deep return 7/10; cross-court dink rally of 10+; punch volley at the kitchen line with compact swing; knows scoring and calls the three-number score in doubles. Rules key: games to 11, win by 2; doubles score 'server score – receiver score – server number (1 or 2)'; first serve of the game starts at '0-0-2'; kitchen = 7 ft non-volley zone; faults include ball out, into the net, volleying in the kitchen, violating the two-bounce rule.

weeks.prep: Get racquets (badminton or tennis), shuttlecocks or tennis balls, a flat wall, and a footwork ladder (or chalk one). Learn the basic grips: badminton forehand ('shake hands') and backhand (thumb on the flat side of the grip); tennis eastern or semi-western forehand.
misconceptions: Students hit with a stiff wrist and arm only. Power comes from the legs, hip and shoulder rotation, then the forearm.
Students stand facing the net on forehands and backhands. Turn sideways (shoulder to the net) to swing through.
Students stop moving after hitting. Recover to the base position after every shot.

days.guide: Teach grips; the student hits 100 forehands against a wall.

questions.q: Which part of the body starts a powerful forehand?
questions.a: The legs and hips rotate first, then the shoulders and arm.

days.guide: Teach backhand technique (one- or two-handed); practice against a wall.

questions.q: Why turn your shoulders before a backhand?
questions.a: To load the body for a full swing and keep the racquet face square.

days.guide: Practice overhead clears and smashes (badminton) or serves/overheads (tennis).

questions.q: What is a badminton clear?
questions.a: A high, deep shot to the opponent's back court that buys time.

days.guide: Lead footwork ladder drills (in-in-out-out, lateral shuffles, crossover steps).

questions.q: Why practice footwork?
questions.a: Getting to the shuttle/ball early and balanced makes every stroke better.

days.guide: Rally for consistency and record the longest rally.

questions.q: Name one adjustment to improve rally length.
questions.a: Hit at medium pace toward the center, keep eyes on the ball, and reset to ready position.

weeks.assessment_key: Rally count: record longest cooperative rally (wall or partner). Benchmarks — beginning: under 10; developing: 10–24; proficient: 25+. Technique checklist: correct grip, side-on stance, swing from low to high (tennis) or high contact (badminton clear), follow-through, recovery to base.

weeks.prep: Racquets and balls/shuttles; a pro match clip (pickleball or badminton) and a shot-charting sheet.
misconceptions: Students hit everything hard. Shot selection (placement, depth, angle) wins more points than power.
Students in doubles both chase the same ball. Communicate ('mine', 'yours') and use a formation.
Students stay where they hit. Recover to the base position (center of the possible returns).

days.guide: Teach singles base position and the cross-court/down-the-line pattern to move the opponent.

questions.q: Why hit cross-court first?
questions.a: Cross-court travels over the lower part of the net with more court length, so it's safer and pulls the opponent wide, opening the down-the-line space.

days.guide: Teach up-and-back (attack) vs. side-by-side (defense) badminton doubles formations and switching on a lob.

questions.q: When do badminton doubles partners switch to side-by-side?
questions.a: When defending, e.g., after hitting a lift/clear, to cover the court against smashes.

days.guide: Watch a pro clip and chart 20 shots by type and placement.

questions.q: What pattern did you see most often?
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers cite counts from the chart.

days.guide: Play three games, each with one strategy goal; tally points won with it.

questions.q: Why set one strategy goal per game?
questions.a: To isolate which tactic works by measuring its results.

days.guide: The student writes which strategy worked best using tally data.

questions.q: What makes a conclusion convincing?
questions.a: Specific numbers from your tallies plus a reason the strategy worked.

weeks.assessment_key: Match analysis rubric: 4 = charts 20 shots by type and placement correctly; tallies points won using each strategy goal across three games; concludes which strategy worked best using numbers (e.g., 'cross-court then down-the-line won 7 of 10 points'); explains why. 3 = data present, reasoning weak. 2 = incomplete data. 1 = opinion only.

weeks.prep: Book courts or set up the driveway court; recruit players (family, friends, co-op) for a round robin; print a bracket and a sportsmanship self-assessment.
misconceptions: Students argue line calls. In recreational play, each player calls their own side; if in doubt, the ball is in.
Students forget the score in doubles pickleball. Call the score before every serve.
Students see officiating as passive. Officials must know rules, signal clearly and stay neutral.

days.guide: Warm up with a skill circuit: 20 serves, 20 dinks/drops, 20 volleys.

questions.q: Why practice a skill circuit before a match?
questions.a: It warms up the specific movements and builds confidence in each shot.

days.guide: Run a round-robin pickleball doubles event rotating partners.

questions.q: In a round robin, how is the winner usually decided?
questions.a: By most games won (then point differential).

days.guide: Play badminton or tennis matches in a short bracket.

questions.q: How is a badminton game scored?
questions.a: Rally scoring to 21, win by 2 (capped at 30).

days.guide: The student officiates one match, calling score, faults and line calls.

questions.q: A pickleball volley is hit while a player's foot is on the kitchen line. What's the call?
questions.a: Fault — a kitchen (non-volley zone) violation.

days.guide: Give the skill test and sportsmanship self-assessment.

questions.q: Name two behaviors of good sportsmanship.
questions.a: Fair line calls, shaking hands, encouraging others, accepting results gracefully.

weeks.assessment_key: Net-sports skill test: 10 serves (in-court) — 8+ proficient; 10 dinks or drop shots into the kitchen/short zone — 7+; 10 volleys/returns over the net and in — 8+; correct score calls. Sportsmanship self-assessment: rates handshake, fair calls, encouragement, calm after errors.

weeks.prep: Gather resistance bands, dumbbells or water jugs (1 gal ≈ 8.3 lb), a sturdy chair, and a training log. Review correct form videos for squat, hip hinge (deadlift), push, pull (row) and carry.
misconceptions: Students round the back in hinges. Keep a neutral spine: push hips back, chest proud, weight in heels.
Students train only 'mirror muscles' (chest, biceps). Balance antagonist pairs (push/pull, quads/hamstrings) to prevent imbalance and injury.
Students increase weight before form is solid. Progress when all reps of all sets are done with good form (e.g., 2 extra reps on the last set).

days.guide: Teach the five patterns with bodyweight or light load; check form with the student watching a video of themselves.

questions.q: What are the cues for a safe squat?
questions.a: Feet shoulder-width, chest up, hips back and down, knees tracking over toes, heels down, neutral spine.

days.guide: Upper-body band workout: rows, presses, face pulls, curls, triceps extensions; 3 × 10–12.

questions.q: What are the antagonist muscles to the biceps?
questions.a: The triceps.

days.guide: Lower-body workout: goblet squats, reverse lunges, Romanian deadlifts with jugs, glute bridges, calf raises.

questions.q: Which muscles does a Romanian deadlift mainly work?
questions.a: Hamstrings and glutes (and spinal erectors).

days.guide: Core circuit: dead bugs, side planks, bird dogs, Pallof press with band.

questions.q: What is the main job of the core in lifting?
questions.a: Stabilizing the spine and transferring force between upper and lower body.

days.guide: The student logs weights and reps and writes next week's progression.

questions.q: What is progressive overload?
questions.a: Gradually increasing the demand (reps, load or sets) so the body keeps adapting.

weeks.assessment_key: Training log: full credit for exercises, sets, reps, load and RPE recorded for each session, and a progression plan (e.g., add 1–2 reps per set or ~5% load when 3 × 12 is completed with good form).
