Key concepts: strength (heavier, 3–6 reps), hypertrophy/endurance (8–15 reps), progressive overload, rest 48 hours for the same muscle group, antagonist pairs (biceps/triceps, quads/hamstrings, chest/back).

weeks.prep: Food log and water log sheets, MyPlate Plan for an active teen, a sleep tracker (paper or app).
misconceptions: Students think sports drinks are always better than water. For most workouts under an hour, water is enough.
Students think teens can thrive on 6 hours of sleep. Teens need 8–10 hours; sleep is when muscles recover and memories consolidate.
Students skip post-workout eating. A carbohydrate-plus-protein snack within a couple of hours aids recovery.

days.guide: The student logs food and water for two days.

questions.q: Name the three macronutrients.
questions.a: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

days.guide: The student compares intake to MyPlate recommendations for active teens.

questions.q: Which macronutrient is the body's main fuel for intense exercise?
questions.a: Carbohydrates.

days.guide: Complete a 40-minute cardio session with hydration checks every 15 minutes.

questions.q: How can you tell if you're dehydrated?
questions.a: Thirst, dark urine, headache, fatigue, dizziness.

days.guide: Track sleep and relate it to energy and performance.

questions.q: How much sleep do teens need?
questions.a: 8–10 hours per night.

days.guide: The student writes a recovery plan.

questions.q: What's a good post-workout snack?
questions.a: Chocolate milk, yogurt with fruit, or a turkey sandwich — carbohydrates plus protein.

weeks.assessment_key: Food and sleep analysis rubric: 4 = two-day food/water log compared to MyPlate (fruit, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy) with specific gaps identified; hydration estimate; sleep tracked for a week with average hours and patterns related to energy and performance; recovery plan with sleep target (8–10 h), hydration, nutrition timing and rest days. 3 = complete but general. 2 = missing comparison. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Set up the same testing equipment and conditions as Week 1. Print the baseline log for comparison. Build the semester written exam from Units 1–5 keys.
misconceptions: Students compare raw scores without considering test conditions. Note weather, time of day and effort.
Students feel discouraged by small gains. Any improvement toward or within the HFZ is progress.
Students revise plans by adding more of everything. Target the specific weakest component.

days.guide: Retest PACER or mile under the same conditions as Week 1.

questions.q: PACER went from 32 to 40 laps. What's the percent change?

days.guide: Retest push-ups and curl-ups with cadence.

questions.q: Why use the same cadence and form standards as before?
questions.a: So results are comparable and changes reflect fitness, not test differences.

days.guide: Retest sit-and-reach and trunk lift.

questions.q: Name one way to improve sit-and-reach.
questions.a: Regular hamstring and lower-back stretching after workouts.

days.guide: Give the semester written exam.

questions.q: Calculate target HR at 70% for a 16-year-old with resting HR 60.

days.guide: The student compares results and revises the fitness plan.

questions.q: If curl-ups improved but push-ups didn't, how might you revise the plan?
questions.a: Add or progress upper-body pushing work (push-up variations 3×/week) while maintaining core work.

weeks.assessment_key: Retest log: full credit for all tests repeated with the same protocol and percent change calculated: (new − old) ÷ old × 100 (e.g., PACER 32 → 40 laps = +25%). Written exam key (sample): FITT; Karvonen calculation; SMART goal; Ten Essentials; LNT principles; compass bearing steps; color codes; breakfall technique; pickleball two-bounce rule and kitchen; badminton scoring; progressive overload; antagonist pairs; teen sleep 8–10 h; 60 min daily activity.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball, 10 cones, tape for targets on a wall or fence or a goal, timer. Find a park field.
misconceptions: Students look down at the ball the whole time. Use quick glances at the ball and head up to see space.
Students pass with the toe. Use the inside of the foot for accurate short passes, ankle locked.
Students shoot with the toe. Use the laces (instep) with toe pointed down and plant foot beside the ball.

days.guide: Dribble a 10-cone slalom with inside/outside touches; time three runs.

questions.q: Which parts of the foot should you use to dribble?
questions.a: Inside, outside and sole — small, frequent touches with both feet.

days.guide: 100 wall passes with each foot, focusing on inside-foot technique and first touch.

questions.q: Where should your plant foot point when passing?
questions.a: At the target, beside the ball.

days.guide: 30 instep shots at taped targets, recording accuracy.

questions.q: Why keep your knee over the ball when shooting?
questions.a: It keeps the shot low and on target.

days.guide: Play 2v2 or 3v3 games to small goals for 30 minutes.

questions.q: Why use small-sided games?
questions.a: More touches and decisions per player.

days.guide: Give the skill test.

questions.q: What makes a good first touch?
questions.a: It cushions the ball and moves it into space away from pressure, ready for the next action.

weeks.assessment_key: Skill test: slalom time (record best of three); 20 passes to a 2-yard target from 10 yards — 14+ proficient; 10 shots on goal (instep) — 6+ on target proficient. Technique checklist: close control with both feet, inside-foot passing with locked ankle, first touch out of feet into space, instep shooting with plant foot beside the ball.

weeks.prep: Ball, cones, a field diagram sheet, and a professional goal clip.
misconceptions: Students all chase the ball ('beehive soccer'). Attackers create width and depth; defenders keep shape.
Students dive in on defense. The first defender delays and contains (pressure) while teammates cover and balance.
Students think a through ball is any long kick. It's a pass into space behind the defense for a teammate running onto it.

days.guide: Teach width, depth and penetration; play a 3v1 rondo.

questions.q: Why do attackers spread wide?
questions.a: It stretches the defense, creating gaps to pass through.

days.guide: Teach pressure–cover–balance; practice 2v2 defending.

questions.q: What does the second defender (cover) do?
questions.a: Positions behind and to the side of the first defender to stop a dribble or pass through.

days.guide: The student diagrams a professional goal sequence.

questions.q: What's a give-and-go?
questions.a: A pass to a teammate followed by a run into space to receive the return pass.

days.guide: Play small-sided games with bonus points for a give-and-go or through ball.

questions.q: When is a through ball the right choice?
questions.a: When a teammate is making a run behind the defense and there's space to pass into.

days.guide: The student reflects on which team role suits them and why.

questions.q: What does a 'connector' player do?
questions.a: Links defense and attack by receiving, keeping possession and distributing passes.

weeks.assessment_key: Tactical diagram rubric: 4 = diagram of a goal sequence with player positions, movement arrows, passes (dashed) and dribbles (wavy), labels for width, depth and penetration, and a sentence explaining why the attack succeeded; plus a defensive diagram showing pressure, cover and balance. 3 = mostly accurate. 2 = incomplete labels. 1 = minimal.

weeks.prep: Get a flying disc (and a football if doing the spiral pass), cones for a field (end zones). Note: today's throwing day names the spiral pass or handball jump shot; if focusing on ultimate, teach the backhand and forehand (flick) throws too. Print play cards and the Spirit of the Game scoring sheet.
misconceptions: Students run with the disc. In ultimate, the thrower must establish a pivot foot and may not run.
Students flick the disc with a big arm swing. Disc throws rely on a snap of the wrist with a flat, level release.
Students argue calls. Ultimate is self-officiated; players resolve disputes respectfully (Spirit of the Game).

days.guide: Practice the spiral pass (or handball jump shot) and/or disc backhand and flick, 50 reps at 10, 15 and 20 yards; catch with 'diamond' hands (thumbs and index fingers forming a diamond) for high balls.

questions.q: Where should a thrower aim a pass to a running teammate?
questions.a: Ahead of them into the space they're running toward (lead the receiver).

days.guide: Draw three offensive plays (slant-flat, curl, post) with routes and timing.

questions.q: What does a 'curl' route do?
questions.a: The receiver runs downfield then turns back toward the thrower to create separation.

days.guide: Practice man-to-man vs. zone coverage with a partner, switching every 5 minutes.

questions.q: What's the difference between man-to-man and zone defense?
questions.a: Man-to-man: each defender guards one player. Zone: each defender guards an area.

days.guide: Play 3-on-3 or 4-on-4 games running your plays and tracking completions.

questions.q: What's the stall count in ultimate?
questions.a: The marker counts to 10; if the disc isn't thrown before 'ten', it's a turnover.

days.guide: The student writes a paragraph comparing space-creation strategy in soccer, ultimate and flag football.

questions.q: What principle do all three sports share in attack?
questions.a: Spreading out and making cutting runs to create open space for passes.

weeks.assessment_key: Spirit score: rate 0–4 in rules knowledge, fouls and body contact, fair-mindedness, attitude and self-control, communication. Skills: backhand and flick completions at 10/15/20 yards (7 of 10 at 10 yards proficient), pancake/two-hand catches, pivoting, marking with a stall count to 10, running routes from the play card. Rules key: 7 players a side (fewer at home); score by catching in the end zone; turnover if the disc is dropped, intercepted, out of bounds, or not thrown before stall 10; no running with the disc; non-contact; self-officiated.

weeks.prep: Equipment for soccer and ultimate (ball, disc, cones), flags if playing flag football, a timer, a measured 400 m (track or route), and an agility ladder. Build the written test on invasion games.
misconceptions: Students drop their team shape during tournament pressure. Remind them of width and pressure–cover before each game.
Students lead warm-ups with only static stretches. Use dynamic, sport-specific moves.
Students pace 400 m repeats too fast at the start. Aim for even splits.

days.guide: Play a small-sided soccer tournament applying width and pressure–cover.

questions.q: When your team wins the ball, what should attackers do?
questions.a: Spread out quickly (width and depth) to offer passing options.

days.guide: Play ultimate games, self-officiating with spirit rules.

questions.q: If you think a foul occurred in ultimate, what do you do?
questions.a: Call 'foul', play stops, discuss calmly; if no agreement, the disc goes back to the last thrower.

days.guide: The student plans and leads a 10-minute dynamic warm-up for the family.

questions.q: What's the order of a good warm-up?
questions.a: General movement to raise heart rate, dynamic stretches, then sport-specific drills that build intensity.

days.guide: Give the written test on invasion games.

questions.q: What's a fast break?
questions.a: A quick transition from defense to attack to score before the defense organizes.

days.guide: Sport-specific conditioning: shuttle runs, agility ladder, 3 × 400 m with 2-minute rests.

questions.q: What energy system do 400 m repeats mainly train?
questions.a: The anaerobic (glycolytic) system, along with aerobic recovery between repeats.

weeks.assessment_key: Written test key (sample): 1) Width, depth, penetration. 2) Pressure, cover, balance. 3) Give-and-go and through ball definitions. 4) Ultimate turnovers — drop, interception, out of bounds, stall 10. 5) Spirit of the Game — self-officiating with respect. 6) No running with the disc; pivot foot. 7) Man vs. zone defense. 8) Fast break — quick transition to attack before the defense sets. 9) Route definitions (slant, flat, curl, post). 10) Offside in soccer — an attacker is offside if nearer to the opponent's goal line than both the ball and the second-to-last defender when the ball is played to them (in the opponent's half). Game-play observation checklist: positioning, decisions, communication, effort, sportsmanship.

weeks.prep: Equipment for soccer and ultimate; observation checklist; written test (reuse a variant of Week 22's).
misconceptions: Students treat assessment games as just play. Share the observation checklist in advance so they know what's being scored.
Students give vague instructions when leading. Leaders demonstrate, use short cues and check understanding.
Students skip cool-down. Include it after every fitness session.

days.guide: Play a soccer tournament; you score the observation checklist.

questions.q: What should the nearest defender do when an opponent receives the ball?
questions.a: Apply pressure quickly but under control — close down, stay on your feet, and delay.

days.guide: Play an ultimate tournament; you score the checklist.

questions.q: What's a 'cut' in ultimate?
questions.a: A sharp run to get open for a pass.

days.guide: The student leads a warm-up for the group.

questions.q: How can a leader check that everyone understands?
questions.a: Demonstrate, have them try it, watch and give quick feedback.

days.guide: Give the written test on rules and strategy.

questions.q: Is a player offside if they are level with the second-to-last defender?
questions.a: No — level is onside.

days.guide: Complete a fitness workout (intervals, strength circuit, cool-down).

questions.q: Why include a cool-down?
questions.a: It gradually lowers heart rate and helps flexibility and recovery.

weeks.assessment_key: Written test: alternate version of Week 22 key (same concepts). Observation checklist (soccer and ultimate): uses width and depth in attack (Y/N), defends with pressure/cover, communicates, makes good pass decisions, follows rules and spirit; 4 = consistently, 3 = usually, 2 = sometimes, 1 = rarely.

weeks.prep: Find videos for a Mexican folklórico zapateado basics tutorial, a salsa basic step tutorial and a line dance (e.g., Cupid Shuffle, Electric Slide or Cha Cha Slide). Clear space; wear supportive shoes (hard-soled shoes for zapateado if available). Heart-rate monitor or pulse checks.
misconceptions: Students think dance isn't real exercise. Track heart rate to show it reaches moderate to vigorous intensity.
Students rush steps off the beat. Count aloud and practice slowly with music at reduced speed.
Students treat cultural dances as costumes. Learn the origin, meaning and respect the traditions.

days.guide: Learn a folklórico zapateado sequence (heel-toe strikes, flat-foot stamps) from video.

questions.q: What is zapateado?
questions.a: Rhythmic footwork of heel, toe and flat-foot strikes used in Mexican folklórico dance.

days.guide: Learn the salsa basic step and a simple turn.

questions.q: How is the salsa basic counted?
questions.a: Step on 1-2-3, pause on 4, step on 5-6-7, pause on 8 ('on 1' style).

days.guide: Learn a line dance.

questions.q: What makes a line dance different from partner dance?
questions.a: Everyone dances the same sequence in lines without partners, usually turning to face a new wall.

days.guide: Track heart rate during dance and compare with the target zone.

questions.q: If your heart rate during salsa was 150 bpm and your zone is 149–177, what intensity is that?
questions.a: Moderate-to-vigorous, at the low end of the target zone.

days.guide: The student performs one dance.

questions.q: Where did salsa develop?
questions.a: In New York City in the 1960s–70s, from Cuban son and other Afro-Caribbean and Latin music styles.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric: 4 = accurate steps, on the beat throughout, smooth transitions, energy and style appropriate to the dance, can explain its cultural origin (folklórico — regional Mexican dances with zapateado footwork; salsa — developed in New York in the 1960s–70s from Cuban son and other Afro-Caribbean styles; line dances — American social dances with repeating patterns). 3 = minor errors. 2 = several timing errors. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Pick a 30-second music-video dance clip for analysis, music for the student's choreography (clean lyrics), a phone on a tripod or stack of books, and a choreography rubric.
misconceptions: Students choreograph without counting. Map moves to eight-counts so the dance repeats reliably and lines up with the music's phrases.
Students use only one level. Include high, middle and low levels and different pathways for interest.
Students judge their performance only by feel. Video review against the beat reveals timing errors.

days.guide: Break down a 30-second dance clip into eight-counts; identify levels, pathways and formations.

questions.q: How many beats are in four eight-counts?

days.guide: The student choreographs a 32-count sequence with at least two levels and one turn.

questions.q: What are the three levels in dance?
questions.a: High (on toes, jumping), middle (standing), low (near or on the floor).

days.guide: Rehearse slowly, then at tempo, fixing transitions.

questions.q: Why rehearse slowly first?
questions.a: To build correct muscle memory and smooth transitions before adding speed.

days.guide: Record a full performance from the front and review timing.

questions.q: How can you check timing on video?
questions.a: Clap or count along with the music while watching to see whether moves land on the beat.

days.guide: The student scores the video and sets two fixes.

questions.q: Write a specific fix.
questions.a: Example: 'Start the turn on count 7 instead of 8 so I finish facing front on 1.'

weeks.assessment_key: Choreography video rubric (4 levels, each scored 1–4): Accuracy (performs the 32 counts as designed), Rhythm (movements land on the beat), Energy/expression, Creativity (uses at least two levels, one turn, varied pathways). Proficient total 12+/16. Self-critique must name two specific fixes with count numbers (e.g., 'arm on count 5 of the second eight is late').

weeks.prep: Find a 30-minute aerobic dance workout video and a Latin-style dance fitness video (Zumba-style). Heart-rate monitor or pulse checks. Prepare the dance rubric and quiz.
misconceptions: Students think low-impact means low intensity. Big arm movements and tempo can still produce vigorous heart rates.
Students teach by doing the dance at full speed. Break it into counts, use cue words and mirror the learner.
Students skip warm-up for dance workouts. Videos usually include one; don't skip it.

days.guide: Complete a 30-minute aerobic dance workout and record peak heart rate.

questions.q: Which fitness component does aerobic dance primarily develop?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance.

days.guide: Complete a Latin-style dance fitness workout and compare RPE to Day 1.

questions.q: Why might RPE differ between the two workouts?
questions.a: Different tempo, movement size and familiarity change perceived effort.

days.guide: The student teaches the 32-count sequence to a family member using counts and cues.

questions.q: What makes a good teaching cue?
questions.a: Short, clear words tied to counts (e.g., 'step-touch, 1-2; turn, 3-4').

days.guide: The student performs polished choreography for an audience.

questions.q: What should you do if you make a mistake during a performance?
questions.a: Keep going, rejoin on the next count, keep your expression.

days.guide: Complete the dance rubric and a short quiz on cultural origins and fitness benefits.

questions.q: Who created Zumba and where?
questions.a: Alberto 'Beto' Pérez, in Colombia, in the 1990s.

weeks.assessment_key: Dance rubric: see Week 25 categories applied to the polished performance. Quiz key: 1) Folklórico — traditional regional Mexican dances, zapateado footwork. 2) Salsa — New York, 1960s–70s, Cuban son roots. 3) Zumba — created in Colombia in the 1990s by Alberto 'Beto' Pérez. 4) Line dance — repeated sequence, facing walls. 5) Dance fitness benefits — cardiorespiratory endurance, coordination, balance, muscular endurance, mood. 6) Eight-count — musical phrase used to structure choreography. 7) RPE moderate ≈ 12–14 (6–20).

weeks.prep: Use thick gymnastics mats or several stacked exercise mats on a soft surface, clear space with no hard edges nearby, and a wall for headstand prep. You serve as spotter; learn spotting positions from a reputable gymnastics video. Skip headstands if the student has neck problems.
misconceptions: Students roll onto the top of their head. Tuck the chin to the chest so the back of the neck and shoulders contact the mat.
Students land jumps with straight legs. Land on the balls of the feet, knees bent and aligned over toes, arms forward for balance.
Students rush to harder skills. Master progressions (log roll → forward roll down an incline → flat forward roll).

days.guide: Teach safe landings, mat setup, spotting roles and progressions.

questions.q: What's the safest landing position from a jump?
questions.a: Feet shoulder-width, knees bent and over toes, hips back, arms forward.

days.guide: Practice forward and backward rolls 10 times each with a spotter, using log-roll progressions as needed.

questions.q: Why tuck the chin in a forward roll?
questions.a: To roll on the back of the neck and shoulders and protect the head and neck.

days.guide: Practice tripod balance, wall headstand prep and partner balances.

questions.q: What shape do your hands and head make in a tripod balance?
questions.a: A triangle, giving a wide base of support.

days.guide: Explain base of support and center of gravity with diagrams; test with a gentle push test in narrow vs. wide stance.

questions.q: Why is a wide, low stance harder to push over?
questions.a: The base of support is larger and the center of gravity lower, so it must be pushed farther before it moves outside the base.

days.guide: The student demonstrates a roll, a balance and a jump; score with the checklist.

questions.q: When does a balance fail, in terms of physics?
questions.a: When the center of gravity moves outside the base of support.

weeks.assessment_key: Skill checklist: forward roll (hands shoulder-width, chin tucked, rounded back, rises to feet without hands), backward roll (or progression), tripod balance held 5 seconds, wall headstand prep held 5 seconds with control, jump with safe landing (bent knees, arms forward, stick 2 seconds). Proficient = all correct with control. Concept: balance improves with a wide base of support and low center of gravity, with the center of gravity over the base.

weeks.prep: Mats, a yoga flow video (sun salutations A and B, warrior series), measuring box or yardstick for sit-and-reach, timer, phone for filming.
misconceptions: Students hold their breath in holds. Breathe steadily; exhale during effort.
Students force stretches. Move to mild tension, never pain.
Students design routines as a list of tricks. Transitions should flow smoothly between elements.

days.guide: Complete a 30-minute yoga flow focused on breath.

questions.q: Name two benefits of yoga for athletes.
questions.a: Improved flexibility and mobility, balance, core strength and relaxation/recovery.

days.guide: Do a hip, shoulder and ankle mobility routine and re-measure sit-and-reach.

questions.q: What's the difference between flexibility and mobility?
questions.a: Flexibility is how far a muscle can lengthen; mobility is active, controlled movement through a joint's range.

days.guide: Practice planks, L-sit prep and hollow holds for max time, 3 rounds each.

questions.q: What type of muscle contraction is a plank?
questions.a: Isometric — the muscle produces force without changing length.

days.guide: The student designs a six-element floor routine linking rolls, balances and a jump.

questions.q: How can you make a transition smooth?
questions.a: End one element in a position that naturally begins the next (e.g., finish a roll in a squat that rises into a balance).

days.guide: Practice the routine five times and film the last attempt.

questions.q: Why film practice?
questions.a: It shows form and timing errors you can't feel.

weeks.assessment_key: Routine draft: six elements (e.g., forward roll, tripod balance, log roll, V-sit or L-sit prep, arabesque or scale balance, straddle jump) with planned transitions, written order, and the filmed fifth attempt. Proficient = all six elements, smooth transitions, held balances 3 seconds, safe landings.

weeks.prep: Mats, the filmed routine, an audience, a routine rubric, and the written test on tumbling safety, spotting and biomechanics.
misconceptions: Students skip the start and finish poses. They frame the routine and show control.
Students say balance is 'just practice'. Explain it with base of support and center of gravity.
Students think only gymnasts need body control. It transfers to almost every sport.

days.guide: Refine weak elements using video feedback.

questions.q: What is one way to fix a wobbly balance?
questions.a: Engage the core, widen the base if allowed, fix the eyes on a point, and shift the center of gravity over the support.

days.guide: Perform the routine for an audience with a clear start and finish pose.

questions.q: Why hold the finish pose?
questions.a: It shows control and signals the end to judges/audience.

days.guide: The student analyzes the video explaining base of support and center of gravity in each balance.

questions.q: In a scale (arabesque) balance, what's the base of support?
questions.a: The standing foot; the body must keep its center of gravity over that foot.

days.guide: Give the written test.

questions.q: What should a spotter do during a forward roll progression?
questions.a: Kneel beside the performer and guide the hips and shoulders, helping them keep the chin tucked and roll straight.

days.guide: The student writes about which body-control skills transfer to other sports.

questions.q: Give an example of transfer.
questions.a: Safe falling helps in soccer and volleyball; core strength and balance help in climbing and martial arts.

weeks.assessment_key: Routine rubric: Execution (form, control) 1–4; Flow (transitions) 1–4; Difficulty/variety (rolls, balances, jump) 1–4; Presentation (start/finish pose, confidence) 1–4; proficient 12+/16. Written test key: 1) Spotter's role — support and guide, not throw. 2) Mat setup — no gaps, clear space. 3) Chin tucked in rolls. 4) Landing — bent knees. 5) Center of gravity must stay over the base of support. 6) Wider base + lower center = more stable. 7) Isometric hold definition. 8) Progressions — learn easier versions first.

weeks.prep: Volleyball (or a softer trainer ball), a wall, a net or rope tied about 7 ft 4 in (girls' height) to 7 ft 11 in (men's) — a lower rope is fine for practice — and target zones taped or marked.
misconceptions: Students swing their arms for a forearm pass. Keep a flat, still platform and move the legs to aim.
Students set with palms. Use finger pads in a triangle/window shape above the forehead.
Students hit the ball twice in a row. A player can't contact the ball twice consecutively (except after a block).

days.guide: Pass against a wall 100 times using a flat platform, then pass to a partner.

questions.q: How do you aim a forearm pass?
questions.a: Angle the platform toward the target and move your feet to face it; don't swing the arms.

days.guide: Practice overhead setting to a target 10 feet high, 50 reps.

questions.q: Where should you contact the ball when setting?
questions.a: Just above the forehead, with finger pads, then extend arms and legs.

days.guide: Practice underhand and overhand serves into target zones.

questions.q: What makes an overhand float serve 'float'?
questions.a: Hitting the center of the ball with a firm, flat hand and no spin.

days.guide: Play 2-on-2 or 3-on-3 with a rope net, requiring three touches.

questions.q: What's the maximum number of team contacts before the ball must cross the net?
questions.a: Three (a block doesn't count as one).

days.guide: Give the skill test.

questions.q: What's the ideal three-touch sequence?
questions.a: Pass (bump), set, attack (hit).

weeks.assessment_key: Skill test: 10 forearm passes to a target (7+ proficient), 10 sets to a 10-foot height and target (7+), 10 serves into target zones (6+). Technique: ready position, platform angle toward target, set from forehead with extension of arms and legs, serve with consistent toss and firm contact.

weeks.prep: Court diagram, volleyball, net/rope. Players: as many as available.
misconceptions: Students rotate the wrong way. Rotate clockwise when your team wins the serve back (side-out).
Students think rotation positions stay fixed during the rally. Players must be in rotational order at the serve, then may switch.
Students stay silent. Calling 'mine' early prevents collisions and dropped balls.

days.guide: Teach the 6-player rotation and positions on a court diagram.

questions.q: Which position serves?
questions.a: Position 1, right back.

questions.q: Which direction do players rotate?
questions.a: Clockwise.

days.guide: Practice pass-set-hit adding an attack approach (left-right-left for right-handers).

questions.q: What's the footwork for a right-handed attack approach?
questions.a: Left, right, left (last two quick), then jump off both feet.

days.guide: Practice calling 'mine' and 'out' in a seam-ball drill.

questions.q: Why call the ball early?
questions.a: It tells teammates who's taking it, preventing collisions and balls dropping between players.

days.guide: Play games tracking successful three-touch sequences.

questions.q: How is volleyball scored?
questions.a: Rally scoring: a point on every rally; sets to 25, win by 2.

days.guide: The student reflects on how communication affected success.

questions.q: Give an example of communication improving play.
questions.a: Calling 'out' on a long serve so the passer lets it go, winning the point.

weeks.assessment_key: Observation rubric: rotation correct (Y/N), uses pass-set-hit sequence (count successful sequences), communicates ('mine', 'out', 'free'), covers hitter. Rules key: positions 1 (right back, server), 2 (right front), 3 (middle front), 4 (left front), 5 (left back), 6 (middle back); rotate clockwise on side-out; rally scoring to 25, win by 2 (deciding set to 15).

weeks.prep: Basketball, a hoop (driveway or park), cones for a dribble course, a partner for pick and roll.
misconceptions: Students shoot with the elbow out. BEEF: Balance, Eyes on the target, Elbow under the ball, Follow-through.
Students set picks while moving. A legal screen is set stationary, feet shoulder-width.
Students dribble with the palm. Use finger pads, keep the ball low and eyes up.

days.guide: Practice BEEF form shooting from five spots, 10 shots each, recording percentages.

questions.q: What does BEEF stand for?
questions.a: Balance, Eyes, Elbow, Follow-through.

days.guide: Ball-handling series: crossovers, between the legs, two-ball dribbling.

questions.q: Why keep your eyes up while dribbling?
questions.a: To see teammates, defenders and open space.

days.guide: Learn and practice the pick and roll with a partner.

questions.q: What makes a screen legal?
questions.a: The screener is stationary with feet about shoulder-width, not moving into the defender.

days.guide: Play 3-on-3 half-court games applying pick and roll and help defense.

questions.q: What is help defense?
questions.a: A defender leaves their player briefly to stop a ball handler driving to the basket, then recovers.

days.guide: Give the skill test.

questions.q: Which foot do you jump off for a right-handed layup?
questions.a: The left foot (step right-left, jump off the left, shoot with the right hand).

weeks.assessment_key: Skill test: layups — 5 attempts each hand (4/5 proficient); free throws — 10 attempts (5+ proficient); dribble course time (record, both hands required). Pick-and-roll concept: screener sets a stationary screen on the ball handler's defender, then rolls to the basket; ball handler reads the defense — drive, pull-up, or pass to the roller.

weeks.prep: Practice plan template, equipment for volleyball or basketball, a whistle, and officiating signal charts (USA Volleyball and NFHS basketball). Build the written test.
misconceptions: Students plan practices that are mostly scrimmage. Include warm-up, skill drills with clear goals and a cool-down.
Students give feedback only on errors. Use specific praise plus one correction.
Students hesitate when officiating. Decide, signal clearly, and keep the game moving.

days.guide: The student writes a 45-minute practice plan.

questions.q: What should come first in a practice plan?
questions.a: A dynamic warm-up.

days.guide: The student leads the practice for siblings or friends.

questions.q: Give an example of specific feedback.
questions.a: 'Great platform — now step toward the target as you pass.'

days.guide: The student officiates a game using correct signals.

questions.q: What's the basketball signal for traveling?
questions.a: Rolling the fists around each other in front of the body.

days.guide: Give the written test.

questions.q: In basketball, what is a double dribble?
questions.a: Dribbling with both hands at once, or stopping the dribble and starting again.

days.guide: The student reflects on leadership strengths and one area to improve.

questions.q: What's one quality of an effective team leader?
questions.a: Communicates clearly, stays positive, includes everyone, models effort.

weeks.assessment_key: Leadership rubric (4 levels): Planning (45-min plan with warm-up, 2–3 drills with objectives, scrimmage, cool-down), Instruction (clear demonstration and cues), Feedback (specific, positive + corrective), Management (safety, time, everyone active), Officiating (correct calls and signals). Written test key: volleyball — rotation, rally scoring to 25, three contacts, positions; basketball — traveling, double dribble, fouls, shot clock basics, three seconds in the lane, pick and roll, zone vs. man defense, fast break.

weeks.prep: Lifetime activity list, local parks and recreation catalog, YMCA and club schedules, a 12-week plan template.
misconceptions: Students pick activities based only on popularity. Choose ones they enjoy and can access affordably.
Students write plans with no progression. Each week should change one FITT variable gradually.
Students assume motivation lasts. Plan for barriers ahead of time.

days.guide: The student ranks 15 lifetime activities by enjoyment, cost and access.

questions.q: What makes an activity 'lifetime'?
questions.a: You can keep doing it as an adult with few people and little equipment (e.g., hiking, cycling, swimming, pickleball, yoga).

days.guide: The student finds three local options with schedules and costs.

questions.q: Name a free community fitness resource.
questions.a: Parks, trails, public courts, library fitness classes, community center open gyms.

days.guide: The student writes a 12-week summer plan with FITT and progression.

questions.q: How much should weekly training volume increase?
questions.a: Gradually — about 10% per week or less.

days.guide: The student identifies barriers and strategies.

questions.q: Strategy for the barrier 'too hot in summer'?
questions.a: Exercise early morning or evening, swim, or work out indoors.

days.guide: The student completes Week 1 Day 1 and logs it.

questions.q: What should a log record?
questions.a: Date, activity, duration, intensity (HR or RPE) and notes.

weeks.assessment_key: Plan rubric: 4 = 12-week plan with FITT details for cardio, strength, flexibility (and balance/skill), clear weekly progression, two or more enjoyable lifetime activities with local access and costs, three barriers with specific strategies, and Week 1 Day 1 completed and logged. 3 = complete but general. 2 = missing components. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Testing equipment from Week 1; baseline and midyear logs; graph paper or spreadsheet.
misconceptions: Students compare only final vs. baseline. Include midyear to see the trend.
Students compute percent change from the new score. Use the original (baseline) as the denominator.
Students set summer goals unrelated to results. Base them on the weakest components.

days.guide: Final PACER or 1-mile run.

questions.q: Mile time improved from 9:30 to 8:24. What's the percent change in time?

days.guide: Final push-up and curl-up tests.

questions.q: Push-ups went from 12 to 20. Percent change?

days.guide: Final sit-and-reach, trunk lift and body composition.

questions.q: Why is body composition only one part of fitness?
questions.a: Fitness also includes aerobic capacity, strength, endurance and flexibility; healthy bodies vary.

days.guide: Graph baseline, midyear and final; calculate percent change.

questions.q: What does a flat line between midyear and final suggest?
questions.a: A plateau; training may need to change (new stimulus or more consistency).

days.guide: The student writes summer goals based on results.

questions.q: Write a SMART summer goal.
questions.a: 'Run 3 times per week and reach 45 PACER laps by August 20.'

weeks.assessment_key: Final test log: full credit for all tests repeated with the same protocols, graphed (baseline, midyear, final), percent change calculated correctly (e.g., push-ups 12 → 20 = +66.7%), HFZ status for each, and summer SMART goals tied to results.

weeks.prep: Review notes, the written final (cumulative: FITT, heart-rate zones, biomechanics, outdoor safety and team strategy), portfolio folder or digital folder, and reflection prompts.
misconceptions: Students cram facts without application. Ask them to apply concepts to their own data.
Students include everything in the portfolio. Curate the best evidence of growth.
Students write reflections that only summarize. Include evidence and future plans.

days.guide: Review FITT, HR zones, biomechanics, outdoor safety and team strategy.

questions.q: Give one example each of a principle from biomechanics and from team strategy.
questions.a: Biomechanics: lower center of gravity increases stability. Strategy: width in attack stretches the defense.

days.guide: Give the written final exam.

questions.q: Calculate the 60% target heart rate for a 16-year-old with RHR 70.

days.guide: The student chooses and leads a favorite activity for the family.

questions.q: What should you explain before starting?
questions.a: Rules, safety and the goal of the activity.

days.guide: The student compiles fitness logs, test results and reflections into a portfolio.

questions.q: Which items best show growth?
questions.a: Baseline vs. final test graphs and logs showing consistent training.

days.guide: The student writes a 300-word reflection on how activity habits changed.

questions.q: What makes a reflection strong?
questions.a: Specific data, honest challenges and concrete plans.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam key (sample): 1) FITT. 2) Karvonen for given age/RHR. 3) SMART goal. 4) Ten Essentials. 5) LNT principles. 6) Naismith's rule. 7) Color codes of awareness. 8) Pickleball kitchen and two-bounce rule. 9) Pressure–cover–balance. 10) Center of gravity and base of support. 11) Volleyball rotation (clockwise; position 1 serves). 12) BEEF. 13) Progressive overload. 14) 60 minutes daily activity. 15) Teen sleep 8–10 h. Portfolio rubric: logs, test graphs, plans, and reflection; 300-word reflection cites specific data.

SCI.overview: Chemistry in the Earth System runs about 60 minutes a day: a short explanation or demonstration, a hands-on investigation or PhET simulation, then practice problems and a written explanation. Insist on units and significant figures in every calculation, balanced equations, and claim-evidence-reasoning writing; supervise all flames, heat and chemicals and require goggles. The burning-candle phenomenon from Week 1 threads through the year, so keep the driving-question board visible and revisit it at the end of each unit.

weeks.prep: Gather a kitchen scale, measuring cups, a thermometer, safety goggles and a notebook to use as a lab notebook all year. Locate the home fire extinguisher and print or write a simple safety contract (goggles on, long hair tied back, no eating in lab, adult present for flames, know where water and the extinguisher are). Preview Khan Academy 'significant figures' and 'scientific notation' videos.
misconceptions: Students think more digits always means more accurate. Distinguish precision (how close repeated measurements are) from accuracy (how close to the true value), and show that a calculator answer cannot be more precise than the least precise measurement.

Trailing and leading zeros confuse students (counting 0.0045 as 4 significant figures). Teach the rules: leading zeros never count, captive zeros always count, trailing zeros count only if there is a decimal point.
Students drop units mid-calculation. Require every number in a dimensional-analysis setup to carry its unit and cancel units visibly.

days.guide: Walk through the safety contract line by line and have the student sign it. Tour the 'lab' (kitchen) together, physically locating the extinguisher, water source and first-aid kit. Then read five hazard scenarios aloud and have the student name the hazard and the correct action for each.

questions.q: A student heats a liquid in a sealed jar. What is the hazard?
questions.a: Pressure builds as the liquid and air heat and the jar can burst; never heat a closed container.

questions.q: Why do we wear goggles even when only mixing vinegar and baking soda?
questions.a: Any splash can reach the eyes, and even mild acids or bases can injure eyes; goggles are worn whenever chemicals or flames are used.

days.guide: Model reading a scale and a thermometer to one estimated digit beyond the smallest marking. The student measures the mass, volume and temperature of the same water sample three times, records all trials, and computes the mean and percent error = |measured − accepted| ÷ accepted × 100. Check that units are recorded on every number.

questions.q: Three volume readings are 99, 101 and 100 mL for a 100.0 mL sample. What is the mean and the percent error?
questions.a: Mean = 100 mL; percent error = 0%. The readings are both precise (close together) and accurate.

questions.q: Readings of 92.1, 92.0 and 92.2 g for a 100.0 g mass are precise or accurate?
questions.a: Precise but not accurate: they agree closely with each other but are about 8% off the true value, which suggests a systematic error such as an untared scale.

days.guide: Teach the significant-figure rules with examples on a whiteboard, then the rules for calculations (multiply/divide: fewest sig figs; add/subtract: fewest decimal places). The student completes the 20 problems using his or her own measurement data, showing the rounding step. Check five problems together before the rest.

questions.q: How many significant figures are in 0.02030?
questions.a: 4 (the leading zeros do not count; the 2, 0, 3 and trailing 0 after the decimal do).

questions.q: Calculate the density of a 25.3 g sample with a volume of 12 mL, with correct sig figs.
questions.a: 25.3 ÷ 12 = 2.108… → 2.1 g/mL (2 sig figs, limited by 12 mL).

questions.q: Write 6,020,000 in scientific notation with 3 significant figures.

days.guide: Light a candle (adult supervision, goggles, hair tied back) and have the student observe silently for five minutes, recording at least 10 observations. Then the student writes 10 questions, including 'Where does the wax go?', on sticky notes and starts a driving-question board that will be revisited all year. Do not answer the questions yet.

questions.q: Is the burning of a candle a physical change, a chemical change, or both?
questions.a: Both: wax melting is a physical change, while wax vapor burning to form carbon dioxide and water is a chemical change.

questions.q: What evidence suggests that the candle is getting lighter?
questions.a: The candle gets shorter over time and wax does not pile up underneath it; the matter is leaving as invisible gases.

days.guide: Give the quiz closed-book (calculator allowed) and grade it together immediately, having the student correct each missed item in a different color. Collect the measurement lab sheet and check it against the key.

questions.q: Convert 450 mg to grams.
Why do scientists use SI units?
questions.a: So measurements are consistent and comparable worldwide; SI units are based on powers of ten, which makes conversions easy.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Name two items of PPE for a home lab — safety goggles and closed-toe shoes or gloves/apron. 2) What to do if clothing catches fire — stop, drop and roll (or smother with a blanket); never run. 3) Sig figs in 0.00450 — 3. 4) Sig figs in 3.040 — 4. 5) Write 0.000365 in scientific notation — 3.65 × 10⁻⁴. 6) 4.56 × 1.4 = 6.4 (2 sig figs). 7) 12.11 + 18.0 + 1.013 = 31.1 (round to the tenths place). 8) Convert 2.5 L to mL — 2.5 × 10³ mL (2500 mL). 9) Convert 65 mi/h to m/s (1 mi = 1609 m) — 65 × 1609 ÷ 3600 = 29 m/s. 10) A student measures 98.5 g for a 100.0 g standard; percent error — |98.5 − 100.0| ÷ 100.0 × 100 = 1.5%. Lab sheet: full credit when all three trials are recorded with units, the mean is correct, and percent error is calculated with the formula shown. 9–10 = mastery; 7–8 = review sig-fig rules; below 7 = reteach.

weeks.prep: Gather tea lights, three glass jars of different sizes, a metal spoon, pickling lime (calcium hydroxide) to make limewater (stir 1 tsp into 1 cup water, let settle, pour off the clear liquid), a straw, fine steel wool (0000), a 9-volt battery, a baking tray and the kitchen scale. Have water and the fire extinguisher nearby. Preview a video of steel wool burning so you know what to expect (it sparks).
misconceptions: Students believe matter is destroyed when something burns. Emphasize that atoms are rearranged into invisible gases (CO₂ and H₂O), and show that steel wool actually gains mass because it combines with oxygen.
Students think the candle flame goes out under a jar because the jar 'runs out of air'. Clarify that it runs low on oxygen specifically; nitrogen, which is most of the air, remains.
Students confuse the wick with the fuel. The wick only carries melted wax upward; the wax vapor is what burns.

days.guide: Light identical tea lights and cover each with a jar of a different size at the same moment; time how long each burns. Measure each jar's volume by filling it with water and pouring into a measuring cup, then graph jar volume (x) vs. burn time (y). Ask the student to explain the trend.

questions.q: Predict what happens to burn time if the jar volume doubles.
questions.a: Burn time roughly doubles, because the jar holds about twice as much oxygen for the flame to use.

questions.q: What reactant from the air does the candle need?
questions.a: Oxygen (O₂).

days.guide: Hold a cool metal spoon briefly above (not in) the flame and observe droplets; then collect candle exhaust in an inverted jar and shake with limewater. Compare with limewater the student has blown into through a straw. Discuss what both cloudy results show.

questions.q: What forms on the cool spoon and where did it come from?
questions.a: Water droplets; hydrogen atoms in the wax combined with oxygen to make water vapor, which condensed on the cool spoon. (Black soot may also appear from incomplete combustion.)

questions.q: Why does limewater turn cloudy?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O.

days.guide: Fluff a pad of steel wool, weigh it on a foil-lined tray, then touch the 9-V battery terminals to it (adult present, goggles, over the tray, nothing flammable nearby). After it cools, reweigh it, including any fallen bits. The student explains why mass increased.

questions.q: The steel wool weighed 5.20 g before and 5.45 g after burning. Explain.
questions.a: Mass increased by 0.25 g because iron atoms combined with oxygen atoms from the air to form iron oxide; the added mass is the oxygen.

questions.q: Write a balanced equation for iron reacting with oxygen to form iron(III) oxide.
questions.a: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃

days.guide: Model drawing methane (one C with four H) and oxygen molecules as circles, then rearranging the same atoms into products. The student draws before/after particle diagrams, writes the word equation and the balanced symbol equation, and counts atoms of each element on both sides.

questions.q: Write the balanced equation for methane combustion.
questions.a: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

questions.q: Count the oxygen atoms on each side of that equation.
questions.a: Left: 2 × 2 = 4. Right: 2 (in CO₂) + 2 (in 2H₂O) = 4. Balanced.

days.guide: Review the claim-evidence-reasoning structure with a model paragraph on a different topic. The student writes the CER paragraph explaining where the candle's mass goes, citing this week's data. Score with the rubric and have the student revise one weak part.

questions.q: What is the difference between evidence and reasoning in a CER?
questions.a: Evidence is the data or observations; reasoning is the scientific principle that explains why the evidence supports the claim (here, conservation of atoms in a chemical reaction).

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric (4 points each for claim, evidence, reasoning): 4 = Claim states that the candle's mass goes into the air as carbon dioxide and water vapor (gases). Evidence cites at least two observations: water condensing on the cool spoon, limewater turning cloudy with candle gases, the candle getting shorter/lighter, and the flame going out sooner under smaller jars (oxygen is a reactant). Reasoning explains that atoms are conserved — carbon and hydrogen atoms from wax combine with oxygen from air to form CO₂ and H₂O, so mass is not destroyed but leaves as gas; the steel wool gaining mass shows that combustion adds oxygen atoms. 3 = correct claim with one piece of evidence and partial reasoning. 2 = claim with evidence but no atomic reasoning. 1 = claim only or incorrect claim (e.g., 'mass is destroyed').

weeks.prep: Gather an empty soda can, a paperclip bent into a stand, a cork or clay base, a ring stand or stack of books with a pencil to hang the can, a thermometer, a 100 mL measuring cup, cheese puffs, cashews (check for nut allergies — use another snack if needed), matches, a lighter, a scale reading to 0.01 g if possible, and nutrition labels. Prepare a fire-safe surface. Look up the California Energy Commission's 'Total System Electric Generation' page for Day 4.
misconceptions: Students mix up the food Calorie (capital C, = 1 kilocalorie) and the calorie. Show that a 100 Calorie snack contains 100,000 calories, or about 418 kJ.

Students think heat and temperature are the same. Heat (q, in joules) is energy transferred; temperature measures average particle kinetic energy. The same heat raises a small mass of water more than a large one.

Students expect their calorimeter result to match the label. Most of the heat escapes to the air and can, so home calorimeters typically capture well under half of the label value; this is the error to analyze, not a mistake.

days.guide: Teach the conversions 1 cal = 4.184 J and 1 food Calorie = 1 kcal = 4184 J. Model one label conversion, then have the student convert three snack labels to kJ per serving and kJ per gram. Check that the student multiplies, not divides, when going from Calories to joules.

questions.q: A granola bar has 190 Calories. How many kilojoules is that?
How many calories (small c) are in one food Calorie?
questions.a: 1000 calories.

days.guide: Build the calorimeter: hang the can with 100 mL (100 g) of water above a food sample stuck on a paperclip stand. Record the water's starting temperature and the food's mass, ignite the food, let it burn out, stir and record the highest temperature, then reweigh the remains. Repeat with the cashew.

questions.q: Why do we measure the food mass both before and after burning?
questions.a: To find the mass that actually burned; energy per gram uses only the mass consumed.

questions.q: Why use water as the substance being heated?
questions.a: Its specific heat (4.184 J/g·°C) is known and it is easy to measure, so the energy absorbed can be calculated from its temperature change.

days.guide: Write q = mcΔT on the board and model it with the student's cheese-puff data. The student calculates energy per gram for both foods, converts the label value to J/g, computes percent error, and lists reasons the measured value is low.

questions.q: 100.0 g of water warms from 21.0 °C to 39.0 °C. How much heat did it absorb?
A cashew lost 0.60 g while releasing 7530 J to the water. What is the measured energy per gram?
questions.a: 7530 ÷ 0.60 = 12,550 J/g ≈ 13 kJ/g (about 3.0 Cal/g); the label value is about 23 kJ/g, so much heat was lost.

questions.q: Give one way to reduce the error.
questions.a: Shield the flame and can from drafts (e.g., a foil chimney), put the can closer to the flame, or use a lid to reduce heat lost to the air.

days.guide: Have the student find California's current electricity sources on the California Energy Commission site and record the top sources (natural gas, solar, wind, hydro, nuclear, etc.). Then compare energy per gram of fuels in a table and discuss why hydrogen is energy-dense by mass but hard to store.

questions.q: Rank gasoline, natural gas (methane) and hydrogen by energy released per gram.
questions.a: Hydrogen (~120–142 kJ/g) > natural gas (~50–55 kJ/g) > gasoline (~46 kJ/g).

questions.q: What product does hydrogen combustion make, and why does that matter for climate?
questions.a: Only water (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O), so burning it produces no CO₂; however, how the hydrogen is produced can still create emissions.

days.guide: Give the five-question energy quiz with a calculator and formula sheet (q = mcΔT, c of water = 4.184 J/g·°C, 1 Cal = 4.184 kJ). Grade together and file corrections in the lab notebook.

questions.q: How much energy is needed to warm 250 g of water by 4.0 °C?

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric (4 levels): 4 = Data table with mass of food before/after, water mass, initial/final temperatures; q = mcΔT calculated correctly for both foods (e.g., 100 g × 4.184 J/g·°C × 18.0 °C = 7530 J); energy per gram = q ÷ mass burned; comparison to label (label kJ/g = Calories per serving × 4.184 ÷ grams per serving); percent error; at least two specific error sources (heat lost to air and can, incomplete burning, soot) with a suggested improvement (shield, lid, closer can). 3 = correct calculations with general error analysis. 2 = calculation errors or missing comparison. 1 = incomplete data. Friday quiz key: 1) 500 Cal = 2092 kJ. 2) 200 g water warmed 20 °C → 45 °C: q = 200 × 4.184 × 25 = 20,900 J (20.9 kJ). 3) 1.20 g of food heats 50.0 g water by 30.0 °C: q = 6276 J; 6276 ÷ 1.20 = 5230 J/g (5.23 kJ/g, about 1.25 Cal/g). 4) 4184 J added to 100 g water: ΔT = 4184 ÷ (100 × 4.184) = 10.0 °C. 5) Which has more energy per gram, gasoline or hydrogen? Hydrogen (~120–142 kJ/g vs. ~46 kJ/g).

weeks.prep: Have a calculator, a periodic table, and the family's recent gas/utility bill and an estimate of weekly car miles and the car's mpg. Open the California Air Resources Board GHG inventory page and a spreadsheet. Print the Unit 1 test you make from the key below.
misconceptions: Students assume 1 gallon of gasoline (about 2.8 kg) cannot produce more than 2.8 kg of CO₂. Show that each carbon atom picks up two oxygen atoms from the air, so the CO₂ mass is about three times the fuel mass.
Students confuse criteria and constraints. Criteria are what a good solution should achieve (cut CO₂, affordable); constraints are hard limits it must work within (budget, existing cars, laws).
Students think 'carbon footprint' counts only driving. Include home heating, electricity and goods.

days.guide: Model the calculation: a gallon of gasoline is about 2.80 kg; treat gasoline as octane, C₈H₁₈ (114.2 g/mol). Moles of octane = 2800 ÷ 114.2 = 24.5 mol; each makes 8 CO₂, so 196 mol CO₂ × 44.0 g/mol ≈ 8.6 kg. The student repeats the reasoning for a 10-gallon tank.

questions.q: How many kg of CO₂ are produced by burning a 10-gallon tank?
questions.a: About 86 kg (10 × 8.6 kg; EPA's figure of 8.89 kg/gal gives 89 kg).

questions.q: Write the balanced equation for octane combustion.
questions.a: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O

days.guide: Help the student gather the family's weekly miles, mpg and natural-gas use (therms). Weekly car CO₂ = miles ÷ mpg × 8.89 kg; natural gas ≈ 5.3 kg CO₂ per therm. The student builds a small spreadsheet and identifies the largest source.

questions.q: A family drives 200 miles a week in a 25-mpg car. How much CO₂ is that?
questions.a: 200 ÷ 25 = 8 gallons × 8.89 kg ≈ 71 kg CO₂ per week.

questions.q: A household uses 10 therms of natural gas in a week. Estimate the CO₂.

days.guide: Define criteria and constraints with examples. The student builds a table for a cleaner transportation fuel (criteria: lower CO₂ per mile, cost per mile, energy density, safety; constraints: existing infrastructure, budget, state law, vehicle range) and ranks the importance of each.

questions.q: Is 'must work in existing gas stations' a criterion or a constraint?
questions.a: A constraint — it is a limit the solution must operate within.

questions.q: Give one criterion for a cleaner fuel.
questions.a: For example: produces less CO₂ per mile than gasoline (or costs no more per mile).

days.guide: Pull out the Week 1 candle questions. The student redraws the candle model, now adding particle diagrams for wax + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O and energy release, and marks which driving questions are answered. Discuss what remains unknown.

questions.q: Using what you know now, where does the energy of the candle flame come from?
questions.a: From the chemical potential energy stored in the bonds of wax and oxygen; forming the stronger bonds in CO₂ and H₂O releases more energy than is needed to break the reactant bonds.

questions.q: Why does the flame need the wick to start?
questions.a: The wick holds melted wax so it can vaporize; wax burns as a vapor, and the wick's flame provides heat to melt and vaporize more wax.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test in one sitting (allow 50 minutes). Grade with the key, then have the student redo missed problems and explain one in writing.

questions.q: Balance: C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O.
questions.a: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test key (sample items): 1) Balance C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. 2) Products of complete hydrocarbon combustion: CO₂ and H₂O. 3) Steel wool gains mass when burned because oxygen atoms bond to iron. 4) 150 g water warmed by 12.0 °C absorbs q = 150 × 4.184 × 12.0 = 7530 J. 5) 300 Cal = 1255 kJ. 6) Sig figs in 0.0500 — 3. 7) 7.21 × 0.32 = 2.3. 8) Burning 1 gal gasoline (2.80 kg, modeled as C₈H₁₈) makes about 8.6 kg CO₂ (EPA uses 8.89 kg). 9) Define criteria vs. constraint (see misconception). 10) Short answer: why the candle went out sooner in a small jar — less oxygen available. Score 1 point each (item 10: 2 points); 90%+ mastery, 70–89% targeted review, below 70% reteach.

weeks.prep: Open PhET 'Build an Atom' and test it. Gather marbles, a large piece of cardboard propped on books, and a hidden shape cut from cardboard (triangle or circle). For 'beanium' gather three kinds of dried beans (e.g., 20 pinto, 15 kidney, 5 lima) and the kitchen scale. Have a periodic table.
misconceptions: Students think the mass number is on the periodic table. The decimal number shown is the average atomic mass; the mass number (protons + neutrons) is a whole number for one isotope.
Students think isotopes of an element have different numbers of protons. Isotopes have the same protons (same element) but different neutrons.
Students treat ions as changes in protons. Ions form by gaining or losing electrons; the number of protons never changes in a chemical reaction.

days.guide: Have the student research each scientist and make an illustrated timeline: Dalton (c. 1803, solid indivisible spheres), Thomson (1897 discovered the electron; plum-pudding model), Rutherford (1911 gold foil; nucleus), Bohr (1913 electrons in fixed energy levels), Schrödinger/quantum model (1920s electron cloud/orbitals). For each, note the evidence that changed the model.

questions.q: What evidence led Thomson to propose that atoms contain smaller particles?
questions.a: Cathode-ray experiments showed beams of negatively charged particles much lighter than any atom, deflected by electric and magnetic fields — electrons.

questions.q: What was wrong with the plum-pudding model?
questions.a: It predicted alpha particles would pass straight through gold foil; Rutherford found a few bounced back, showing charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

days.guide: Hide a shape under the cardboard without letting the student see it. The student rolls marbles under it from many directions, marks where each enters and exits, and infers the shape. Connect: Rutherford never saw the nucleus either; he inferred it from deflections.

questions.q: In Rutherford's experiment, what did it mean that most alpha particles went straight through?
questions.a: The atom is mostly empty space.

questions.q: How is the marble activity like the gold-foil experiment?
questions.a: Both use the paths of projectiles to infer the size and shape of something that cannot be seen directly.

days.guide: In PhET Build an Atom, the student builds H, He, C, O and Na, then makes ions (e.g., O²⁻, Na⁺) and records protons, neutrons, electrons, charge and mass number in a table. Ask what determines the element's identity.

questions.q: An atom has 8 protons, 8 neutrons and 10 electrons. What is it?
questions.a: An oxide ion, O²⁻ (oxygen-16 with a 2− charge).

questions.q: What determines which element an atom is?
questions.a: The number of protons (atomic number).

days.guide: Sort the beans by type, count each type and weigh each group. Model the weighted average: (fraction of type A × average mass of A) + … The student calculates the atomic mass of beanium and explains why it is not simply the average of the three masses.

questions.q: Chlorine is about 75% Cl-35 and 25% Cl-37. Estimate its average atomic mass.
Why is boron's average atomic mass (10.81) closer to 11 than to 10?
questions.a: Boron-11 is much more abundant (about 80%) than boron-10.

days.guide: Give the 10-item quiz and grade it together; collect the beanium lab sheet. Have the student redo missed isotope calculations.

questions.q: How many neutrons are in uranium-238 (Z = 92)?
questions.a: 238 − 92 = 146 neutrons.

weeks.assessment_key: Beanium lab: full credit if mass of each bean type, count, percent abundance, and weighted average are correct. Example: 20 beans at 0.50 g, 15 at 0.80 g, 5 at 1.20 g (40 beans) → abundances 50%, 37.5%, 12.5%; average = 0.50(0.50) + 0.375(0.80) + 0.125(1.20) = 0.70 g. Quiz key: 1) Protons, neutrons, electrons in ⁵⁶Fe: 26, 30, 26. 2) Electrons in Na⁺: 10. 3) Electrons in O²⁻: 10. 4) Why most alpha particles passed through gold foil — atoms are mostly empty space. 5) Why some bounced back — a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus. 6) Define isotope — atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. 7) Copper: 69.15% ⁶³Cu (62.93 u) and 30.85% ⁶⁵Cu (64.93 u); average = 63.55 u. 8) Order the models Dalton → Thomson → Rutherford → Bohr → quantum (electron cloud). 9) Mass number of an atom with 17 protons and 20 neutrons — 37 (chlorine-37). 10) Which subatomic particle has almost no mass — the electron.

weeks.prep: Build the spectroscope ahead with the student: a cereal box, an old CD (or DVD) as the diffraction grating, a narrow slit cut from foil, and tape (search 'CD spectroscope cereal box' for a template). Find incandescent, LED and fluorescent light sources at home. Queue a flame-test demonstration video and PhET 'Models of the Hydrogen Atom'. Print a blank periodic table.
misconceptions: Students think the color in a flame test comes from the flame itself. The colored light comes from electrons in the metal ions dropping from excited energy levels to lower levels.
Students fill 3d before 4s or forget the order. Use the diagonal (Aufbau) chart: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p.
Students count all electrons as valence electrons. Valence electrons are in the outermost s and p sublevels (main-group elements: the group number's ones digit, e.g., Cl has 7).

days.guide: Assemble the spectroscope and have the student look at a bright incandescent bulb, a white LED, and a fluorescent tube or CFL (never look at the Sun). The student sketches each spectrum with colored pencils and describes the differences.

questions.q: Which light source shows a continuous spectrum, and which shows bright lines?
questions.a: Incandescent shows a continuous spectrum (a hot glowing filament); fluorescent shows bright lines from excited mercury atoms.

questions.q: What does the CD do in the spectroscope?
questions.a: Its closely spaced tracks act as a diffraction grating, spreading light into its component wavelengths.

days.guide: Watch a flame-test video, pausing before each reveal so the student predicts. The student records element and color, then uses a reference table to identify two 'unknown' flame colors you describe.

questions.q: An unknown salt gives a crimson-red flame. Which ions could it contain?
questions.a: Lithium (crimson) or strontium (red).

questions.q: Why are fireworks different colors?
questions.a: Different metal salts are added; each metal's electrons emit characteristic wavelengths when excited (e.g., strontium red, barium green, copper blue, sodium yellow).

days.guide: Use PhET Models of the Hydrogen Atom (Bohr view) to show an electron jumping up when absorbing a photon and dropping down emitting one. Model on paper: a larger drop gives a higher-energy, shorter-wavelength photon. The student explains in writing why spectra act like fingerprints.

questions.q: In hydrogen, does a drop from level 3 to 2 or from level 4 to 2 give the higher-energy photon?
questions.a: 4 → 2, because it is a larger energy difference (it produces blue-green light, 486 nm, versus red, 656 nm, for 3 → 2).

questions.q: Why can't a hydrogen atom emit any color it wants?
questions.a: Electrons can only occupy specific energy levels, so only specific energy differences — specific photon energies — are possible.

days.guide: Teach the Aufbau order and orbital diagrams (boxes with up/down arrows, Hund's rule: fill singly before pairing). The student writes configurations for elements 1–36, using noble gas shorthand after neon, and highlights valence electrons. Point out the exceptions Cr ([Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵) and Cu ([Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰).

questions.q: Write the electron configuration and orbital diagram for nitrogen.
questions.a: 1s² 2s² 2p³; the three 2p electrons each occupy a separate box with parallel spins (Hund's rule).

questions.q: Write the configuration of calcium in noble gas notation.
questions.a: [Ar] 4s²

days.guide: Give the quiz and grade it together. Collect the spectroscope sketches and observation write-up.

questions.q: How many valence electrons does phosphorus have?
questions.a: 5 (3s² 3p³).

weeks.assessment_key: Spectroscope observations: full credit for sketches of each light — incandescent: continuous rainbow; fluorescent: continuous dim background with distinct bright lines (violet, green, yellow-orange lines from mercury); white LED: smooth band strongest in blue and yellow-green with a weak gap — and a sentence explaining continuous vs. line spectra. Quiz key: 1) Configuration of O: 1s² 2s² 2p⁴. 2) Na: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. 3) Fe: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶ ([Ar] 4s² 3d⁶). 4) Br valence electrons: 7. 5) Why each element has a unique spectrum — each has a unique set of energy levels, so the energy differences (photon colors) are unique. 6) Higher-energy photon: violet or red? Violet. 7) Flame color of sodium — yellow-orange; copper — blue-green; strontium/lithium — red. 8) What happens when an electron absorbs energy — it jumps to a higher energy level (excited state). 9) Noble gas notation for K — [Ar] 4s¹. 10) Element with configuration [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁵ — bromine.

weeks.prep: Make 20 element cards (name, symbol, atomic mass, a property such as metal/nonmetal, reactivity, formula of oxide). Gather graph paper or a spreadsheet with atomic radius and first ionization energy data for elements 1–20 (from PubChem or a textbook appendix). Queue an alkali-metals-in-water video (e.g., Royal Institution or Open University).
misconceptions: Students think atoms get bigger across a period because they gain electrons. Across a period, added protons increase nuclear charge while shielding stays about the same, so electrons are pulled in and the radius shrinks.
Students think metals 'want' to lose electrons. Atoms do not have wants; lower ionization energy means the outer electron is held less tightly and is removed more easily.
Students reverse ionization energy and radius trends. Remind them that they are inverse: small atoms hold electrons tightly (high IE).

days.guide: Shuffle the element cards. The student sorts them into groups by similar properties, then by increasing atomic mass, and explains the arrangement. Tell how Mendeleev (1869) left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties.

questions.q: Why was Mendeleev's table convincing to other scientists?
questions.a: He predicted properties of undiscovered elements (e.g., 'eka-silicon' = germanium) that were later found to match closely.

questions.q: Today the table is ordered by what instead of atomic mass?
questions.a: Atomic number (number of protons), which fixes cases like tellurium/iodine.

days.guide: The student plots atomic radius and first ionization energy versus atomic number (1–20) and describes repeating patterns. Prompt: where are the peaks and valleys?

questions.q: Which elements are at the peaks of the ionization energy graph?
questions.a: Noble gases: He, Ne, Ar.

questions.q: What happens to atomic radius going from Li to Ne?
questions.a: It decreases.

days.guide: Draw Bohr-style shells for Na and Cl side by side. Explain effective nuclear charge (protons minus inner shielding electrons) and shielding. The student writes explanations for each trend using these two ideas.

questions.q: Explain why K is larger than Na.
questions.a: K has an additional occupied electron shell (4 vs. 3), so its outer electron is farther from the nucleus, even though K has more protons.

questions.q: Why is the first ionization energy of F greater than that of Li?
questions.a: F has a much larger effective nuclear charge pulling on electrons in the same shell, so its electrons are held more tightly.

days.guide: Before showing the video, the student predicts the reaction of Li, Na and K with water, then watches and checks. Write the equation for sodium and connect reactivity to ionization energy.

questions.q: Write the balanced equation for sodium and water.
questions.a: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂

questions.q: Predict how cesium reacts compared with potassium.
questions.a: More violently: cesium's outer electron is farther from the nucleus and easier to remove.

days.guide: Give the 10-question quiz and grade it together. Collect the graphs.

questions.q: Which has a larger radius, Mg or Mg²⁺?
questions.a: Mg — losing the two 3s electrons removes the outer shell, so Mg²⁺ is smaller.

weeks.assessment_key: Graphs: full credit for correctly plotted radius and ionization energy vs. atomic number for Z = 1–20, axes labeled with units (pm, kJ/mol), and written patterns: IE peaks at noble gases (He, Ne, Ar) and drops sharply at alkali metals (Li, Na, K); radius peaks at alkali metals and decreases across each period. Quiz key: 1) Larger atom: Na or Cl? Na. 2) Larger atom: Li or K? K. 3) Higher first ionization energy: Mg or Ba? Mg. 4) Most electronegative element: fluorine. 5) More reactive: Na or K? K, its outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded. 6) Explain the radius decrease across period 3 — more protons (greater effective nuclear charge) with the same number of shells/shielding. 7) Why does IE jump from Na to Ne? Ne has a full shell with electrons close to the nucleus; Na's lone 3s electron is far away and shielded. 8) Group 17 name — halogens; Group 18 — noble gases. 9) Mendeleev left gaps — he predicted undiscovered elements such as gallium and germanium. 10) Rank by electronegativity: Na < C < O.

weeks.prep: Gather 100 pennies (or M&Ms), a shoebox with a lid, graph paper. Review the nuclear symbols (mass number on top, atomic number on bottom). Read a short overview of Diablo Canyon Power Plant (PG&E) and fusion (ITER or the 2022 National Ignition Facility result at Lawrence Livermore, California).
misconceptions: Students think half-life means the sample is gone after two half-lives. After each half-life, half of what remains decays: 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5%.
Students think radioactive decay is a chemical reaction. Decay changes the nucleus (it can change the element); chemical reactions involve only electrons.
Students mix up fission (splitting heavy nuclei) and fusion (joining light nuclei). Use 'fusion = fuse together'.

days.guide: Teach nuclear notation and the three decay types: alpha (emits ⁴₂He, mass −4, atomic number −2), beta (a neutron becomes a proton, emits an electron, atomic number +1), gamma (high-energy photon, no change). Model two equations and have the student balance five more by checking that top and bottom numbers add up.

questions.q: Complete: ²³⁸₉₂U → ? + ⁴₂He
questions.a: ²³⁴₉₀Th (thorium-234).

questions.q: Complete: ¹³¹₅₃I → ? + ⁰₋₁e
questions.a: ¹³¹₅₄Xe (xenon-131).

days.guide: Put 100 pennies in the box, shake, remove all heads (they 'decayed'), and record the count. Repeat until none remain. The student graphs shakes vs. pennies remaining and finds the half-life from the graph.

questions.q: Starting with 100 pennies, about how many remain after 3 shakes?
Can you predict exactly which penny will 'decay' next?
questions.a: No; decay is random for individual nuclei, but predictable for large numbers.

days.guide: Model: number of half-lives = time ÷ half-life, and fraction left = (1/2)ⁿ. Work a C-14 and a U-238 example together, then the student solves six problems.

questions.q: A wooden tool has 12.5% of its original C-14. How old is it?
questions.a: 12.5% = (1/2)³, so 3 half-lives × 5,730 yr = 17,190 years.

questions.q: Why isn't C-14 used to date dinosaur bones?
questions.a: Dinosaurs died over 66 million years ago; after ~50,000 years almost no C-14 remains. Longer-lived isotopes in surrounding volcanic rock (e.g., U-238, K-40) are used instead.

days.guide: Compare fission and fusion in a T-chart: fuel, products, where it happens (Diablo Canyon reactor splits U-235; the Sun fuses hydrogen), waste, and energy source. Work an E = mc² example.

questions.q: How much energy is released if 1.0 g (0.0010 kg) of mass is converted to energy?
Give one advantage and one challenge of fission power.
questions.a: Advantage: no CO₂ emissions during operation. Challenge: long-lived radioactive waste and safety concerns.

days.guide: Give the quiz with a periodic table. Grade together and collect the half-life graph.

questions.q: Polonium-210 has a half-life of 138 days. What fraction remains after 276 days?
questions.a: One quarter (two half-lives).

weeks.assessment_key: Lab: full credit for a data table of remaining pennies each shake, a graph with a smooth decay curve, and a half-life of about 1 shake (half remain each round). Quiz key: 1) Alpha decay of radium-226: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He. 2) Beta decay of thorium-234: ²³⁴₉₀Th → ²³⁴₉₁Pa + ⁰₋₁e. 3) Beta decay of carbon-14: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e. 4) Gamma radiation changes neither mass number nor atomic number. 5) 80 g of iodine-131 (half-life 8 days) after 24 days: 10 g. 6) A bone has 25% of its original C-14 (half-life 5,730 yr): age 11,460 years. 7) A rock has half its original U-238 (half-life 4.5 billion yr): about 4.5 billion years old. 8) Most penetrating radiation: gamma; least: alpha. 9) Fission splits a heavy nucleus such as U-235; fusion joins light nuclei such as hydrogen into helium. 10) Source of energy in both: a small amount of mass converted to energy (E = mc²).

weeks.prep: Bookmark NASA's 'Star Life Cycle' and 'The Sun' pages and print a periodic table color-coded by origin (search 'Jennifer Johnson nucleosynthesis periodic table' by NASA/SDSS) to check the student's version. Gather colored pencils.
misconceptions: Students think stars 'burn' like fire. Stars release energy through nuclear fusion, not chemical combustion; there is no oxygen burning.

Students think all elements are made in supernovae. Hydrogen and helium come from the Big Bang; carbon and nitrogen largely come from dying low-mass stars; elements up to iron form by fusion in massive stars; many heavy elements like gold come from neutron-star mergers.
Students think the Sun will become a black hole. The Sun is too small; it will become a red giant, then a white dwarf.

days.guide: Model the proton-proton chain simply: four hydrogen nuclei (protons) eventually fuse into one helium-4 nucleus, releasing positrons, neutrinos and energy. The products have about 0.7% less mass than the reactants; that mass becomes energy (E = mc²). The student draws a flow diagram.

questions.q: Four hydrogen atoms have a mass of 4.0313 u; one helium-4 atom is 4.0026 u. What fraction of the mass is converted to energy?
Why does fusion require the extreme temperature of the Sun's core (~15 million K)?
questions.a: Nuclei are positively charged and repel; only at very high speeds (temperature) and pressure can they get close enough for the strong force to fuse them.

days.guide: Using NASA resources, the student draws two branching paths: a Sun-like star (nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf) and a massive star (… → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole). Label what fuses in each stage.

questions.q: What determines whether a star ends as a white dwarf or a supernova?
questions.a: Its mass; stars more than about 8 times the Sun's mass end in supernovae.

questions.q: Where is the Sun in its life cycle?
questions.a: On the main sequence, about halfway through its roughly 10-billion-year lifetime.

days.guide: The student color-codes a blank periodic table by origin: Big Bang (H, He, some Li), low-mass dying stars (e.g., C, N, many heavy elements via slow neutron capture such as barium and lead), massive stars and supernovae (O through Fe and others), neutron-star mergers (e.g., gold, platinum), and human-made (Tc, elements beyond U). Compare to the NASA version.

questions.q: Where did the iron in your blood come from?
questions.a: Fusion and supernova explosions of stars (especially massive stars and white-dwarf supernovae).

questions.q: Which two elements were made mainly in the Big Bang?
questions.a: Hydrogen and helium.

days.guide: The student writes the 1-page explainer 'You are made of stardust', using at least three specific elements in the human body (oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, calcium, iron) and their origins. Score with the rubric and have the student revise once.

questions.q: Is the hydrogen in water molecules in your body 'stardust'? Explain.
