questions.a: Not exactly: hydrogen formed in the Big Bang, before stars; most other elements in the body were formed in stars.

questions.q: What evidence tells astronomers which elements are in distant stars?
questions.a: Their absorption/emission spectra — each element produces a unique set of lines.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test (50 minutes) with a periodic table. Grade together and log errors for review.

questions.q: Write the configuration of sulfur and state its valence electrons.
questions.a: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴; 6 valence electrons.

weeks.assessment_key: Explainer rubric (4 levels): 4 = Explains that hydrogen in our bodies formed in the Big Bang, carbon/oxygen/nitrogen formed by fusion in stars and were spread by stellar winds and supernovae, iron is the endpoint of fusion in massive stars, and heavier elements (e.g., gold, iodine) form in supernovae and neutron-star mergers; cites at least two pieces of evidence (stellar spectra showing elements, solar fusion, observed 2017 neutron-star merger GW170817 with heavy-element signatures). Unit 2 test key (sample): 1) ²³⁹₉₄Pu alpha decay → ²³⁵₉₂U + ⁴₂He. 2) Half-lives in 15 days for a 5-day isotope: 3; fraction left 1/8. 3) Fe configuration [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. 4) Larger radius: Ca or Br — Ca. 5) Ions: Mg²⁺ has 12 p, 10 e. 6) Average mass of Ga (60.1% Ga-69 at 68.93; 39.9% Ga-71 at 70.92) = 69.72. 7) The Sun's energy source: fusion of hydrogen into helium. 8) Fate of a star 20× the Sun's mass: supernova, then neutron star or black hole. 9) Why fusion stops at iron: fusing iron absorbs rather than releases energy. 10) Line spectra show which elements are in stars.

weeks.prep: Gather table salt, a magnifier, a jar, string or a pencil for crystal growth, and parts for a conductivity tester: a 9-V battery, an LED, two insulated wires (or alligator clips), and tape. Prepare distilled or tap water, sugar and salt. Make a polyatomic ion reference card (nitrate NO₃⁻, sulfate SO₄²⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, hydroxide OH⁻, phosphate PO₄³⁻, ammonium NH₄⁺, acetate C₂H₃O₂⁻).
misconceptions: Students write NaCl as a molecule. Ionic compounds are lattices of alternating ions; the formula shows the simplest ratio (a formula unit).
Students forget parentheses for multiple polyatomic ions, writing CaNO₃₂. Polyatomic ions stay intact: Ca(NO₃)₂.
Students think solid salt conducts because it is made of ions. Ions must be free to move (dissolved or melted) to conduct.

days.guide: Model Lewis dot diagrams for Na and Cl, then draw an arrow showing the electron transfer and the resulting ions in brackets with charges. The student repeats for MgO and CaCl₂, checking that total charge is zero.

questions.q: Show electron transfer in CaCl₂.
questions.a: Ca (2 valence electrons) gives one electron to each of two Cl atoms → Ca²⁺ and 2 Cl⁻; charges total zero.

questions.q: Why does sodium form Na⁺ rather than Na⁻?
questions.a: Na has one valence electron that is easily lost (low ionization energy), leaving a stable neon-like configuration.

days.guide: Teach the criss-cross method and naming rules (metal name + nonmetal ending in -ide; polyatomic names unchanged; Roman numerals for transition metals). The student writes and names 30 compounds; check the first five together.

questions.q: Write the formula for aluminum sulfate.
questions.a: Al₂(SO₄)₃

questions.q: Name Cu₂O.
questions.a: Copper(I) oxide.

days.guide: Dissolve salt in hot water until no more dissolves (saturated). Pour into a shallow dish and leave a few days (or hang a string). Examine crystals with a magnifier and sketch their cubic shape. Relate the shape to the lattice.

questions.q: Why do salt crystals form cubes?
questions.a: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions stack in a repeating cubic lattice; the visible crystal reflects that arrangement.

questions.q: What makes a solution 'saturated'?
questions.a: It holds the maximum dissolved solute at that temperature; extra solute will not dissolve.

days.guide: Build the tester: battery to LED to one probe; second probe from the battery's other terminal (adult checks LED polarity). Test dry salt, salt water, sugar water and plain water, recording brightness. The student explains each result.

questions.q: Why does salt water light the LED but sugar water does not?
questions.a: Salt dissociates into mobile Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that carry charge; sugar dissolves as neutral molecules.

questions.q: Predict whether melted salt would conduct.
questions.a: Yes — in the liquid state the ions can move.

days.guide: Give the 10-item quiz with the polyatomic ion card allowed. Grade together and collect the conductivity data table.

questions.q: Write the formula for sodium hydroxide and for barium hydroxide.
questions.a: NaOH; Ba(OH)₂.

weeks.assessment_key: Conductivity table: dry salt — LED off (ions locked in a lattice); salt water — LED on (mobile ions); sugar water — LED off (molecules, no ions); tap water — dim or off. Quiz key: 1) Formula of magnesium chloride — MgCl₂. 2) Aluminum oxide — Al₂O₃. 3) Calcium nitrate — Ca(NO₃)₂. 4) Ammonium sulfate — (NH₄)₂SO₄. 5) Name Na₂CO₃ — sodium carbonate. 6) Name Fe₂O₃ — iron(III) oxide. 7) Name K₃PO₄ — potassium phosphate. 8) Lewis diagram of MgO: Mg transfers 2 electrons to O, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻. 9) Why ionic compounds have high melting points — strong electrostatic attractions among many ions in a lattice. 10) Name CuSO₄ — copper(II) sulfate.

weeks.prep: Gather gumdrops (two or three colors) and toothpicks, a plastic comb, and a faucet that can make a thin steady stream. Open PhET 'Molecule Shapes' and test it. Make an electronegativity reference (H 2.2, C 2.6, N 3.0, O 3.4, Cl 3.2).
misconceptions: Students draw CO₂ as bent like water. Carbon in CO₂ has no lone pairs and two double bonds, so it is linear (180°).
Students think any molecule with polar bonds is polar. A symmetric shape (CO₂, CH₄) cancels bond dipoles, making the molecule nonpolar.
Students forget lone pairs when predicting shape. Lone pairs repel more strongly and squeeze bond angles (109.5° → 107° in NH₃ → 104.5° in H₂O).

days.guide: Model the steps: count valence electrons, place the least electronegative atom (not H) in the center, connect with single bonds, complete octets, and form multiple bonds if electrons run short. The student draws H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, NH₃, O₂ and N₂ and checks electron totals.

questions.q: How many valence electrons are in CO₂, and what is its Lewis structure?
questions.a: 16 (4 + 6 + 6); O=C=O with two lone pairs on each oxygen.

questions.q: Why does N₂ have a triple bond?
questions.a: Each N has 5 valence electrons (10 total); a triple bond plus one lone pair on each N gives both atoms an octet.

days.guide: Build gumdrop models with toothpicks, using a different color for lone pairs (or leaving a bare toothpick). The student photographs and names each shape.

questions.q: Name the shape of NH₃ and explain why it is not flat.
questions.a: Trigonal pyramidal; the lone pair on nitrogen pushes the three N–H bonds down.

questions.q: What shape is CH₄?
questions.a: Tetrahedral, 109.5°.

days.guide: In PhET Molecule Shapes, the student adds bonds and lone pairs to a central atom and records the electron geometry, molecular shape and bond angle for 2–6 electron domains. Discuss why lone pairs compress angles.

questions.q: A central atom has 4 electron domains: 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. What is the molecular shape?
questions.a: Bent (about 104.5°, like water).

questions.q: A central atom has 3 bonding domains and no lone pairs. Shape and angle?
questions.a: Trigonal planar, 120° (e.g., BF₃).

days.guide: Explain bond polarity using electronegativity differences (O–H is polar because O pulls electrons more). Rub a comb on hair or wool and bring it near a thin water stream; the stream bends. The student classifies the six molecules as polar or nonpolar with reasons.

questions.q: Is CH₄ polar? Explain.
questions.a: No; C–H bonds are only slightly polar and the tetrahedral shape is symmetric, so dipoles cancel.

questions.q: Why is water polar?
questions.a: O–H bonds are polar, and the bent shape means the dipoles do not cancel; oxygen is partially negative and the hydrogens partially positive.

days.guide: Give the quiz, then grade together. Collect model photos.

questions.q: Draw the Lewis structure of HCl and state whether it is polar.
questions.a: H–Cl with three lone pairs on Cl; polar because Cl is more electronegative than H.

weeks.assessment_key: Model photos: full credit for correct shapes of H₂O (bent), CO₂ (linear), CH₄ (tetrahedral), NH₃ (trigonal pyramidal) with labels. Quiz key: 1) Lewis structure of H₂O: O with two single bonds to H and two lone pairs. 2) CO₂: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O. 3) N₂: triple bond, one lone pair on each N. 4) Shape and angle of CH₄: tetrahedral, 109.5°. 5) NH₃: trigonal pyramidal, ~107°. 6) H₂O: bent, ~104.5°. 7) Is CO₂ polar? No — linear and symmetric so dipoles cancel. 8) Is NH₃ polar? Yes. 9) Bond type in O₂: double. 10) Why a water stream bends toward a charged comb: water molecules are polar and their partial charges are attracted to the charged comb.

weeks.prep: Gather pennies, an eyedropper, water, 70% or 91% rubbing alcohol, vegetable oil, paper towels, a thermometer, and a timer. Prepare a boiling-point data table: H₂O 100 °C, H₂S −60 °C, CH₄ −162 °C, ethanol 78 °C; halogens F₂ −188 °C, Cl₂ −34 °C, Br₂ 59 °C, I₂ 184 °C; noble gases He −269, Ne −246, Ar −186, Kr −153 °C. Keep alcohol away from flames.
misconceptions: Students confuse intermolecular forces with covalent bonds. Boiling water separates molecules from each other (breaking hydrogen bonds); it does not break O–H bonds inside molecules.
Students think hydrogen bonds are bonds to any hydrogen. A hydrogen bond is an attraction between H attached to N, O or F and a lone pair on another N, O or F.
Students assume heavier molecules always boil higher. True within a family (London forces grow with size), but hydrogen bonding makes water boil far higher than heavier H₂S.

days.guide: Using the eyedropper, the student adds drops of water one at a time onto a clean, dry penny until it spills, records the count, and repeats with alcohol and oil (cleaning and drying between). Discuss why water forms a tall dome.

questions.q: Which liquid fit the most drops, and why?
questions.a: Water (typically 20–40+ drops), because hydrogen bonding gives it the strongest cohesion and highest surface tension.

questions.q: What would adding a drop of dish soap to the water do?
questions.a: Fewer drops would fit; soap disrupts hydrogen bonding at the surface and lowers surface tension.

days.guide: Wrap a thermometer bulb in a strip of paper towel. Dip in water, record the temperature every 30 seconds for 4 minutes while fanning gently; repeat with alcohol. Also time how long equal wet spots take to evaporate.

questions.q: Which liquid cooled the thermometer more, and why?
questions.a: Rubbing alcohol; it evaporates faster because its intermolecular forces are weaker, and evaporation removes energy from the bulb.

questions.q: Why does sweating cool you?
questions.a: Water molecules with the most energy escape when sweat evaporates, lowering the average kinetic energy (temperature) of what remains on the skin.

days.guide: Introduce the three forces: London dispersion (all molecules, stronger with more electrons), dipole-dipole (polar molecules), and hydrogen bonding (H on N, O, F). The student ranks water, isopropyl alcohol and oil by force strength using two lines of evidence from this week.

questions.q: Rank water, alcohol and oil by surface tension and support with evidence.
questions.a: Water highest (most drops on penny); alcohol and oil lower. Water's extensive hydrogen bonding creates the strongest cohesion.

questions.q: Which force is present in all molecules?
questions.a: London dispersion forces.

days.guide: Give the boiling-point table. The student graphs boiling point vs. molar mass for the noble gases and halogens and explains the trend, then explains why H₂O (18 g/mol) boils at 100 °C while H₂S (34 g/mol) boils at −60 °C.

questions.q: Why does boiling point increase from F₂ to I₂?
questions.a: Larger molecules have more electrons, so London dispersion forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them.

questions.q: Why does water have such a high boiling point for its size?
questions.a: Strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules must be overcome; H₂S has no hydrogen bonding.

days.guide: The student writes the full lab report connecting bulk properties to particle forces. Review it with the rubric and have the student revise the reasoning paragraph.

questions.q: Predict whether glycerin (many O–H groups) would evaporate faster or slower than water.
questions.a: Slower — more hydrogen bonding sites and larger molecules mean stronger attractions.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric (HS-PS1-3), 4 levels: 4 = Question and hypothesis; procedure with controlled variables (same penny, same dropper, same height); data tables (drops on a penny, evaporation time, temperature drop); claim ranking water > alcohol, oil for surface tension and alcohol evaporating faster with larger cooling; reasoning that stronger intermolecular attractions (water's hydrogen bonding) hold molecules together, producing higher surface tension and slower evaporation; error sources (drop size, room air) and a next step. 3 = correct claim and data, reasoning mentions forces but not hydrogen bonding specifically. 2 = data with weak reasoning. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather aluminum foil, white school glue (PVA), borax (or contact-lens saline with boric acid plus baking soda), measuring cups, food coloring, zip bags, an HDPE bag (crinkly grocery bag, recycling code 2) and an LDPE bag (bread or zip bag, code 4), and a ruler. Borax should not be ingested; wash hands after slime.
misconceptions: Students think metals are malleable because metal atoms are soft. Metal cations sit in a sea of mobile electrons; layers can slide without breaking the bonding, unlike ionic crystals that shatter.
Students think slime is a new compound like a reaction product. Borate ions cross-link existing PVA chains with weak, reversible bonds; that is why slime flows slowly yet stretches.
Students think 'plastic' is one material. Different polymers have different chain structures and properties (HDPE vs. LDPE).

days.guide: Model metallic bonding with a diagram of positive ions in a sea of electrons. Bend and fold aluminum foil and compare to tapping a salt crystal (which shatters). The student explains malleability, ductility and conductivity using the model.

questions.q: Why do metals conduct electricity?
questions.a: Their valence electrons are delocalized and free to move through the metal.

questions.q: Why does a salt crystal shatter when hit but a metal bends?
questions.a: Shifting an ionic lattice lines up like charges, which repel and split the crystal; in metals the electron sea keeps holding the ions together as layers slide.

days.guide: Mix ½ cup glue with ½ cup water, then slowly stir in a borax solution (1 tsp borax in 1 cup warm water) until slime forms. The student observes stretch, flow and bounce and draws polymer chains before and after cross-linking.

questions.q: What does borax do to the glue?
questions.a: Borate ions form cross-links between long PVA polymer chains, turning the liquid into a stretchy gel.

questions.q: Predict what adding more borax solution does.
questions.a: More cross-links make the slime stiffer and less stretchy (more rubbery).

days.guide: Cut equal 2 cm × 10 cm strips from an HDPE and an LDPE bag. The student pulls each slowly by hand, measuring how far it stretches before breaking, and compares. Draw linear vs. branched chains.

questions.q: Which bag stretched more, and why?
questions.a: LDPE usually stretches more because its branched chains cannot pack tightly, so they slide past each other; HDPE's linear chains pack tightly, making it stiffer and stronger.

questions.q: What does the 2 in a recycling triangle mean?
questions.a: The item is high-density polyethylene (HDPE).

days.guide: The student researches one designed material using reliable sources and fills a chart: material, molecular structure, property, use, how structure causes property. Check the explanation is at the molecular level, not just 'it is strong'.

questions.q: How does Kevlar's structure explain its strength?
questions.a: Long rigid chains align parallel and are held together by many hydrogen bonds between chains, so it resists pulling apart.

questions.q: Why is nonstick PTFE coating slippery?
questions.a: Its surface is covered with fluorine atoms that are tightly held and have very weak attractions to other molecules.

days.guide: The student presents a 3-minute explanation with a diagram; you ask one question. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: What is the general rule connecting structure and properties of materials?
questions.a: The arrangement of particles and the strength of forces between them determine bulk properties like strength, flexibility, melting point and conductivity.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric (4 levels): 4 = Names the material and its use; describes the molecular structure accurately (e.g., Kevlar: rigid, aligned polyamide chains with hydrogen bonds between chains → high tensile strength; Gore-Tex: expanded PTFE membrane with pores far smaller than liquid water droplets but larger than water vapor molecules → waterproof and breathable; PTFE nonstick: carbon chain shielded by fluorine atoms, very strong C–F bonds and weak surface attractions → nothing sticks); a clear diagram linking structure to function; within 3 minutes; answers one question. 3 = accurate but structure–function link vague. 2 = describes uses with little structure. 1 = inaccurate or incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather uncooked rice, a measuring cup, sugar, salt, water, and the kitchen scale. Make a periodic table available with atomic masses. Write key numbers on a card: 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ particles; molar mass of water 18.02 g/mol, NaCl 58.44 g/mol, sucrose (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) 342.30 g/mol.
misconceptions: Students think a mole is a mass. A mole is a count (6.022 × 10²³); its mass depends on the substance.
Students add atomic masses without multiplying by subscripts (H₂O = 1 + 16 = 17). Multiply each atomic mass by the number of atoms: 2(1.01) + 16.00 = 18.02.
Students flip conversion factors. Set up units so they cancel: grams × (1 mol / g) → mol.

days.guide: Weigh 100 grains of rice, then weigh a full cup. The student calculates the number of grains in the cup without counting, then connects to how chemists count atoms by weighing.

questions.q: 100 rice grains weigh 2.0 g and a cup of rice weighs 185 g. How many grains are in the cup?
Why do chemists count atoms by weighing?
questions.a: Atoms are far too small and numerous to count; if you know the mass of one mole, weighing tells you how many particles you have.

days.guide: Model molar mass: sum (atomic mass × number of atoms). The student calculates 15 molar masses; check H₂O, CO₂, NaCl, C₆H₁₂O₆ and Ca(NO₃)₂ first.

questions.q: Molar mass of CO₂?
Molar mass of Ca(NO₃)₂?
Molar mass of C₆H₁₂O₆?

days.guide: Draw the mole map: grams ⇄ moles (molar mass) ⇄ particles (Avogadro's number). Model two problems with full units, then assign ten.

questions.q: How many moles are in 36.0 g of water?
How many molecules is that?
questions.a: 2.00 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.20 × 10²⁴ molecules.

questions.q: What is the mass of 0.250 mol of NaCl?

days.guide: Weigh out one mole each of sugar (342 g), salt (58.4 g) and water (18.0 g, which is 18 mL) and compare their volumes in measuring cups. Discuss why the same number of particles takes up different amounts of space.

questions.q: Why does a mole of sugar take up far more space than a mole of water?
questions.a: Each sucrose molecule is much larger and heavier (342 g/mol vs. 18 g/mol), so the same number of molecules has more mass and volume.

questions.q: How many molecules are in the 18 mL of water?
questions.a: About 6.02 × 10²³ (one mole).

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test with a periodic table and polyatomic ion card. Grade together and log errors.

questions.q: How many moles of NaCl are in 117 g?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key (sample): 1) NaCl is ionic; CH₄ covalent; Cu metallic. 2) Formula of calcium phosphate — Ca₃(PO₄)₂. 3) Shape of H₂O — bent; polar. 4) Highest boiling point: H₂O, H₂S, CH₄ — H₂O (hydrogen bonding). 5) Molar mass of CaCO₃ — 100.09 g/mol. 6) 36.0 g of H₂O = 2.00 mol = 1.20 × 10²⁴ molecules. 7) Mass of 0.500 mol NaCl — 29.2 g. 8) Moles in 90.0 g glucose (180.16 g/mol) — 0.500 mol. 9) Why salt water conducts but sugar water does not — mobile ions vs. neutral molecules. 10) Why metals are malleable — mobile electron sea allows layers to slide. 11) Molecules in 1.00 g H₂O: 3.34 × 10²² (1.00 ÷ 18.02 × 6.022 × 10²³). Score: 90%+ mastery; reteach mole conversions if items 6–8 are missed.

weeks.prep: Gather clear cups, food coloring, hot (not boiling) and ice-cold water, a timer, a pot, ice, a stove, a thermometer that reads to at least 100 °C (candy or digital probe), and a clock. Open PhET 'States of Matter'. Supervise all stove work.
misconceptions: Students think temperature rises steadily while ice melts. During a phase change, added energy goes into separating particles (potential energy), so temperature stays constant.
Students say 'cold' flows into objects. Heat (energy) always flows from hotter to colder; cold is just less thermal energy.
Students think particles stop moving in solids. Particles in solids vibrate in place; only at absolute zero would motion be minimal.

days.guide: Fill two clear cups, one with hot water and one with cold, let them settle, then add one drop of food coloring to each simultaneously. Time how long until the color is evenly spread. The student explains using particle motion.

questions.q: Why did the color spread faster in hot water?
questions.a: Water molecules in hot water have greater average kinetic energy, so they collide with dye particles more often and harder, spreading them faster.

questions.q: What is temperature, at the particle level?
questions.a: A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles.

days.guide: In PhET States of Matter, the student heats and cools water, argon and oxygen, observing particle motion in each phase and recording what changes at phase transitions.

questions.q: What happens to particle motion when a solid is heated to its melting point?
questions.a: Particles vibrate faster until they break free of fixed positions and slide past each other as a liquid.

questions.q: In the simulation, what happens to particle spacing during boiling?
questions.a: It increases greatly as particles escape into the gas phase.

days.guide: Fill a pot with ice and a little water; record the temperature every minute while heating on medium until it has boiled for 5 minutes (stir gently; adult at the stove). The student graphs temperature vs. time and labels phases.

questions.q: What did the temperature do while ice was still present?
questions.a: Stayed near 0 °C until all the ice melted.

questions.q: Why might your water boil below 100 °C?
questions.a: At higher altitude, air pressure is lower, so water boils at a lower temperature.

days.guide: Use the graph to explain plateaus: during melting and boiling, energy goes into overcoming attractions (raising potential energy) rather than raising kinetic energy. Compare the length of the melting and boiling plateaus.

questions.q: Why is the boiling plateau longer than the melting plateau?
questions.a: Vaporization requires much more energy (2260 J/g) than melting (334 J/g) because molecules must separate completely.

questions.q: Does steam at 100 °C or water at 100 °C cause a worse burn? Why?
questions.a: Steam — it releases its large heat of vaporization as it condenses on skin, in addition to the heat from cooling.

days.guide: Give the quiz and grade together. Collect the heating-curve graph.

questions.q: When you hold an ice cube, which way does heat flow?
questions.a: From your hand into the ice.

weeks.assessment_key: Heating curve graph: full credit for time on x-axis, temperature on y-axis, plotted points, plateau near 0 °C while ice melts, rising section, and plateau near 100 °C (slightly lower at high altitude) while boiling, each section labeled with the phase(s) present. Quiz key: 1) Temperature measures average kinetic energy of particles. 2) Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. 3) Food coloring spreads faster in hot water because particles move faster. 4) Why the temperature is flat at 0 °C — energy breaks attractions between molecules (increasing potential energy), not speeding them up. 5) Thermal equilibrium — two objects in contact reach the same temperature and net heat flow stops. 6) A hot spoon in cool water: heat flows from spoon to water. 7) Which has more thermal energy: a cup of boiling water or a bathtub of warm water? The bathtub (far more particles). 8) Name the phase change at the 100 °C plateau — boiling/vaporization. 9) In which state do particles have the most freedom? Gas. 10) Absolute zero is 0 K (−273.15 °C).

weeks.prep: Gather foam cups with lids (nest two for insulation), a thermometer, metal washers (about 50 g), a pot of boiling water, tongs, a kitchen scale, dry sand, two identical containers and a lamp. Prepare a spreadsheet. Formula card: q = mcΔT; c(water) = 4.184 J/g·°C; heat lost by hot = heat gained by cold.
misconceptions: Students average temperatures without weighting by mass (100 g at 80 °C + 200 g at 20 °C → 50 °C). The final temperature is mass-weighted: 40 °C.
Students think materials with high specific heat get hot quickly. High specific heat means more energy is needed per degree, so water warms and cools slowly.
Students forget that ΔT is final minus initial and get sign errors. Use magnitudes and the idea 'heat lost = heat gained'.

days.guide: The student predicts the final temperature of 100 g of 70 °C water mixed with 100 g of 20 °C water, then tests it in a lidded foam cup. Repeat with unequal masses. Compare predictions and measurements.

questions.q: Predict the final temperature when 100 g of water at 70 °C mixes with 100 g at 20 °C.
questions.a: 45 °C (equal masses, so the simple average).

questions.q: Predict the final temperature for 100 g at 80 °C mixed with 200 g at 20 °C.

days.guide: Weigh the washers, heat them in boiling water for 5 minutes (they reach ~100 °C), then transfer quickly with tongs into a cup with a known mass of room-temperature water. Record the highest temperature. Model the calculation: heat gained by water = heat lost by metal.

questions.q: 50.0 g of metal at 100.0 °C goes into 100.0 g water at 20.0 °C; final 24.0 °C. Find the metal's specific heat.
Why must the transfer be quick?
questions.a: The hot metal loses heat to the air while it travels, which would make the calculated specific heat too low.

days.guide: Build a spreadsheet with inputs m₁, T₁, m₂, T₂ (and c₁, c₂) and a formula for Tf. The student tests it against Day 1 data and then explores 'what if' cases.

questions.q: What does the model predict for 150 g at 50 °C mixed with 150 g at 10 °C?
50 g of iron (c = 0.45) at 100 °C is dropped into 50 g of water at 20 °C. Will the final temperature be near 60 °C, above it, or below it? Why?
questions.a: Well below 60 °C (about 27.7 °C): water's specific heat is about nine times larger, so the water's temperature changes much less.

days.guide: Put equal masses of dry sand and water in identical containers under the same lamp for 15 minutes, recording temperatures every 3 minutes, then turn off the lamp and record cooling. Connect to coastal vs. inland California.

questions.q: Which heated faster, sand or water, and why?
questions.a: Sand, because its specific heat (~0.8 J/g·°C) is much lower than water's (4.18), so less energy raises its temperature.

questions.q: Why are summers milder in San Francisco than in Sacramento?
questions.a: The Pacific Ocean's high specific heat keeps coastal air cooler in summer (and milder in winter); inland land heats up much more.

days.guide: The student writes the lab report on energy conservation using this week's data. Review with the rubric.

questions.q: State the second law of thermodynamics in your own words for this lab.
questions.a: Thermal energy spontaneously flows from hotter to colder objects until they reach the same temperature; the energy becomes more evenly spread out.

weeks.assessment_key: Spreadsheet model: full credit if Tf = (m₁c₁T₁ + m₂c₂T₂) ÷ (m₁c₁ + m₂c₂) is entered with cell references and gives 40.0 °C for 100 g at 80 °C + 200 g at 20 °C water, and 30.0 °C for 150 g at 50 °C + 150 g at 10 °C. Lab report rubric: 4 = predictions vs. measured values, percent difference, correct metal specific heat calculation (e.g., 50.0 g washers at 100.0 °C into 100.0 g water at 20.0 °C, final 24.0 °C: water gains 100 × 4.184 × 4.0 = 1674 J; c = 1674 ÷ (50.0 × 76.0) = 0.440 J/g·°C, close to iron/steel at 0.45), explanation of heat lost to cup and air, and a statement of energy conservation and the second law (heat flows hot → cold until equilibrium).

weeks.prep: Gather a clear heat-safe pot (or glass saucepan), water, food coloring, a few grains of uncooked rice, and the stove. For the solar heater: a cardboard box, aluminum foil, black paint or black paper, plastic wrap, clear plastic tubing or a black-painted bottle, thermometer. Print a seismic-wave diagram showing P- and S-wave shadow zones (USGS or IRIS).
misconceptions: Students think the mantle is liquid lava. The mantle is solid rock that flows extremely slowly (centimeters per year) over long times; only small portions melt.
Students think Earth's heat comes from the Sun. Internal heat comes from leftover (primordial) heat from Earth's formation and from radioactive decay of uranium, thorium and potassium-40.
Students think plates float on a liquid layer. They ride on the slowly flowing asthenosphere and are pulled/pushed by slab pull and mantle convection.

days.guide: Show the seismic diagram. Explain that S-waves cannot travel through liquids and P-waves bend at boundaries. The student infers the layers (crust, mantle, liquid outer core, solid inner core) and labels depths.

questions.q: What evidence shows Earth's outer core is liquid?
questions.a: S-waves do not pass through it, creating an S-wave shadow zone on the far side of Earth from an earthquake.

questions.q: Why is the inner core solid even though it is hotter than the outer core?
questions.a: The enormous pressure at the center keeps iron-nickel in a solid state.

days.guide: Fill the pot with water, add a few rice grains, and heat from one side or the center. Add a drop of food coloring at the bottom near the heat. The student sketches the circulation and labels where water rises and sinks.

questions.q: Why does warm water rise?
questions.a: It expands and becomes less dense than surrounding cooler water, so it is pushed upward; cooler, denser water sinks to replace it.

questions.q: How is this like the mantle?
questions.a: Hot mantle rock rises, spreads under the plates, cools and sinks, forming slow convection cells that help move plates.

days.guide: Explain the two internal heat sources and connect to last unit's nuclear chemistry. The student writes a paragraph explaining how decay of U-238, Th-232 and K-40 keeps the mantle convecting.

questions.q: Name two sources of Earth's internal heat.
questions.a: Primordial heat from Earth's formation and radioactive decay of isotopes such as uranium-238, thorium-232 and potassium-40.

questions.q: What would happen to plate tectonics if Earth's interior cooled completely?
questions.a: Convection would stop and plate motion would eventually stop, as appears to have happened on Mars.

days.guide: Use a plate map of California. Explain that the San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary where the Pacific Plate moves northwest relative to the North American Plate (~3–5 cm/yr). The Sierra Nevada granite formed from magma generated by subduction of the Farallon plate; the range was later uplifted and tilted along faults on its east side.

questions.q: What type of plate boundary is the San Andreas Fault?
questions.a: A transform boundary (plates slide past each other).

questions.q: How did the granite of Yosemite form?
questions.a: Magma produced by subduction of the Farallon plate cooled slowly deep underground, forming granite that was later uplifted and exposed by erosion.

days.guide: The student designs and builds a solar water heater, then measures the temperature of a known mass of water before and after 30 minutes in sun. Calculate energy gained with q = mcΔT.

questions.q: 500 g of water warms from 20 °C to 32 °C. How much energy was absorbed?
Why paint the absorber black?
questions.a: Black surfaces absorb more visible light and convert it to thermal energy.

weeks.assessment_key: Device and model rubric: 4 = Labeled diagram of mantle convection (hot material rises, spreads, cools, sinks) linked to plate motion; solar heater data table with start/end temperatures, water mass and energy gained (e.g., 500 g water warming 12 °C gains 500 × 4.184 × 12 = 25,100 J); written explanation of design features (black absorbs radiation, foil reflects light onto the absorber, plastic wrap reduces convective loss) and one improvement. 3 = data and diagram correct, explanation brief. 2 = missing calculations. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather the solar heater, semester notes, and a practice set. Build the semester exam from the key below (about 30 items), allowing 60 minutes with a periodic table, formula sheet and calculator.
misconceptions: Students memorize formulas without units. Require units at every step on review problems.
Students review only what they like. Use the Week 1–17 quiz error logs to target weak areas.
Students treat the engineering summary as a list of changes. It must explain trade-offs (e.g., better insulation vs. cost or weight).

days.guide: The student changes one variable of the solar heater (more insulation, a reflector, a glazing layer), retests under similar sun, and writes an engineering summary comparing results and trade-offs.

questions.q: Why should you change only one design feature at a time?
questions.a: So you can tell which change caused the difference in performance.

questions.q: Give an example of a trade-off in the heater design.
questions.a: Adding a second plastic layer reduces heat loss but also blocks some sunlight and costs more material.

days.guide: Mixed practice: configurations, trends, ionic formulas, Lewis structures, moles. The student works problems, checking each with you before moving on; reteach anything missed twice.

questions.q: Name and give the formula of the compound formed by magnesium and nitrogen.
questions.a: Magnesium nitride, Mg₃N₂.

questions.q: Which is more electronegative, N or P?
questions.a: N.

days.guide: Mixed practice on q = mcΔT, mixing problems, specific heat and phase-change plateaus.

questions.q: How much heat is released when 300 g of water cools from 90 °C to 40 °C?
A 40 g metal sample absorbs 720 J and warms 20 °C. Find its specific heat.
questions.a: c = 720 ÷ (40 × 20) = 0.90 J/g·°C (close to aluminum).

days.guide: Give the semester exam in one 60-minute sitting with standard reference sheets. Do not help during the exam.

questions.q: (Exam day) After the exam, have the student name the topic that felt hardest.
questions.a: Answers vary; use it to plan the Day 5 corrections.

days.guide: Return the exam. The student corrects every missed item with an explanation, then updates the driving-question board, moving answered candle questions to 'answered' with the evidence.

questions.q: Which driving question about the candle can you now answer fully?
questions.a: Example: 'Where does the wax go?' — wax vapor reacts with oxygen to form CO₂ and H₂O gases, conserving atoms and mass.

weeks.assessment_key: Semester exam key (sample of 15 core items): 1) Sig figs in 0.07020 — 4. 2) Balance C₂H₆ + O₂ — 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. 3) 250 g water warmed 8.0 °C: 8370 J. 4) Average mass: 90% X-20, 10% X-22 → 20.2 u. 5) Configuration of Cl: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵. 6) Larger: Na or Mg — Na. 7) Alpha decay of U-238 → Th-234. 8) 64 g of an isotope after 3 half-lives — 8 g. 9) Formula of aluminum chloride — AlCl₃. 10) Shape of NH₃ — trigonal pyramidal. 11) Why H₂O has a high boiling point — hydrogen bonding. 12) Moles in 88.0 g CO₂ — 2.00 mol. 13) Mixing 200 g water at 60 °C with 100 g at 30 °C — 50 °C. 14) Why ice-water temperature stays at 0 °C — energy goes into melting (breaking attractions). 15) Driver of mantle convection — internal heat (radioactive decay + primordial heat). Engineering summary rubric: 4 = states original vs. revised temperature gain with numbers, explains why the change worked, and discusses at least two trade-offs (cost, materials, time, size).

weeks.prep: Gather baking soda, vinegar, a sturdy zip-top bag, a small cup that fits inside the bag, a balloon, a bottle, and the kitchen scale (0.1 g if possible). Open PhET 'Balancing Chemical Equations'. Print 20 skeleton equations (key below includes the core ones).
misconceptions: Students balance by changing subscripts (making H₂O into H₂O₂). Changing a subscript changes the substance; only coefficients may change.
Students think mass is lost in the open-system reaction. The 'missing' mass left as CO₂ gas; in a closed bag the mass stays the same.
Students forget that a coefficient multiplies every atom in the formula (2H₂O has 4 H and 2 O).

days.guide: Put 1 tablespoon of baking soda in the bag and 50 mL of vinegar in a small cup standing upright inside; seal, weigh, then tip the cup to react and reweigh. Repeat in an open cup. The student records both masses and explains the difference.

questions.q: Why did the closed bag's mass stay the same?
questions.a: No matter could enter or leave; the CO₂ produced stayed in the bag, so total mass was conserved.

questions.q: Write the word equation for baking soda and vinegar.
questions.a: Sodium bicarbonate + acetic acid → sodium acetate + water + carbon dioxide.

days.guide: Model the atom-inventory method with a table of each element on each side, adjusting coefficients one at a time (save H and O for last; balance polyatomic ions as units). The student balances 20 equations, drawing particle diagrams for three.

questions.q: Balance: Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃
questions.a: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃

questions.q: Balance: C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
questions.a: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O

days.guide: The student plays PhET Balancing Chemical Equations levels 1–3 and records any equations that took more than two tries, then explains the fix for each.

questions.q: Balance: Fe + Cl₂ → FeCl₃
questions.a: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃

questions.q: How many oxygen atoms are in 3Ca(NO₃)₂?

days.guide: The student writes a CER explaining why the open system lost mass, using Day 1 data and the balanced equation. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: If the open cup lost 2.3 g, what does that number represent?
questions.a: The mass of CO₂ gas that escaped into the air (plus a little evaporated water).

questions.q: How could you show the gas has mass?
questions.a: Collect it in a balloon over the bottle; the inflated balloon traps it, or weigh the sealed system.

days.guide: Give the 10-equation balancing quiz. Grade together and have the student check each answer by atom inventory.

questions.q: Balance: H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂
questions.a: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = Claim that the open system lost mass because CO₂ gas escaped; evidence with numbers (e.g., closed: 152.4 g before, 152.4 g after; open: 152.4 g → 150.1 g, a 2.3 g loss; bubbling observed); reasoning that atoms are rearranged, not destroyed (NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → NaCH₃COO + H₂O + CO₂), so mass is conserved in a closed system and the gas carried mass away in the open one. Balancing quiz key: 1) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 2) 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. 3) C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. 4) 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂. 5) N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. 6) 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. 7) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. 8) 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. 9) Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O. 10) C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O.

weeks.prep: Gather 3% hydrogen peroxide, active dry yeast, a tall glass or bottle, wooden splints or long matches, an iron nail (sanded clean), copper sulfate root killer (toxic — gloves, goggles, keep from children and pets, dispose per label) or vinegar + salt with dull pennies, Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate), washing soda (sodium carbonate — irritant, gloves), and clear cups. Print an activity series (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Ag, Au).
misconceptions: Students think any metal can replace any other. A metal replaces another only if it is higher on the activity series.
Students think the precipitate is the original solid coming back. It is a new insoluble compound formed by swapping ion partners.
Students classify combustion and synthesis interchangeably. Combustion is a reaction with oxygen releasing energy (often a hydrocarbon making CO₂ and H₂O); synthesis is any A + B → AB.

days.guide: Pour ~50 mL of 3% peroxide into a tall glass and add a teaspoon of yeast. Light a splint, blow it out so it glows, and lower it into the foam (adult present). The student records observations and writes the balanced equation.

questions.q: Why does the glowing splint relight?
questions.a: The reaction produces oxygen gas, which makes the glowing wood burn faster.

questions.q: What role does the yeast play?
questions.a: It contains the enzyme catalase, a catalyst that speeds decomposition; it is not used up.

days.guide: With gloves and goggles, place a clean iron nail in copper sulfate solution (or soak pennies in vinegar + salt, then add a nail). Observe over 20 minutes and the next day. The student writes the equation and explains using the activity series.

questions.q: What is the reddish coating on the nail?
questions.a: Copper metal; iron replaced copper in solution because iron is more active.

questions.q: Why does the blue color fade?
questions.a: Blue Cu²⁺ ions are being removed from the solution and replaced by pale Fe²⁺ ions.

days.guide: Dissolve a spoon of Epsom salt in one cup of water and a spoon of washing soda in another, then mix. The student observes the precipitate, writes the equation, and identifies the swapped partners.

questions.q: Write the balanced equation and name the precipitate.
questions.a: MgSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → MgCO₃(s) + Na₂SO₄; the precipitate is magnesium carbonate.

questions.q: Why is this called double replacement?
questions.a: The cations and anions of two compounds swap partners.

days.guide: Model how to use the activity series. The student predicts whether 12 reactions occur and writes products for those that do.

questions.q: Will Al react with CuCl₂? If so, write the products.
questions.a: Yes; 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu.

questions.q: Will Pb react with ZnCl₂?
questions.a: No — lead is below zinc.

days.guide: Give the quiz and grade together. Collect the lab notebook.

questions.q: Classify: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂
questions.a: Decomposition.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab notebook: full credit for observations, balanced equations and reaction types for all three labs: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (decomposition; splint relights); Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (single replacement; copper coating, blue fades); MgSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → MgCO₃(s) + Na₂SO₄ (double replacement; white precipitate). Quiz key: 1) 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO — synthesis. 2) CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ — decomposition. 3) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ — single replacement. 4) AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃ — double replacement. 5) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O — combustion. 6) Does Cu + ZnSO₄ react? No (Cu below Zn). 7) Does Zn + CuSO₄ react? Yes → ZnSO₄ + Cu. 8) Does Ag + HCl react? No (Ag below H). 9) Does Mg + 2HCl react? Yes → MgCl₂ + H₂. 10) Does Fe + 2AgNO₃ react? Yes → Fe(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag.

weeks.prep: Gather baking soda, vinegar, a cup, balloons, and the kitchen scale (0.01 g ideal). Formula card: NaHCO₃ = 84.01 g/mol; CO₂ = 44.01 g/mol; NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → NaCH₃COO + H₂O + CO₂.
misconceptions: Students convert grams of A directly to grams of B using the coefficients. Coefficients are mole ratios; always convert to moles first.
Students use the mole ratio upside down. Write the ratio with the unknown substance on top and the known on the bottom.
Students think percent yield over 100% is great. It signals an error (e.g., wet product or measurement error).

days.guide: Model reading mole ratios from coefficients. The student writes all ratios for N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ and solves mole-to-mole problems.

questions.q: How many moles of NH₃ form from 6.0 mol H₂ (with enough N₂)?
questions.a: 6.0 mol H₂ × (2 mol NH₃ / 3 mol H₂) = 4.0 mol NH₃.

questions.q: In 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O, how many mol O₂ burn 1.0 mol octane?
questions.a: 12.5 mol O₂.

days.guide: Model the three-step road map: grams A → moles A → moles B → grams B. Work two examples, then assign eight problems.

questions.q: How many grams of water form when 16.0 g of CH₄ burns completely?
How many grams of NH₃ form from 28.0 g of N₂?

days.guide: The student predicts the mass of CO₂ from 5.0 g baking soda, then weighs a cup of excess vinegar plus the baking soda on paper, adds the baking soda slowly, waits until bubbling stops, swirls, and reweighs everything (including the paper). Mass lost = CO₂ released.

questions.q: Predict the mass of CO₂ produced from 5.0 g of NaHCO₃.
Why add the baking soda slowly?
questions.a: To avoid foam overflowing, which would lose liquid mass and make the CO₂ loss appear too large.

days.guide: The student calculates percent yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100 and analyzes errors.

questions.q: You measured 2.1 g of CO₂ lost; the theoretical value is 2.6 g. What is the percent yield?
Why might the measured CO₂ be low?
questions.a: Some CO₂ stays dissolved in the liquid; also the reaction may not be complete or readings may be imprecise.

days.guide: Give the stoichiometry quiz with a periodic table. Grade together and redo missed problems.

questions.q: How many grams of O₂ are needed to burn 16.0 g of CH₄?

weeks.assessment_key: Lab: full credit for predicted CO₂ (5.0 g ÷ 84.01 = 0.0595 mol → 0.0595 × 44.01 = 2.6 g), measured mass loss, percent yield, and two error sources (CO₂ staying dissolved in the liquid, splashing, water evaporating, incomplete reaction). Quiz key: 1) In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, mol H₂O from 4.0 mol O₂ — 8.0 mol. 2) In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, mol H₂ needed for 5.0 mol N₂ — 15 mol. 3) Grams NH₃ from 28.0 g N₂ — 34.1 g. 4) Grams H₂O from 16.0 g CH₄ burned — 35.9 g. 5) Grams O₂ needed to burn 16.0 g CH₄ — 63.9 g (≈ 64 g). 6) Theoretical yield 2.6 g, actual 2.1 g — 81% (80.8%). 7) Grams CO₂ from 10.0 g C₃H₈ (C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O): 10.0 ÷ 44.09 = 0.227 mol × 3 × 44.01 = 29.9 g.

weeks.prep: Gather bread and cheese slices (or cards labeled as such), baking soda, vinegar (5% acetic acid), five identical bottles and balloons, a measuring spoon or scale, and a flexible measuring tape. Open PhET 'Reactants, Products and Leftovers'.
misconceptions: Students assume the reactant with the smaller mass is limiting. Compare moles needed vs. moles available using the balanced ratio.
Students think that once one reactant is used up the other keeps reacting. The reaction stops when the limiting reactant is gone; the excess remains.
Students calculate product from both reactants and add them. The smaller amount of product is the correct (theoretical) yield.

days.guide: Model making sandwiches (2 bread + 1 cheese). Give different quantities and have the student find how many sandwiches can be made, what runs out, and what is left over.

questions.q: You have 12 slices of bread and 4 slices of cheese. How many sandwiches, and what is limiting?
questions.a: 4 sandwiches; cheese is limiting; 4 slices of bread are left.

questions.q: Relate this to a chemical reaction.
questions.a: The balanced equation is the recipe; the reactant that runs out first limits how much product forms.

days.guide: In PhET, the student completes the sandwich and molecule screens, predicting products and leftovers before checking. Record three cases.

questions.q: With 4 N₂ and 9 H₂ molecules (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃), what forms and what is left?
questions.a: H₂ limits: 9 H₂ make 6 NH₃ using 3 N₂; 1 N₂ is left over.

questions.q: With 3 CH₄ and 4 O₂ (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O), what forms?
questions.a: O₂ limits: 2 CH₄ react making 2 CO₂ and 4 H₂O; 1 CH₄ left over.

days.guide: Put 100 mL of vinegar in each of five bottles. Put 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 g of baking soda into balloons, stretch each over a bottle, then lift to dump. After reactions stop, measure balloon circumference and graph.

questions.q: Why do the last balloons end up about the same size?
questions.a: The vinegar ran out (became limiting), so extra baking soda could not make more CO₂.

questions.q: Estimate the baking soda mass at which 100 mL of 5% vinegar becomes limiting.
questions.a: ≈ 5 g acetic acid ÷ 60.05 = 0.083 mol → 0.083 × 84.01 ≈ 7 g baking soda.

days.guide: Model a limiting reactant problem for methane combustion; the student solves four more for fuels.

questions.q: 10.0 g CH₄ reacts with 32.0 g O₂. Which is limiting and how much CO₂ forms?
questions.a: CH₄: 0.623 mol needs 1.25 mol O₂, but only 1.00 mol O₂ is available → O₂ limits. CO₂ = 1.00 ÷ 2 = 0.500 mol × 44.01 = 22.0 g.

questions.q: In a car engine with too little air, what forms instead of CO₂, and why is it dangerous?
questions.a: Carbon monoxide (CO) and soot from incomplete combustion; CO binds to hemoglobin and blocks oxygen transport.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Grade together and collect the balloon graph.

questions.q: 4.0 mol Al reacts with 4.0 mol Cl₂ (2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃). Which is limiting and how much AlCl₃ forms?
questions.a: Cl₂ limits (4.0 mol Al needs 6.0 mol Cl₂); AlCl₃ = 4.0 × 2/3 = 2.7 mol.

weeks.assessment_key: Balloon lab: full credit for a graph of baking soda mass (x) vs. balloon circumference (y) that rises and then levels off; identification of the leveling point. With 100 mL vinegar (≈0.083 mol acetic acid), growth should stop near 7 g baking soda (0.083 × 84.01). Explanation: before that point baking soda is limiting; after it vinegar is limiting. Quiz key: 1) 10 slices of bread and 8 cheese, sandwich = 2 bread + 1 cheese: 5 sandwiches, bread limiting, 3 cheese left. 2) 10.0 g CH₄ + 32.0 g O₂: O₂ limiting (needs 1.25 mol O₂, has 1.00 mol); CO₂ = 0.500 mol = 22.0 g; leftover CH₄ = 1.98 g. 3) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O with 4.0 mol H₂ and 3.0 mol O₂: H₂ limiting; 4.0 mol H₂O; 1.0 mol O₂ left. 4) N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ with 2.0 mol N₂ and 3.0 mol H₂: H₂ limiting; 2.0 mol NH₃.

weeks.prep: Gather baking soda, vinegar, 3% hydrogen peroxide, yeast, two cups, and a thermometer. Prepare a bond-energy table (kJ/mol): C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O (in CO₂) 799, O–H 463, H–H 436, N≡N 945, N–H 391. Build the Unit 5 test from the key.
misconceptions: Students think breaking bonds releases energy (like breaking a stick). Breaking bonds always requires energy; forming bonds releases energy.
Students reverse the sign: ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed; a negative ΔH is exothermic.
Students think exothermic reactions need no activation energy. Even exothermic reactions (like burning wood) need an initial energy input to start.

days.guide: Mix baking soda and vinegar in a cup with a thermometer and record the temperature change; then mix yeast into peroxide and record. The student classifies each as endo- or exothermic.

questions.q: The baking soda reaction dropped from 21 °C to 17 °C. Endothermic or exothermic?
questions.a: Endothermic — it absorbed energy from the surroundings.

questions.q: The peroxide reaction rose from 21 °C to 35 °C. What does that tell you about bonds?
questions.a: Exothermic — more energy was released forming bonds in H₂O and O₂ than was absorbed breaking bonds in H₂O₂.

days.guide: Model an energy diagram: reactant level, hump (activation energy), product level, and ΔH arrow. The student draws one for each Day 1 reaction and labels them.

questions.q: On an exothermic energy diagram, are products higher or lower than reactants?
questions.a: Lower — energy is released.

questions.q: What does a catalyst do to the diagram?
questions.a: It lowers the activation energy hump; ΔH is unchanged.

days.guide: Model ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) for methane combustion step by step. The student then does H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl and 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

questions.q: Calculate ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
Calculate ΔH for 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

days.guide: Use two magnets as a model: pulling them apart takes energy (breaking), letting them snap together releases energy (forming). The student builds a written or physical model explaining why combustion is exothermic overall.

questions.q: Why is burning methane exothermic overall if breaking its bonds absorbs energy?
questions.a: The bonds formed in CO₂ and H₂O are stronger in total, releasing more energy (3450 kJ) than was absorbed breaking the reactant bonds (2648 kJ).

questions.q: What does the magnet model represent?
questions.a: Atoms attracting; separating them requires energy input and bringing them together releases energy.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test (50 minutes) with periodic table, bond-energy table and activity series. Grade together.

questions.q: Is photosynthesis endothermic or exothermic?
questions.a: Endothermic — it absorbs light energy to make glucose.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test key (sample): 1) Balance Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. 2) Classify AgNO₃ + KCl → AgCl + KNO₃: double replacement. 3) Grams CO₂ from 12.0 g C burned (C + O₂ → CO₂): 44.0 g. 4) 5.0 mol H₂ and 2.0 mol O₂ (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O): O₂ limits, 4.0 mol H₂O. 5) Percent yield, 18.0 g theoretical, 15.3 g actual: 85.0%. 6) ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O from bond energies: −802 kJ/mol. 7) ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl (H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431): (436 + 242) − 2(431) = −184 kJ (exothermic). 8) Endothermic or exothermic: baking soda + vinegar — endothermic (temperature drops). 9) Label an energy diagram: reactants, products, activation energy, ΔH. 10) Explain why forming bonds releases energy — atoms reach a lower, more stable energy state.

weeks.prep: Gather two identical jars, plastic wrap, a rubber band, two thermometers, a lamp with an incandescent or halogen bulb (or sunlight), and black and white paper. Bookmark NASA's Earth energy budget diagram and PhET 'Greenhouse Effect'. Make a data table.
misconceptions: Students think the greenhouse effect is the ozone hole. They are different problems; ozone depletion lets in more UV, while greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared.
Students think greenhouse gases trap sunlight coming in. Most incoming sunlight is visible light that passes through; greenhouse gases absorb the infrared Earth emits.
Students think the greenhouse effect is entirely bad. Without it Earth's average temperature would be about −18 °C instead of about +15 °C; the problem is the enhanced effect from added gases.

days.guide: Using NASA's diagram, the student draws Earth's energy budget: incoming sunlight (~340 W/m² average), ~30% reflected by clouds, air and surface, ~70% absorbed, and outgoing infrared, with the atmosphere re-radiating some back down. Discuss what 'balance' means.

questions.q: What happens to Earth's temperature if more energy comes in than goes out?
questions.a: Earth warms until outgoing infrared increases enough to restore balance.

questions.q: About what fraction of incoming sunlight is reflected?
questions.a: About 30%.

days.guide: Wrap one thermometer bulb in black paper and one in white; place both in sun for 15 minutes, reading every 3 minutes. The student graphs and explains in terms of albedo.

questions.q: Which warmed more and why?
questions.a: Black paper — it has low albedo, absorbing more light and converting it to thermal energy.

questions.q: Why does Arctic sea ice loss speed up warming?
questions.a: Dark ocean replaces reflective ice, lowering albedo so more sunlight is absorbed.

days.guide: Place thermometers in two jars under a lamp; cover one with plastic wrap. Record temperatures every 5 minutes for 30 minutes and graph. Discuss honestly what the model does and does not show.

questions.q: Why did the covered jar get warmer?
questions.a: Mostly because the cover traps warm air (stops convection and mixing with room air); it is a model of energy trapping but not the same mechanism as CO₂ absorbing infrared.

questions.q: How could you better model the real greenhouse effect?
questions.a: Compare two covered jars, one filled with extra CO₂ (from baking soda and vinegar), keeping everything else the same.

days.guide: In PhET Greenhouse Effect (photon absorption screen), the student shines infrared on N₂, O₂, CO₂, H₂O and CH₄ and records which absorb it and how they move. Explain using bond vibrations that change the molecule's charge distribution.

questions.q: Why does CO₂ absorb infrared but N₂ does not?
questions.a: CO₂ can bend and stretch in ways that create a temporary dipole, letting it absorb IR; N₂ is a symmetric diatomic whose vibration produces no dipole change.

questions.q: After a CO₂ molecule absorbs infrared, what happens to the energy?
questions.a: It is re-emitted in a random direction (some back toward Earth) or transferred to nearby molecules by collisions, warming the air.

days.guide: Give the energy-balance quiz and grade together. Collect lab data.

questions.q: Why is water vapor considered a feedback rather than a driver of climate change?
questions.a: Its amount depends on temperature: warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases like CO₂.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab data: full credit for temperature tables every 5 minutes, graphs of both trials, and correct conclusions (black paper warmed more than white; covered jar warmed more than open). The write-up should note honestly that a sealed jar warms mainly because it blocks convection, which is different from how CO₂ works in the atmosphere. Quiz key: 1) Earth reflects about 30% of incoming sunlight (albedo ≈ 0.3). 2) Earth emits energy as infrared radiation. 3) Greenhouse gases include CO₂, H₂O, CH₄, N₂O. 4) Why N₂ and O₂ don't absorb IR — symmetric two-atom molecules; vibrating doesn't change their dipole. 5) Without greenhouse gases Earth would average about −18 °C. 6) Melting ice lowers albedo, so more sunlight is absorbed. 7) If incoming energy exceeds outgoing, Earth warms until balance returns. 8) Black surfaces have low albedo and absorb more.

weeks.prep: Print a NOAA or NASA carbon-cycle diagram with reservoirs (GtC) and fluxes (GtC/yr). Gather chalk or limestone (or seashells), vinegar, a calculator and a spreadsheet. Approximate values to use: atmosphere ~875 GtC (pre-2020 diagrams; about 900 today), surface ocean ~900, deep ocean ~37,000, vegetation ~450–650, soils ~1,500–2,400, fossil fuel reserves ~1,000+, sedimentary rocks ~60–100 million GtC; human emissions ~10 GtC/yr; 1 ppm CO₂ ≈ 2.13 GtC.
misconceptions: Students think carbon is 'used up' in the cycle. Carbon atoms are conserved; they move among reservoirs.
Students think all human CO₂ stays in the air. About half is absorbed by oceans and land; roughly 45% remains in the atmosphere.
Students confuse reservoirs (amounts, GtC) with fluxes (rates, GtC/yr). Use units to tell them apart.

days.guide: Using the diagram, the student makes a table of reservoirs (GtC) and fluxes (GtC/yr): photosynthesis, respiration/decay, ocean uptake/release, volcanism, fossil fuel burning. Ask which reservoir is largest and which flux humans added.

questions.q: Which reservoir holds the most carbon?
questions.a: Sedimentary rocks (limestone and organic carbon) — tens of millions of GtC; among the fast-cycle reservoirs, the deep ocean (~37,000 GtC).

questions.q: What process moves carbon from the atmosphere to the biosphere?
questions.a: Photosynthesis (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂).

days.guide: Build a spreadsheet box model: Year, Atmospheric carbon, Natural in, Natural out (equal). Start with natural fluxes balanced so the line stays flat. The student explains why a balanced system is steady.

questions.q: If natural inflows equal outflows, what happens to atmospheric carbon over time?
questions.a: It stays constant (steady state).

questions.q: Convert 875 GtC of atmospheric carbon to ppm of CO₂.

days.guide: Add human emissions (10 GtC/yr) with 55% taken up by sinks. The student graphs 50 years, converts to ppm, and compares the slope to the Keeling Curve's recent ~2.4 ppm/yr.

questions.q: With 10 GtC/yr emitted and 45% remaining, how fast does atmospheric CO₂ rise in ppm/yr?
questions.a: 4.5 GtC/yr ÷ 2.13 ≈ 2.1 ppm/yr.

questions.q: Why might the model underestimate the real rise?
questions.a: Emissions are growing rather than constant, and sinks may absorb a smaller fraction over time.

days.guide: Drop vinegar on chalk or limestone and observe fizzing. Write the reaction and connect to carbon stored in rocks and the slow carbon cycle (weathering, burial, volcanic release).

questions.q: Write the equation for vinegar reacting with limestone.
questions.a: CaCO₃ + 2CH₃COOH → Ca(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂O + CO₂

questions.q: How did carbon get into limestone originally?
questions.a: Marine organisms built shells from dissolved calcium and carbonate; the shells accumulated and became rock.

days.guide: The student writes a model explanation with the spreadsheet graph, explaining reservoirs, fluxes, human perturbation and limitations. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Why is burning fossil fuels a problem for the carbon cycle if the carbon was originally in the atmosphere?
questions.a: It moves carbon stored over millions of years in the slow cycle into the atmosphere in decades, much faster than natural processes can remove it.

weeks.assessment_key: Model rubric (4 levels): 4 = Spreadsheet with year column, atmospheric carbon (starting ~875 GtC), natural fluxes in and out balanced, human emissions (~10 GtC/yr) with about 55% absorbed by sinks, conversion to ppm (÷ 2.13), and a graph over 50 years showing ~2.1 ppm/yr increase (close to the observed ~2.4 ppm/yr); written explanation of assumptions, comparison to Keeling Curve data, and one limitation (e.g., constant emissions or constant sink fraction). 3 = working model but weak comparison. 2 = model errors (mixing reservoirs and fluxes). 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Download NOAA Mauna Loa annual mean CO₂ (gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends) and Vostok ice core CO₂ and temperature data (NOAA Paleoclimatology or CDIAC). Open NASA Climate 'Vital Signs' and Cal-Adapt (cal-adapt.org) for California projections. Prepare a spreadsheet.
misconceptions: Students think correlation in ice cores proves CO₂ alone drove past cycles. In ice ages, orbital changes started warming and CO₂ then amplified it (a feedback); today CO₂ is rising first because of human emissions.
Students think the yearly Keeling sawtooth is pollution changing seasonally. It is Northern Hemisphere plants taking up CO₂ in summer and releasing it in winter.
Students think 'positive feedback' means good. Positive feedback amplifies a change; negative feedback dampens it.

days.guide: The student graphs Mauna Loa annual mean CO₂ from 1959 to the latest year, calculates the average yearly increase overall and for the last ten years, and describes the shape (accelerating). Discuss the monthly sawtooth.

questions.q: CO₂ was about 317 ppm in 1960 and 425 ppm in 2024. What is the average annual increase?
Why does CO₂ drop each Northern Hemisphere summer?
questions.a: Plants in the Northern Hemisphere, which has most of the land, absorb CO₂ through photosynthesis during the growing season.

days.guide: Graph Vostok CO₂ and temperature on the same time axis (or a scatter plot). The student describes the correlation and compares the maximum ice-core value with today.

questions.q: What relationship do the Vostok data show?
questions.a: A strong positive correlation: warm interglacials have high CO₂ (~280–300 ppm) and ice ages have low CO₂ (~180 ppm).

questions.q: How do the bubbles in ice record past CO₂?
questions.a: Air trapped in the ice as snow compacts preserves samples of the ancient atmosphere.

days.guide: The student draws loop diagrams for the ice-albedo and permafrost feedbacks, with + signs on each arrow, and one negative feedback for contrast (e.g., warmer Earth radiates more infrared).

questions.q: Explain the permafrost feedback.
questions.a: Warming thaws frozen soil; microbes decompose organic matter, releasing CO₂ and methane, which cause more warming.

questions.q: Give an example of a negative feedback.
questions.a: A warmer Earth emits more infrared radiation to space, which tends to cool it.

days.guide: Use Cal-Adapt or NASA projections to compare a lower-emissions and higher-emissions scenario for the student's region in 2050 (temperature, extreme-heat days, Sierra snowpack). The student writes a short forecast with numbers and sources.

questions.q: Why do forecasts give two or more scenarios?
questions.a: Future warming depends on how much greenhouse gas humans emit, which is uncertain; scenarios show outcomes for different emission paths.

questions.q: Why does Sierra snowpack matter to California?
questions.a: It stores water that melts in spring and summer, supplying a large share of the state's water; less snowpack means less stored water when it's needed.

days.guide: Give the data-analysis quiz (graph reading and calculations). Grade together.

questions.q: A graph shows global temperature rising 0.2 °C per decade. How much warming is that over 30 years?

weeks.assessment_key: Forecast write-up rubric: 4 = Uses NASA/Cal-Adapt projections to state a 2050 California temperature change under lower and higher emissions (roughly +2 to +4 °F above late-20th-century averages, larger under high emissions) and the direction of snowpack change (substantial decline, larger under high emissions), cites the data source and explains uncertainty and the role of feedbacks. Quiz key: 1) Mauna Loa CO₂ rose from about 317 ppm (1960) to about 425 ppm (2024): average ≈ 1.7 ppm/yr; recent decade ≈ 2.4–2.5 ppm/yr. 2) Vostok CO₂ ranged ~180–300 ppm over 400,000 years. 3) Today's ~425 ppm is far above any value in the 800,000-year ice-core record. 4) Ice-albedo feedback: warming melts ice → lower albedo → more absorption → more warming (positive). 5) Permafrost feedback: thawing releases CO₂ and CH₄ → more warming (positive). 6) The seasonal cycle is caused by Northern Hemisphere photosynthesis/respiration.

weeks.prep: Gather research sources: NREL or Department of Energy pages on solar and EVs, IEA or DOE pages on carbon capture, California Air Resources Board pages on cap-and-trade (renamed cap-and-invest when extended in 2025) and SB 32. Build the Unit 6 test from the key.
misconceptions: Students think EVs produce zero emissions under all conditions. Their emissions depend on how electricity is generated and on battery manufacturing, though lifetime emissions are generally lower than gasoline cars.
Students think one solution will solve climate change. Use the trade-off matrix to show that combinations are needed.
Students confuse SB 32 targets with AB 32. AB 32 (2006): return to 1990 levels by 2020. SB 32 (2016): 40% below 1990 levels by 2030.

days.guide: The student researches solar PV, EVs and carbon capture, filling a table: how it works chemically, CO₂ reduced, cost, limitations. Check that chemistry is explained (e.g., electrons freed in silicon by light).

questions.q: How does a solar cell produce electricity?
questions.a: Photons give energy to electrons in a silicon semiconductor; an internal electric field at the p-n junction pushes them through a circuit.

questions.q: How does a common carbon-capture method trap CO₂?
questions.a: Flue gas passes through an amine solution that chemically binds CO₂; heating later releases pure CO₂ for storage underground.

days.guide: Build a decision matrix: rows = solutions, columns = criteria (cost, CO₂ reduction, feasibility, time to deploy), weighted by importance. The student scores each and totals.

questions.q: Why weight criteria differently?
questions.a: Some criteria matter more to the decision-maker (e.g., CO₂ reduction may count double), so weights reflect priorities.

questions.q: What is a trade-off?
questions.a: Giving up some of one desirable quality to gain another (e.g., higher cost for greater CO₂ reduction).

days.guide: Read about California's cap-and-trade program (started 2013, extended in 2025 as cap-and-invest) and the SB 32 goal. The student summarizes how a cap works and lists one argument for and one against.

questions.q: What does SB 32 require?
questions.a: That California cut greenhouse gas emissions to 40% below 1990 levels by 2030.

questions.q: How does cap-and-trade reduce emissions?
questions.a: The state sets a declining cap on total emissions and issues allowances; companies that cut emissions cheaply can sell spare allowances, so reductions happen where cheapest.

days.guide: The student writes a 1-page brief recommending one solution for the city, with evidence and trade-offs. Score with the rubric; revise once.

questions.q: What should the brief's recommendation sentence include?
questions.a: The specific action, who should do it, and the main benefit (e.g., 'The city should install solar panels on all public buildings by 2030 to cut X tons of CO₂ per year').

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test. Grade together.

questions.q: What is the chemistry behind an EV battery's charge and discharge?
questions.a: Lithium ions move from the anode to the cathode through the electrolyte while electrons flow through the circuit (discharge); charging reverses the flow.

weeks.assessment_key: Position brief rubric: 4 = Clear recommendation for the student's city; explains the chemistry (e.g., photovoltaic silicon converting light to electricity; lithium-ion batteries moving Li⁺ ions; amines binding CO₂); uses data (cost, tons of CO₂ avoided); acknowledges trade-offs; cites ≥3 sources. Unit 6 test key (sample): 1) Albedo of Earth ≈ 0.3. 2) Why CO₂ absorbs IR — vibrations change its dipole. 3) 1 ppm CO₂ ≈ 2.13 GtC; adding 4.26 GtC raises CO₂ by 2 ppm. 4) Largest active reservoir — deep ocean. 5) Ice-albedo feedback is positive. 6) SB 32 target — 40% below 1990 by 2030. 7) Cap-and-trade sets a declining limit on total emissions and lets companies buy/sell allowances. 8) One trade-off of carbon capture — high energy cost and expense. 9) The Keeling Curve's seasonal cycle comes from Northern Hemisphere photosynthesis. 10) Mitigation vs. adaptation: mitigation reduces emissions; adaptation copes with impacts.

weeks.prep: Gather Alka-Seltzer tablets (6+), clear cups, ice water, room-temperature water and hot tap water (~45–50 °C), a thermometer, a stopwatch, a spoon or mortar for crushing, 3% hydrogen peroxide and yeast. Open PhET 'Reactions & Rates'.
misconceptions: Students think a catalyst is consumed. It speeds the reaction by providing a lower-activation-energy pathway and is recovered unchanged.
Students say heat makes particles collide only more often. Higher temperature also makes a larger fraction of collisions energetic enough to exceed the activation energy — the bigger effect.
Students think crushing a tablet changes how much gas forms. It changes the rate, not the total amount of product.

days.guide: In PhET Reactions & Rates, the student runs single collisions with low and high energy, then many-molecule runs at different temperatures, recording how often reactions happen. Introduce the four factors (temperature, concentration, surface area, catalyst).

questions.q: According to collision theory, what two conditions must a collision meet to cause a reaction?
questions.a: Enough energy (at least the activation energy) and the correct orientation.

questions.q: Why does increasing concentration speed a reaction?
questions.a: More particles per volume means more frequent collisions.

days.guide: Put equal volumes of ice water, room-temperature water and hot water in three cups, record temperatures, and time a whole tablet dissolving in each. Repeat once. The student graphs temperature vs. time.

questions.q: Predict the effect of raising the temperature by 10 °C.
questions.a: The reaction speeds up — for many reactions roughly doubling the rate.

questions.q: Explain the result with collision theory.
questions.a: Particles in hot water move faster, colliding more often and with more energy, so more collisions exceed the activation energy.

days.guide: Time a whole tablet and a crushed tablet (same mass) in equal room-temperature water. The student explains the difference and connects to real examples (flour-dust explosions, kindling vs. logs).

questions.q: Which dissolved faster and why?
questions.a: The crushed tablet — more surface area exposes more particles to collisions with water.

questions.q: Why do grain silos risk dust explosions?
questions.a: Fine dust has an enormous surface area, so it can burn extremely rapidly when ignited.

days.guide: Pour peroxide into two cups; add yeast to one only. Compare bubbling. The student draws an energy diagram showing the catalyzed and uncatalyzed paths.

questions.q: How does catalase speed the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide?
questions.a: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed.

questions.q: Is the yeast used up?
questions.a: No — the enzyme is a catalyst; it is not consumed (though it can eventually denature).

days.guide: The student writes the rate lab report. Score with the rubric and have the student revise the explanation section.

questions.q: Why do we refrigerate food?
questions.a: Lower temperature slows the chemical reactions and bacterial growth that spoil food.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: 4 = Question, hypothesis, controlled variables (same water volume, tablet size), data table with times for cold/room/hot and whole/crushed (with trials), graph of temperature vs. dissolving time showing time decreases as temperature rises; explanation using collision theory (faster particles → more frequent collisions and more collisions with energy ≥ activation energy; crushing increases surface area so more particles are exposed; yeast's catalase lowers activation energy); error analysis and improvement. 3 = correct data and partial collision-theory explanation. 2 = data with little explanation. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather two identical clear cups, water, two straws of different diameters, a measuring cup or ruler, and graph paper. Open a sealed bottle of soda for Day 4 discussion.
misconceptions: Students think at equilibrium the amounts of reactants and products are equal. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations are constant but usually not equal.
Students think reactions stop at equilibrium. Both reactions continue (dynamic); there is no net change.
Students include solids and pure liquids in K expressions. Only gases and dissolved species appear.

days.guide: Introduce reversible reactions with examples (N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂, water evaporating and condensing in a closed bottle). The student defines dynamic equilibrium and sketches a concentration vs. time graph showing curves leveling off.

questions.q: In a sealed water bottle, why does the water level stop dropping?
questions.a: The evaporation rate becomes equal to the condensation rate.

questions.q: What does the double arrow ⇌ mean?
questions.a: The reaction is reversible; it proceeds in both directions.

days.guide: Fill cup A with 200 mL water and leave cup B empty. Each 'turn,' the student uses the wide straw to move water A → B and the partner (or student, second hand) uses the narrow straw B → A simultaneously by pinching the straw top. Record levels every turn for 20 turns and graph.

questions.q: Why did the levels stop changing even though water kept moving?
questions.a: The amount moved A → B each turn equaled the amount moved B → A — equal forward and reverse rates.

questions.q: Were the final volumes equal? Why or why not?
questions.a: No; the different straw sizes mean equal transfer happens only when the cup with the narrow straw is much fuller.

days.guide: Teach K = [products]^coefficients ÷ [reactants]^coefficients. The student writes K for five reactions and interprets large and small values.

questions.q: Write K for 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃.
questions.a: K = [SO₃]² ÷ ([SO₂]²[O₂])

questions.q: If K = 5 × 10⁻¹⁰, which side is favored?
questions.a: Reactants — very little product at equilibrium.

days.guide: Discuss a sealed soda: CO₂(g) above the liquid ⇌ CO₂(aq), and CO₂(aq) + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃. Open the bottle and observe. The student explains what changes when the cap comes off.

questions.q: Why doesn't a sealed soda keep bubbling?
questions.a: The CO₂ in the gas space and dissolved CO₂ are at equilibrium; escape and dissolving rates are equal.

questions.q: Why does it fizz when opened?
questions.a: Pressure of CO₂ above the liquid drops, so CO₂ comes out of solution faster than it dissolves until a new equilibrium (mostly flat soda) is reached.

days.guide: Give the equilibrium quiz and grade together.

questions.q: Write K for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g).
questions.a: K = [CO₂] (solids are left out).

weeks.assessment_key: Model graph: full credit for water level vs. transfer number for both cups, curves that level off at unequal heights, and the explanation that equilibrium was reached when the amount moved each way per turn became equal. Quiz key: 1) Define dynamic equilibrium — forward and reverse rates equal; concentrations constant. 2) K for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: K = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³). 3) K for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI: [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]). 4) K = 1 × 10⁸ means products are strongly favored. 5) K = 1 × 10⁻⁵ means reactants favored. 6) In a sealed soda, CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) at equilibrium. 7) Why the water levels weren't equal — different straw sizes make different transfer rates; equilibrium is about equal rates. 8) Is equilibrium static? No — dynamic.

weeks.prep: Make red cabbage indicator: chop 2 cups of red cabbage, cover with boiling water, steep 15 minutes, strain and refrigerate. Gather vinegar, baking soda, clear cups, two sodas (one cold, one warm), and ice/warm water baths. Print a description of the Haber process.
misconceptions: Students think Le Chatelier means the system returns to its original state. It shifts to partially counteract the stress and settles at a new equilibrium.
Students think adding a catalyst shifts equilibrium. A catalyst speeds both directions equally; it gets to equilibrium faster without changing the yield.
Students treat temperature like concentration without considering ΔH. For an exothermic reaction, heat is a 'product', so raising temperature shifts left.

days.guide: Teach Le Chatelier's principle with stresses: add/remove reactant or product, change temperature, change pressure. The student predicts shifts for 10 cases using N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat and explains each.

questions.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat, what happens if the temperature is raised?
questions.a: The equilibrium shifts left (toward N₂ and H₂), absorbing the added heat; less NH₃.

questions.q: What happens if N₂ is added?
questions.a: Shifts right, using up some added N₂ and producing more NH₃.
