days.guide: Put cabbage indicator in three cups: add vinegar to one and baking-soda solution to another; keep one neutral. Then add base to the acid cup drop by drop and watch the color shift back. Explain that indicator molecules exist in an equilibrium between acid and base forms.

questions.q: What color is cabbage indicator in vinegar and in baking-soda solution?
questions.a: Pink/red in vinegar (acid); blue-green in baking-soda solution (base); purple near neutral.

questions.q: Why does adding base to the pink cup change its color?
questions.a: Base removes H⁺ ions, shifting the indicator's equilibrium toward its base-colored form.

days.guide: Open a cold soda and a warm soda (in a sink!) and compare fizz. The student explains with equilibrium: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) + heat.

questions.q: Which soda fizzed more and why?
questions.a: The warm soda; gas solubility decreases at higher temperature, so the equilibrium shifts toward gaseous CO₂.

questions.q: Why does warm lake water hold less oxygen for fish?
questions.a: Gases are less soluble in warmer water, so less O₂ stays dissolved.

days.guide: Present the Haber process and real conditions (~200 atm, ~400–450 °C, iron catalyst, NH₃ removed by cooling). The student proposes conditions to maximize yield and explains the trade-offs.

questions.q: Why not run the Haber process at room temperature if low temperature favors ammonia?
questions.a: The reaction would be far too slow; a moderate temperature with a catalyst gives an acceptable rate with a reasonable yield.

questions.q: Why does high pressure increase the yield?
questions.a: The product side has fewer gas molecules (2 vs. 4), so increasing pressure shifts toward ammonia.

days.guide: Give the Le Chatelier quiz and collect the design proposal.

questions.q: For CO(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ CH₄(g) + H₂O(g), which way does decreasing pressure shift it?
questions.a: Left, toward the side with more gas molecules (4 vs. 2).

weeks.assessment_key: Design proposal rubric: 4 = For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH = −92 kJ): high pressure (shifts toward fewer gas moles, 2 vs. 4); removing NH₃ by condensing it; adding excess N₂/H₂; a compromise moderate temperature (~400–450 °C) because low temperature favors yield but is too slow; iron catalyst for rate; trade-offs of cost and safety of high pressure. Quiz key: 1) Adding H₂ shifts right. 2) Removing NH₃ shifts right. 3) Raising temperature of an exothermic reaction shifts left. 4) Increasing pressure for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ shifts right. 5) Increasing pressure for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI: no shift (2 gas moles each side). 6) Catalyst: no shift. 7) Cold soda holds more CO₂ because CO₂ dissolving is exothermic / gas solubility is higher at low temperature. 8) Adding acid to cabbage indicator turns it pink-red (shifts the indicator's equilibrium to its acid form).

weeks.prep: Print overviews of the Contact process for sulfuric acid (2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH ≈ −198 kJ, vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, ~400–450 °C, near 1–2 atm with excess air) or methanol synthesis (CO + 2H₂ ⇌ CH₃OH, ΔH ≈ −91 kJ, copper/zinc oxide catalyst, ~250 °C, 50–100 atm). Build the Unit 7 test from the key.
misconceptions: Students choose the highest-yield conditions regardless of cost or speed. Industrial chemists optimize rate, yield, cost and safety together.
Students think pressure always helps. Pressure only shifts equilibria involving unequal moles of gas, and high pressure is expensive and hazardous.
Students forget that recycling unreacted gases is a key way to improve overall yield.

days.guide: The student reads the case study and summarizes the equation, ΔH, catalyst, conditions and uses (sulfuric acid: fertilizers, batteries; methanol: fuels, plastics).

questions.q: For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (exothermic), why is a catalyst used?
questions.a: To speed the reaction at a moderate temperature where yield is still good.

questions.q: What is sulfuric acid mostly used for?
questions.a: Making phosphate fertilizers (also batteries and chemical processing).

days.guide: The student proposes changes to temperature, pressure, concentrations and catalyst and explains each effect on rate and yield in a table, plus trade-offs.

questions.q: For methanol synthesis (CO + 2H₂ ⇌ CH₃OH, exothermic), what pressure change improves yield?
questions.a: Higher pressure — 3 gas moles become 1.

questions.q: What is a trade-off of very high pressure?
questions.a: Stronger, costlier equipment and greater safety risk.

days.guide: The student presents the design to you; ask probing questions (Why that temperature? What happens to unreacted gas? Is it safe?). The student records questions he or she could not answer.

questions.q: How can a plant increase overall yield without changing equilibrium?
questions.a: Separate the product and recycle the unreacted reactants back through the reactor.

questions.q: Does the catalyst change the equilibrium yield?
questions.a: No, only how fast equilibrium is reached.

days.guide: The student revises the proposal to address feedback, marking changes.

questions.q: Why might an engineer accept a lower yield per pass?
questions.a: Higher temperature gives a much faster rate, so more product is made per hour overall, especially with recycling.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test. Grade together.

questions.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), does increasing pressure change the yield?
questions.a: No — there are 2 moles of gas on each side.

weeks.assessment_key: Design proposal rubric: 4 = Correct equation and ΔH; predicted effect of temperature, pressure, concentration and catalyst on both rate and yield; chosen operating conditions with justification; at least two trade-offs (cost, safety, energy, rate); revision based on feedback. Unit 7 test key (sample): 1) Four factors affecting rate: temperature, concentration, surface area, catalyst. 2) Why temperature speeds reactions — more frequent, more energetic collisions; more exceed Ea. 3) Catalyst lowers activation energy; does not change K or yield. 4) K for 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄: [N₂O₄] ÷ [NO₂]². 5) For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (exothermic): increasing pressure shifts right; raising temperature shifts left; adding O₂ shifts right. 6) Equilibrium means equal rates, not equal amounts. 7) Why industry recycles unreacted gases — to convert more feedstock over repeated passes.

weeks.prep: Gather a plastic water bottle (not glass), a marker, a ruler, the freezer, sugar cubes, chalk (calcium carbonate sidewalk chalk works), water, vinegar, a baking pan, sand, a cup with a small hole for steady flow, and books to tilt the pan.
misconceptions: Students think ice is denser than water because solids usually are. Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open hexagonal lattice, making it about 9% less dense than liquid water, so it floats and expands when freezing.
Students think dissolving means disappearing. The solute is still present, spread out as particles or ions among water molecules.
Students think erosion only happens in big floods. Slow, repeated processes (frost wedging, dissolution) shape landscapes over long times.

days.guide: Review hydrogen bonding. The student lists water's unique properties (high specific heat, ice less dense than liquid, high surface tension, excellent solvent, high heat of vaporization) and links each to hydrogen bonding and an Earth effect.

questions.q: Why does ice float?
questions.a: Hydrogen bonds lock molecules into an open lattice, making ice less dense than liquid water.

questions.q: How does water's high specific heat affect Earth's climate?
questions.a: Oceans absorb and release large amounts of heat with little temperature change, moderating coastal climates.

days.guide: Fill a plastic bottle to the brim, cap it, mark dimensions, and freeze overnight. Measure the bulge, or fill a container to a line and measure the new height after freezing. Connect to frost wedging in rock cracks.

questions.q: If 500 mL of water freezes, about what volume of ice forms?
questions.a: About 545 mL (roughly 9% larger).

questions.q: Explain frost wedging.
questions.a: Water seeps into cracks, freezes and expands, pushing the crack wider; repeated freeze-thaw breaks rocks apart.

days.guide: Drop a sugar cube and a piece of chalk into water, and another of each into vinegar; time dissolving and observe bubbles.

questions.q: Why does chalk fizz and dissolve in vinegar but not much in water?
questions.a: Chalk is calcium carbonate, which reacts with acid: CaCO₃ + 2CH₃COOH → Ca(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂O + CO₂.

questions.q: How does this model chemical weathering?
questions.a: Rainwater containing dissolved CO₂ forms weak carbonic acid that slowly dissolves limestone, forming caves and sinkholes.

days.guide: Build a sand slope in a baking pan, then pour water at slow and fast rates from the same height. The student sketches channels, deltas and where sediment is deposited.

questions.q: Where did sand get deposited and why?
questions.a: Where the water slowed (at the bottom of the slope or on inside bends), because slower water has less energy to carry sediment.

questions.q: How did faster flow change erosion?
questions.a: It cut deeper, wider channels and carried more and larger particles.

days.guide: The student writes the investigation report. Score with the rubric and revise.

questions.q: Give one California example of water shaping the land.
questions.a: Examples: frost wedging of Sierra granite creating talus slopes; rivers carving canyons; waves eroding coastal cliffs; limestone caves such as those in the Sierra foothills.

weeks.assessment_key: Investigation report rubric (HS-ESS2-5): 4 = Includes all three investigations with data (bottle volume increase ≈ 9%; chalk fizzes and dissolves faster in vinegar than water while sugar dissolves faster in water; faster flow carries more and larger sediment, cutting deeper channels); explains each with water's properties (expansion on freezing due to hydrogen-bonded lattice → frost wedging; water as a polar solvent and weak acids from dissolved CO₂ → chemical weathering of limestone; water's cohesion/mass and flow energy → erosion and deposition); connects to a California example (Sierra granite frost wedging, limestone caves, coastal and river erosion). 3 = data plus partial explanations. 2 = data only. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather table salt, the kitchen scale, measuring cups, a 1-cup (≈ 250 mL) container, cabbage indicator, 10 household solutions (lemon juice, vinegar, soda, coffee, milk, tap water, baking soda solution, soap solution, diluted ammonia cleaner — never mix ammonia with bleach), droppers, and clear cups. Open PhET 'pH Scale'.
misconceptions: Students think pH 6 is twice as acidic as pH 3. Each pH unit is a factor of 10: pH 3 has 1,000 times more H₃O⁺ than pH 6.
Students think molarity uses liters of water added. Molarity = moles of solute per liter of total solution.
Students think neutralization makes something disappear. Acid and base form water and a salt.

days.guide: Model M = mol ÷ L. The student makes 250 mL of a 0.50 M salt solution (7.31 g NaCl dissolved, then water added to 250 mL total) and solves concentration problems.

questions.q: How many grams of NaCl are needed for 250 mL of 0.50 M solution?
What is the molarity of 10.0 g of NaOH (40.00 g/mol) in 500 mL of solution?

days.guide: The student adds indicator to each household solution, records colors, and ranks them by pH using a cabbage color chart (red ~1–2, pink ~3–4, purple ~5–7, blue ~8, green ~9–11, yellow ~12+).

questions.q: Which household items are acids?
questions.a: Lemon juice, vinegar, soda, coffee (and slightly, milk).

questions.q: What color would you expect for ammonia cleaner?
questions.a: Green (strongly basic).

days.guide: In PhET pH Scale, the student tests items and relates [H₃O⁺] to pH using the logarithmic scale; record a table of pH vs. [H₃O⁺].

questions.q: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁵ M. What is its pH, and is it acidic?
questions.a: pH 5; acidic.

questions.q: How does [H₃O⁺] change if you dilute an acid tenfold?
questions.a: It drops by a factor of 10, so the pH rises by 1.

days.guide: Measure 10.0 mL of vinegar into a cup with indicator. Add 0.50 M baking-soda solution (2.1 g NaHCO₃ in 50 mL solution) a milliliter at a time, swirling, until the color turns purple-blue and stays. Calculate vinegar's molarity from the volume used.

questions.q: It took 16.6 mL of 0.50 M NaHCO₃ to neutralize 10.0 mL of vinegar. What is the vinegar's molarity?
questions.a: 0.0166 L × 0.50 = 0.0083 mol NaHCO₃ = 0.0083 mol acetic acid (1:1); 0.0083 ÷ 0.0100 L = 0.83 M (about 5% acetic acid).

questions.q: Why add base slowly near the endpoint?
questions.a: To avoid overshooting the exact point where the acid is just neutralized.

days.guide: Give the quiz with a calculator; collect the pH chart and titration data.

questions.q: How many times more H₃O⁺ is in lemon juice (pH 2) than in milk (pH 6.5)?
questions.a: About 10^4.5 ≈ 32,000 times.

weeks.assessment_key: pH chart: full credit for 10 solutions ranked with color observations and approximate pH (lemon ~2, vinegar ~2.5–3, soda ~3, coffee ~5, milk ~6.5, water ~7, baking soda ~8–8.5, soap ~9–10, ammonia ~11–12). Titration data: volume of baking-soda solution needed to reach the endpoint (purple/blue color change) in a measured vinegar sample, with mole calculation (e.g., 10.0 mL of 0.83 M vinegar contains 0.0083 mol acetic acid; with 0.50 M NaHCO₃ the endpoint is about 16.6 mL). Quiz key: 1) Molarity of 0.50 mol NaCl in 2.0 L — 0.25 M. 2) Grams of NaCl for 250 mL of 0.50 M — 7.31 g. 3) pH when [H₃O⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ M — 3. 4) How many times more acidic is pH 3 than pH 5 — 100. 5) Products of HCl + NaOH — NaCl + H₂O. 6) Acidic, basic or neutral: pH 9 — basic. 7) Moles of HCl in 25.0 mL of 0.100 M — 0.00250 mol.

weeks.prep: Gather cabbage indicator, a straw, eggshells (from about 4 eggs, rinsed and dried) or seashells, vinegar, water, two jars, and the kitchen scale. Bookmark NOAA's Hawaii Ocean Time-series (HOT) pH/pCO₂ graph (Station ALOHA) and readings on California oyster hatcheries and pteropods (NOAA Ocean Acidification Program). Build the Unit 8 test from the key.
misconceptions: Students think the ocean is becoming acidic (below pH 7). Seawater is still basic (~pH 8.05); 'acidification' means it is shifting toward acidic — a ~0.1 drop since preindustrial times, about a 26–30% increase in H⁺.
Students think acid directly dissolves all shells in the ocean now. The bigger problem is reduced carbonate ion availability, which makes building shells harder, especially for larvae and pteropods.
Students think vinegar is a realistic ocean model. It is far more acidic; it models the direction of the effect, not its speed.

days.guide: Put purple cabbage indicator water in a cup and have the student blow gently through a straw (never suck) for 1–3 minutes, watching for a color change. Write the equations.

questions.q: Why does the indicator turn pinker when you exhale into it?
questions.a: Exhaled CO₂ dissolves and forms carbonic acid (CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻), lowering the pH.

questions.q: How is this like the ocean?
questions.a: The ocean absorbs about a quarter of human CO₂ emissions, which forms carbonic acid and lowers seawater pH.

days.guide: Weigh equal masses of eggshell into a jar of vinegar and a jar of water. Each day for three days, remove, pat dry, weigh, and return. The student calculates percent mass change.

questions.q: Shells in vinegar went from 10.0 g to 6.5 g. What percent was lost?
Why is there a control jar of water?
questions.a: To show that the mass loss is caused by the acid, not by soaking or handling.

days.guide: Using the HOT/Station ALOHA graph, the student describes trends in seawater pCO₂ and pH since 1988 and calculates the approximate rate of pH change.

questions.q: What relationship do the HOT data show between ocean CO₂ and pH?
questions.a: As dissolved CO₂ rises (tracking atmospheric CO₂), pH falls — an inverse relationship.

questions.q: If pH fell from 8.11 to 8.05 over 30 years, what is the rate?
questions.a: 0.06 ÷ 30 = 0.002 pH units per year (0.02 per decade).

days.guide: The student researches effects on California and West Coast shellfish: oyster hatchery larvae failures in the late 2000s when corrosive upwelled water reached hatcheries, monitoring and buffering now used by hatcheries, and pteropod shell dissolution observed off the West Coast. Write a summary with sources.

questions.q: Why are oyster larvae especially vulnerable?
questions.a: They must build their first shells quickly, and low carbonate water makes that harder and more energy-costly.

questions.q: Why do pteropods matter to the food web?
questions.a: These tiny swimming snails are food for fish such as salmon, so their decline can ripple up the food chain.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test. Grade together and collect the shell lab.

questions.q: Write the equation showing how added H⁺ reduces carbonate ions in seawater.
questions.a: H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻

weeks.assessment_key: Shell lab: full credit for daily mass table for shells in vinegar vs. water, percent mass lost (vinegar shells lose much more; water shells nearly constant), bubbles noted, equation CaCO₃ + 2CH₃COOH → Ca(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂O + CO₂, and a caveat about vinegar being far more acidic than seawater. Unit 8 test key (sample): 1) Water expands ~9% when it freezes because of its open hydrogen-bonded lattice. 2) Molarity of 1.5 mol in 3.0 L — 0.50 M. 3) pH 4 vs. pH 7: 1,000× more H₃O⁺. 4) CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. 5) Added H⁺ combines with CO₃²⁻ to make HCO₃⁻, lowering carbonate available for CaCO₃ shells. 6) Surface ocean pH dropped from about 8.2 to about 8.1 (now ~8.05). 7) Breathing into indicator turns it from purple toward pink (more acidic). 8) A buffer resists changes in pH. 9) Neutralization: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. 10) Chalk dissolves faster in vinegar than water — acid reacts with carbonate.

weeks.prep: Help the student choose a challenge and gather supplies for the prototype (e.g., for a water filter: a cut plastic bottle, coffee filter, sand, gravel, activated charcoal from a pet store, muddy water — the filtered water is not safe to drink; for an insulated container: boxes, foam, foil, thermometer). Prepare the capstone rubric to share at the start.
misconceptions: Students start building before defining criteria. Require written criteria and constraints first so the test has something to measure.
Students cite only one website. Require three sources, including one government or peer-reviewed source.
Students treat a prototype failure as failure. A failed test produces data for redesign; that is engineering.

days.guide: Discuss three options. The student chooses one and writes a problem statement, at least three criteria (measurable) and two constraints.

questions.q: For an activated-charcoal water filter, give a measurable criterion.
questions.a: Example: reduces turbidity so text is readable through 10 cm of water, or removes a set amount of food dye color within 2 minutes.

questions.q: Give a constraint.
questions.a: Example: total materials cost under $10, or uses only household materials.

days.guide: The student finds three sources (at least one .gov, .edu or peer-reviewed) and writes notes on the chemistry of the problem and solution, with citations.

questions.q: How does activated charcoal remove contaminants?
questions.a: Adsorption: molecules stick to the charcoal's enormous internal surface area (hundreds of m² per gram).

questions.q: Why is source quality important?
questions.a: Reliable sources reduce the chance of basing the design on wrong information.

days.guide: The student builds and tests the prototype, recording quantitative data and at least two trials.

questions.q: Why run more than one trial?
questions.a: To check that results are repeatable and to estimate variability.

questions.q: Is filtered muddy water safe to drink?
questions.a: No — the filter does not reliably remove bacteria or viruses; it must be disinfected or boiled.

days.guide: The student evaluates the prototype against each criterion in a table (met / partly / not met) and lists trade-offs and improvements.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'evaluating' and 'describing' a design?
questions.a: Evaluating judges performance against criteria using data; describing only tells what was built.

days.guide: The student drafts a slide presentation (8–10 slides). Review with the rubric and give two specific suggestions.

questions.q: What should the data slide include?
questions.a: A graph or table with labeled units and a one-sentence takeaway.

weeks.assessment_key: Capstone checkpoint rubric (4 levels): 4 = Problem statement; at least three measurable criteria and two constraints; chemistry explained with three cited sources (e.g., adsorption of contaminants onto activated carbon's huge surface area; insulation reducing conduction/convection/radiation); prototype built and tested with quantitative data (e.g., turbidity rating before/after, temperature drop over time); evaluation against each criterion with trade-offs; draft slides with title, problem, chemistry, design, data, evaluation, next steps. 3 = all parts present but data or chemistry thin. 2 = missing testing or sources. 1 = idea only.

weeks.prep: Arrange the capstone presentation with family. Build a cumulative final exam from the key (about 40 items, 90 minutes, periodic table and formula sheet allowed). Have the Week 1 candle questions and the driving-question board ready.
misconceptions: Students memorize answers to past quizzes rather than practicing new problems. Use fresh numbers in review.
Students skip units on the final. Deduct for missing units on calculations.
Students write the final candle explanation as a list. It should be a connected explanation linking atoms, bonds, energy and the Earth system.

days.guide: The student presents the capstone (10 minutes) and answers questions. Score with the capstone rubric and share one strength and one improvement.

questions.q: Ask: What would you change if you had another month?
questions.a: A strong answer names a specific weakness shown by the data and a concrete redesign.

days.guide: Mixed review covering all units: equations, stoichiometry, energy, bonding, equilibrium, pH, climate. Reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many grams of CO₂ form from 0.10 mol of NaHCO₃ reacting with excess vinegar?
A reaction is endothermic. On an energy diagram, are the products higher or lower than the reactants?
questions.a: Higher.

days.guide: Give the final exam in one 90-minute sitting.

questions.q: (After the exam) Which unit felt strongest and which weakest?
questions.a: Answers vary; use them to guide Day 4 corrections.

days.guide: Return the exam. The student corrects every missed item and writes the reason for each error (concept, careless, units).

questions.q: Why categorize errors?
questions.a: It shows whether mistakes come from misunderstanding or carelessness, guiding what to practice.

days.guide: The student writes a final, connected explanation of the burning candle using ideas from every unit and compares it to the Week 1 questions.

questions.q: In one sentence, where does the candle's mass go and where does its energy come from?
questions.a: The wax's carbon and hydrogen atoms combine with oxygen to form CO₂ and H₂O gases that enter the air (conserving mass), and the energy comes from forming stronger bonds in those products than were broken in the wax and oxygen.

weeks.assessment_key: Capstone rubric: 4 = clear problem and criteria, accurate chemistry, data-driven evaluation, trade-offs, confident delivery, answers questions. Final exam key (sample core items): 1) Balance C₃H₈ + O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O with 5O₂. 2) 200 g water warmed 15 °C absorbs 12,550 J. 3) Neutrons in ¹⁴C — 8. 4) 40 g of an isotope with half-life 10 yr after 30 yr — 5 g. 5) Ionic formula of calcium chloride — CaCl₂. 6) Shape of CO₂ — linear, nonpolar. 7) Moles in 88 g CO₂ — 2.0. 8) Grams CO₂ from 8.4 g NaHCO₃ (0.10 mol) — 4.4 g. 9) Limiting reactant: 3.0 mol H₂ and 1.0 mol O₂ → O₂ limits, 2.0 mol H₂O. 10) ΔH for CH₄ combustion from bond energies — −802 kJ/mol. 11) Exothermic reaction, temperature raised — shifts left. 12) pH 3 vs. pH 6 — 1,000× more acidic. 13) Why CO₂ is a greenhouse gas — absorbs infrared. 14) Ocean acidification reduces carbonate ions. 15) Positive feedback example — ice-albedo. Final candle explanation rubric: 4 = connects wax hydrocarbon structure, combustion equation and conservation of mass, bond energies explaining the release of energy, CO₂'s role in the greenhouse effect and the carbon cycle, and ocean uptake.

VAPA.overview: Music & Media Arts runs about 45 minutes a day: Semester 1 builds music literacy (notation, rhythm, scales, chords), beat-making, songwriting and listening across Western, American and world traditions; Semester 2 moves to media arts — photography, design, copyright, sound design, podcasting, film language, video, scoring and a capstone. Each lesson is a short demonstration followed by hands-on creating with free tools (musictheory.net, BandLab, MuseScore/Noteflight, Audacity, a free photo/video editor), and every project ends with feedback, revision and a short written reflection. Keep a portfolio from day one and require proper credits and licenses for anything not original.

weeks.prep: Bookmark musictheory.net (Lessons and Exercises → Note Identification). Install a free keyboard app or use a piano/keyboard. Print a blank grand staff and a 30-note quiz (mix treble and bass, include middle C and a few ledger-line notes). Read the student's musical autobiography prompt yourself.
misconceptions: Students read bass clef as if it were treble (seeing a G line and calling it E). Teach bass clef separately: lines G-B-D-F-A ('Good Boys Do Fine Always'), spaces A-C-E-G ('All Cows Eat Grass').
Students think middle C is in the middle of the treble staff. Middle C sits on one ledger line below the treble staff (or above the bass staff).
Students think an octave is eight different note names. An octave spans eight letter steps from one note to the next with the same name (C to C), seven distinct letters.

days.guide: The student writes a one-page musical autobiography: songs from childhood, family music, favorite artists, any instruments, and three goals for the year. Discuss it together.

questions.q: What's one goal that is specific and measurable for this course?
questions.a: Example: 'Name any note on the grand staff within 3 seconds by Week 5' or 'Record an original song by Week 13.'

days.guide: The student completes musictheory.net treble-clef lessons and drills until 90% accuracy.

questions.q: Name the notes on the treble-clef lines from bottom to top.
questions.a: E, G, B, D, F.

questions.q: Name the treble-clef spaces.
questions.a: F, A, C, E.

days.guide: The student completes bass-clef lessons and drills, then labels a printed grand staff.

questions.q: Name the bass-clef lines bottom to top.
questions.a: G, B, D, F, A.

questions.q: Where is middle C on the grand staff?
questions.a: On the ledger line between the staves — one ledger line below treble, one above bass.

days.guide: The student finds all C's (left of the two black keys), F's (left of the three black keys) and G's on a keyboard, then plays a C-major scale with fingering: right hand 1-2-3-1-2-3-4-5 (thumb tucks under after E); left hand 5-4-3-2-1-3-2-1.

questions.q: How do you find C on a keyboard?
questions.a: It is the white key just to the left of each group of two black keys.

days.guide: Give the 30-note, 2-minute quiz; review misses with mnemonics.

questions.q: A note sits on the top line of the bass staff. What is it?
questions.a: A.

weeks.assessment_key: Note-naming quiz: 30 notes in 2 minutes; 27+ correct (90%) = mastery, 21–26 = more drill, under 21 = reteach with mnemonics. Answer key reference: treble lines E-G-B-D-F, spaces F-A-C-E; bass lines G-B-D-F-A, spaces A-C-E-G; middle C = one ledger line below treble/above bass; treble ledger below staff: D (space below), C (first ledger line); bass ledger above: B (space above), C (first ledger line).

weeks.prep: Metronome app, musictheory.net rhythm lessons, Chrome Music Lab Rhythm, a printed rhythm ladder (whole → half → quarter → eighth → sixteenth), and an 8-measure body-percussion score (stomp/pat/clap/snap rows). Phone for video.
misconceptions: Students hold notes the wrong length after dotted notes. A dot adds half the note's value: dotted half = 3 beats in 4/4.
Students rush rests. Rests are counted silence; say the counts aloud.
Students think the top number of a time signature names the note type. Top = beats per measure; bottom = which note gets one beat (4 = quarter).

days.guide: The student learns note and rest values and claps a rhythm ladder while counting ('1-e-&-a').

questions.q: In 4/4, how many eighth notes equal one half note?
questions.a: Four.

days.guide: Count and clap rhythms in 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 with the metronome at 80 bpm.

questions.q: What does 3/4 mean?
questions.a: Three beats per measure; the quarter note gets one beat.

questions.q: How many beats does a dotted half note get in 3/4?
questions.a: Three — a full measure.

days.guide: The student notates four 2-measure rhythms you clap or play in Chrome Music Lab.

questions.q: Tip for dictation?
questions.a: Count the beats aloud while listening, first mark where each beat falls, then fill in subdivisions.

days.guide: The student performs an 8-measure body-percussion piece reading notation.

questions.q: What should you do if you make a mistake while performing?
questions.a: Keep the beat going and rejoin on the next measure.

days.guide: Record the rhythm reading assessment on video and score with the rubric.

questions.q: How many sixteenth notes fit in one quarter note?
questions.a: Four.

weeks.assessment_key: Recorded rhythm performance rubric: 4 = steady tempo with metronome at 80 bpm, all note and rest values correct, counts spoken or clear, 8 measures without stopping; 3 = 1–2 errors; 2 = several errors or tempo drift; 1 = cannot complete. Theory checks: whole = 4 beats, half = 2, quarter = 1, eighth = ½, sixteenth = ¼ (in 4/4); 3/4 has three quarter-note beats per measure.

weeks.prep: Keyboard app, musictheory.net (Scales, Key Signatures, Intervals), a circle-of-fifths printout, and song references for intervals.
misconceptions: Students think there is no half step between E–F and B–C. Those white-key pairs are half steps (no black key between).
Students read key signatures by counting accidentals only. Sharp key: the note a half step above the last sharp. Flat key: the second-to-last flat (F major has one flat, B♭).
Students name intervals only by letter distance. Quality matters too: C–E is a major 3rd (4 half steps); C–E♭ is a minor 3rd (3 half steps).

days.guide: The student builds C, G, D and F major scales on the keyboard using W-W-H-W-W-W-H.

questions.q: Build the D major scale.
questions.a: D E F♯ G A B C♯ D.

days.guide: Teach the circle of fifths for sharp keys and the order of sharps.

questions.q: How many sharps are in E major, and which?
questions.a: Four: F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯.

days.guide: The student identifies flat key signatures.

questions.q: A key signature has B♭, E♭ and A♭. What major key is it?
questions.a: E♭ major (second-to-last flat).

days.guide: Identify and sing intervals using song references.

questions.q: What interval begins 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' (on 'twinkle, twinkle')?
questions.a: A perfect 5th.

questions.q: How many half steps are in a perfect 4th?
questions.a: Five.

days.guide: Give the scales and intervals quiz.

questions.q: What's the relative minor of C major?
questions.a: A minor (no sharps or flats).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Major scale pattern — W-W-H-W-W-W-H. 2) G major scale — G A B C D E F♯ G. 3) D major — D E F♯ G A B C♯ D. 4) F major — F G A B♭ C D E F. 5) Order of sharps — F C G D A E B. 6) Order of flats — B E A D G C F. 7) Key with 3 sharps — A major. 8) Key with 4 flats — A♭ major. 9) C to G — perfect 5th. 10) C to F — perfect 4th. 11) C to E — major 3rd. 12) C to A — major 6th. 13) 'Here Comes the Bride' opening — P4; 'Twinkle Twinkle' first leap — P5; 'Happy Birthday' first step — M2; 'Somewhere Over the Rainbow' first leap — octave.

weeks.prep: Keyboard, voice, ukulele or recorder; three 8-bar sight-reading melodies (e.g., from sightreadingfactory.com free trial or a beginner method book); a simple piece (Ode to Joy or a folk song); practice log; performance rubric.
misconceptions: Students practice pieces from the beginning every time. Isolate hard measures, play slowly, then connect.
Students ignore dynamics until the end. Add expression from the start of practice.
Students stop at every mistake when sight-reading. Keep the beat and keep going.

days.guide: Teach dynamics, tempo and articulation markings with examples.

questions.q: What does mf mean?
questions.a: Mezzo forte — moderately loud.

questions.q: What's the difference between staccato and legato?
questions.a: Staccato is short and detached; legato is smooth and connected.

days.guide: The student sight-reads three 8-bar melodies, first scanning key, time signature and tricky spots.

questions.q: What should you check before sight-reading?
questions.a: Key signature, time signature, tempo marking, and any tricky rhythms or accidentals.

days.guide: The student selects a short piece to perform and marks phrases and breaths.

questions.q: What is a phrase in music?
questions.a: A musical 'sentence', often 4 bars, ending with a cadence or breathing point.

days.guide: Use a practice log and slow practice on difficult measures.

questions.q: Describe an effective slow-practice strategy.
questions.a: Play the hard measure slowly with a metronome until correct 3 times, then raise the tempo gradually.

days.guide: Record a performance and self-evaluate with the rubric.

questions.q: What's the Italian term for gradually slowing down?
questions.a: Ritardando (rit.).

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric (4 levels): pitch accuracy, rhythm/steady tempo, expression (dynamics and articulation as marked), tone and posture, and self-evaluation with two specific goals. Proficient = few errors, clear dynamic contrast, steady tempo. Markings key: p (piano) soft, f (forte) loud, mp/mf medium soft/loud, crescendo gets louder, decrescendo/diminuendo softer; allegro fast, andante walking, adagio slow, ritardando gradually slower; staccato short/detached, legato smooth, accent emphasized.

weeks.prep: Buckets, pots and wooden spoons for drums; claves or two sticks; salsa recordings; Smithsonian Folkways recordings of Brazilian samba, Ghanaian drumming and Indian classical tala.
misconceptions: Students think syncopation is random off-beat notes. It's deliberate emphasis on weak beats or off-beats against a steady pulse.
Students play 3-against-2 by guessing. Use 'nice cup of tea' or count 6 pulses: 3-beat part on 1, 3, 5; 2-beat part on 1, 4.
Students think clave patterns change direction randomly. The 3-2 or 2-3 direction is set by the song and stays consistent.

days.guide: Clap and count syncopated rhythms (e.g., eighth-quarter-eighth patterns, ties across beats).

questions.q: What is syncopation?
questions.a: Emphasis on normally weak beats or off-beats.

days.guide: Learn the son clave (3-2: beats 1, 2&, 4 | 2, 3) and play it with salsa recordings.

questions.q: Write the counts of a 3-2 son clave in two bars of 4/4.

days.guide: Layer 3-against-2 polyrhythms with family on household drums.

questions.q: How do you count 3 against 2?
questions.a: Use six pulses: one part plays on 1, 3, 5 (three notes); the other plays on 1 and 4 (two notes).

days.guide: Listen to rhythms from Brazil, Ghana and India and log features.

questions.q: What is a tala in Indian classical music?
questions.a: A repeating rhythmic cycle of a fixed number of beats (e.g., teental has 16).

days.guide: Perform a polyrhythm ensemble.

questions.q: What is an ostinato?
questions.a: A short pattern repeated persistently.

weeks.assessment_key: Ensemble performance rubric: steady pulse maintained by all parts; correct polyrhythm (3:2 aligned on beat 1); son clave played correctly (3-2: beats 1, 2&, 4 | 2, 3); dynamics/balance; 1–2 minutes without breaking. Proficient = all parts locked with at most minor slips. Listening log key features: samba (Brazil) — surdo bass drums, interlocking percussion, 2/4 feel; Ghana (Ewe) — bell timeline, layered polyrhythms, master drum; India — tala cycles such as teental (16 beats), tabla, improvisation within the cycle.

weeks.prep: Set up a free BandLab account (parent-managed for under-18 privacy settings) and explore the Studio and drum sequencer. Headphones help.
misconceptions: Students put snare on every beat in a rock beat. Standard rock: kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4 (backbeat), hi-hat eighth notes.
Students quantize everything to 100%, making grooves stiff. Swing or slight humanization creates feel, especially in hip-hop.
Students confuse BPM with loudness. BPM is tempo (beats per minute).

days.guide: Tour the DAW interface: tracks, timeline, transport, mixer, instruments.

questions.q: What does DAW stand for?
questions.a: Digital Audio Workstation.

days.guide: Program a basic rock beat at 100 bpm.

questions.q: On which beats does the snare play in a rock beat?
questions.a: Beats 2 and 4 (the backbeat).

days.guide: Program a hip-hop beat with swing.

questions.q: What does swing do to eighth or sixteenth notes?
questions.a: Delays the off-beat notes slightly, creating a long-short lilt.

days.guide: Program a reggaeton dembow and a four-on-the-floor house beat.

questions.q: What does 'four-on-the-floor' mean?
questions.a: The kick drum hits on every quarter-note beat.

days.guide: Share four beats with labeled screenshots.

questions.q: What is quantizing?
questions.a: Snapping recorded notes to the nearest grid position to correct timing.

weeks.assessment_key: Beat portfolio: four beats with labeled screenshots. Rock (100 bpm): kick 1 and 3, snare 2 and 4, closed hi-hat eighths. Hip-hop (85–95 bpm): kick pattern syncopated, snare/clap on 2 and 4, hi-hats with swing (~55–65%). Reggaeton dembow (~90–100 bpm): kick on every beat; snare on the 'a' of 1, '&' of 2, 'a' of 3, '&' of 4. House (120–128 bpm): kick on every beat (four-on-the-floor), clap/snare on 2 and 4, open hi-hat on the off-beats. Proficient = correct patterns, tempos and labels.

weeks.prep: BandLab; a favorite song (clean) for form analysis; feedback form for family.
misconceptions: Students write bass lines with random notes. Start with chord roots on beat 1, then add passing tones.
Students stack loops that clash in key. Check loop key and tempo before layering.
Students make songs with no change. Arrangement means adding and removing parts to create sections.

days.guide: The student writes a bass line using chord roots of a progression (e.g., C–G–Am–F).

questions.q: What notes would a root-note bass line play over C–G–Am–F?
questions.a: C, G, A, F.

days.guide: Explore the loop library and layer three loops in the same key and tempo.

questions.q: Why check a loop's key?
questions.a: Loops in different keys can clash harmonically.

days.guide: The student analyzes a favorite song's form with timestamps.

questions.q: What's the difference between a verse and a chorus?
questions.a: Verses change lyrics and tell the story; the chorus repeats the main hook and lyrics.

days.guide: Arrange a 90-second instrumental with clear sections.

questions.q: How can you make a 'drop' or chorus feel bigger?
questions.a: Add layers (bass, drums, synths), raise energy, or remove parts just before it for contrast.

days.guide: Get family feedback and revise.

questions.q: What makes feedback useful?
questions.a: It's specific (time stamp and element) and suggests a change.

weeks.assessment_key: Draft track rubric: 90 seconds, at least three sections (e.g., intro, verse, drop/chorus) with clear changes; bass line following chord roots; three or more layered loops in the same key; revisions noted from family feedback. Form analysis key example: Intro – Verse 1 – Pre-chorus – Chorus – Verse 2 – Pre-chorus – Chorus – Bridge – Chorus – Outro.

weeks.prep: BandLab; criteria sheet for the listening party; headphones and speakers to compare.
misconceptions: Students make everything loud. Balance levels so the main element is clear and the mix doesn't clip (meters stay out of the red).
Students pan everything center. Panning places sounds left-right for space; keep kick, bass and lead vocal centered.
Students write artist statements that just list software steps. Explain artistic choices and intent.

days.guide: Teach volume balance and panning.

questions.q: Which elements are usually panned center?
questions.a: Kick drum, bass and lead vocal or main melody.

days.guide: Refine with automation and fades.

questions.q: What is automation in a DAW?
questions.a: Programmed changes over time to settings like volume or panning.

days.guide: The student writes a 150-word artist statement.

questions.q: What should an artist statement include?
questions.a: What you made, your intent or mood, influences, and key choices and why.

days.guide: Share the track with family and collect criteria-sheet feedback.

questions.q: Why use a criteria sheet?
questions.a: It focuses feedback on specific elements instead of 'I like it'.

days.guide: Submit the final track.

questions.q: What does 'clipping' mean?
questions.a: The signal exceeds the maximum level and distorts.

weeks.assessment_key: Track and statement rubric: Mix (balanced levels, no clipping, purposeful panning, fades), Arrangement (clear sections, development), Creativity, Artist statement (150 words: intent, influences, specific choices and why). Each 1–4; proficient 12+/16.

weeks.prep: Keyboard (and ukulele/guitar if available), Roman numeral chart for C and G major, five pop songs using I–V–vi–IV (e.g., 'Let It Be', 'Don't Stop Believin'', 'Someone Like You', 'With or Without You', 'I'm Yours'), and the chords quiz.
misconceptions: Students build minor triads by lowering the root. Lower the third: C major C–E–G → C minor C–E♭–G.
Students capitalize all Roman numerals. Uppercase = major, lowercase = minor, ° = diminished.
Students think the I–V–vi–IV songs are copies. A shared progression is common and not copyrightable; melody and lyrics differ.

days.guide: Build major and minor triads on the keyboard.

questions.q: Build an F major triad.
questions.a: F A C.

questions.q: Change F major to F minor.
questions.a: F A♭ C.

days.guide: Label chords in a key with Roman numerals.

questions.q: In G major, what chord is vi?
questions.a: E minor (Em).

days.guide: Identify the four-chord progression in five pop songs.

questions.q: Write I–V–vi–IV in D major.
questions.a: D A Bm G.

days.guide: Play a 12-bar blues progression.

questions.q: Write the 12-bar blues in G.
questions.a: G G G G | C C G G | D C G G (or D).

days.guide: Give the chords quiz.

questions.q: What is a chord inversion?
questions.a: A chord with a note other than the root in the bass (e.g., C/E).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) C major triad — C E G. 2) A minor — A C E. 3) G major — G B D. 4) D minor — D F A. 5) Chords in C major — I C, ii Dm, iii Em, IV F, V G, vi Am, vii° Bdim. 6) I–V–vi–IV in C — C G Am F; in G — G D Em C. 7) 12-bar blues in C — C C C C | F F C C | G F C C (or G turnaround). 8) First inversion of C — E G C. 9) Major triad = root + major 3rd + minor 3rd (4 + 3 half steps). 10) The chord built on the 5th scale degree is the dominant (V).

weeks.prep: Install MuseScore or open Noteflight (free). Queue Beethoven's Symphony No. 5, mvt. 1 opening and a pop song with a clear motif. Print staff paper for contour sketches.
misconceptions: Students write melodies with constant leaps. Good melodies mostly move by step with occasional leaps, often followed by a step in the opposite direction.
Students end melodies anywhere. Strong endings resolve to the tonic (do) over the I chord (authentic cadence).
Students think a motif must be long. A motif can be 2–4 notes, like Beethoven's short-short-short-long.

days.guide: Analyze motifs in Beethoven's Fifth (short-short-short-long: G-G-G-E♭) and a pop song.

questions.q: Describe the rhythm of Beethoven's Fifth opening motif.
questions.a: Three short notes followed by a long one (short-short-short-long).

days.guide: Sketch melodic contours (arch, wave, ascending) and turn them into notation.

questions.q: What is melodic contour?
questions.a: The overall shape of a melody — rising, falling, arch, wave.

days.guide: Compose an 8-bar melody over I–IV–V–I.

questions.q: Which notes fit well over a C major chord on a strong beat?
questions.a: Chord tones C, E and G.

days.guide: Revise for cadence and singability.

questions.q: What is an authentic cadence?
questions.a: V to I, ending on the tonic; it sounds final.

days.guide: Share notation and a recording.

questions.q: What makes a melody memorable?
questions.a: A clear motif that repeats with variation, a singable range and a strong rhythm.

weeks.assessment_key: Melody composition rubric: 8 bars over I–IV–V–I (e.g., C–F–G–C, two bars each), uses a motif that repeats or varies, mostly stepwise with purposeful leaps, chord tones on strong beats, singable range (about an octave), ends on the tonic with an authentic cadence (V–I); notation correct; recording included. Proficient = all criteria with minor issues.

weeks.prep: Lyric notebook; lyrics of a classic song (e.g., 'Yesterday' by the Beatles or 'Respect' by Aretha Franklin) printed for analysis; rhyme scheme examples.
misconceptions: Students force rhymes that change meaning. Use near rhymes (slant rhymes) when perfect rhymes distort the message.
Students write verses that repeat the chorus idea. Verses add details and story; the chorus states the main idea.
Students ignore natural word stress. Prosody means stressed syllables land on strong beats.

days.guide: Analyze a classic song's hook and rhyme scheme.

questions.q: Label the rhyme scheme of four lines ending 'day/night/away/light'.
questions.a: ABAB.

days.guide: Brainstorm themes and write a chorus with a hook.

questions.q: What is a hook?
questions.a: A short, catchy musical or lyrical phrase that sticks in the listener's mind, usually in the chorus.

days.guide: Write two verses with imagery.

questions.q: Turn 'I was sad' into an image.
questions.a: Example: 'Rain on the window, cold cup in my hand.'

days.guide: Match lyric stresses to musical rhythm (prosody).

questions.q: Where should the stress fall in 'tomorrow'?
questions.a: On the second syllable: to-MOR-row — place it on a strong beat.

days.guide: Share a lyric draft.

questions.q: What's a slant rhyme?
questions.a: A near rhyme with similar but not identical sounds (e.g., 'home'/'stone').

weeks.assessment_key: Lyric draft rubric: chorus with a clear, repeatable hook; two verses with concrete imagery that develop the theme; consistent rhyme scheme (e.g., ABAB or AABB) with natural phrasing; prosody check marks stressed syllables. Proficient = all present with mostly natural stresses.

weeks.prep: BandLab with a USB or phone microphone, the lyric draft, a chord progression, and an 'I like / I wonder / What if' feedback sheet.
misconceptions: Students write bridges that sound like the chorus. A bridge contrasts: new chords (e.g., starting on vi or IV), different melodic range or rhythm.
Students over-produce demos. A demo captures the song's structure and melody; polish comes later.
Students defend every line in feedback. Listen first; decide later.

days.guide: Sing or play the lyric over the progression, adjusting so stressed syllables land on strong beats.

questions.q: Which beats are strong in 4/4?
questions.a: Beats 1 and 3 (beat 1 strongest).

days.guide: Write a 4–8 bar bridge that contrasts with the chorus.

questions.q: Give two ways to make a bridge contrast.
questions.a: Start on a different chord like vi or IV, change melodic range or rhythm, or change lyric perspective.

days.guide: Record a rough demo in BandLab with a simple part and scratch vocal.

questions.q: What is a scratch vocal?
questions.a: A temporary guide vocal recorded to hear the song, replaced later.

days.guide: Play the demo for a listener and collect feedback with 'I like / I wonder / What if'.

questions.q: Why use a structured protocol?
questions.a: It balances positives, questions and suggestions so feedback is useful and kind.

days.guide: Revise a lyric line, a melodic phrase and the arrangement; save version 2.

questions.q: Why save versions?
questions.a: To compare and go back if a change doesn't work.

weeks.assessment_key: Demo checkpoint: complete song form (verse–chorus–verse–chorus–bridge–chorus), lyric set with prosody, contrasting bridge, rough recording with accompaniment and scratch vocal, documented feedback, version 2 with three specific revisions (lyric line, melodic phrase, arrangement). Proficient = all present.

weeks.prep: BandLab, microphone, MuseScore/Noteflight for the lead sheet, and the song rubric.
misconceptions: Students record one take and keep it. Record three or more and choose (or comp) the best.
Students add heavy reverb to hide problems. Light reverb adds space; too much muddies the mix.
Students leave chord symbols out of lead sheets. A lead sheet has melody, chord symbols above the staff and lyrics below.

days.guide: Record final vocal or lead tracks with at least three takes.

questions.q: What helps a vocal recording sound clear?
questions.a: A quiet room with soft surfaces, consistent distance from the mic (about 6–12 inches), and a pop filter.

days.guide: Mix: balance levels, pan supporting parts and add light reverb.

questions.q: What does reverb simulate?
questions.a: The reflections of sound in a space, like a room or hall.

days.guide: Create a lead sheet with melody, chord symbols and lyrics.

questions.q: Where do chord symbols go on a lead sheet?
questions.a: Above the staff, over the beat where each chord changes.

days.guide: Present the song and explain how melody, harmony and form support the lyric.

questions.q: Give an example of music supporting lyrics.
questions.a: A rising melody on a hopeful line, or a minor chord on a sad word.

days.guide: Write a 250-word reflection and score on the rubric.

questions.q: What should a process reflection discuss?
questions.a: Challenges, decisions, feedback used and what you'd do differently.

weeks.assessment_key: Song rubric (each 1–4): Lyrics (hook, imagery, prosody), Melody (motif, singable, cadences), Harmony (fitting progression, contrasting bridge), Form, Production (balance, panning, light reverb, no clipping), Lead sheet accuracy, Presentation and reflection (250 words). Proficient 21+/28.

weeks.prep: Recordings: Bach, Brandenburg Concerto No. 3 in G (mvt. 1); Mozart, Symphony No. 40 in G minor, K. 550 (mvt. 1); Chopin, Nocturne in E-flat, Op. 9 No. 2. A timeline template. A listening quiz of 8–10 short excerpts.
misconceptions: Students think 'classical' means all old music. The Classical period (c. 1750–1820) is one era; others include Baroque (c. 1600–1750) and Romantic (c. 1820–1900).
Students confuse texture terms. Polyphonic = several independent melodies (Bach); homophonic = melody with accompaniment (much Mozart, Chopin).
Students think sonata form is a piece for one instrument. Sonata form is a structure (exposition–development–recapitulation) used in symphony and sonata movements.

days.guide: Listen to Brandenburg No. 3 and describe the texture.

questions.q: What texture dominates the Brandenburg Concerto No. 3?
questions.a: Polyphonic (contrapuntal) — several string parts weaving independent lines, with continuo.

days.guide: Listen to Mozart's Symphony No. 40, mvt. 1 and map sonata form with timestamps.

questions.q: What are the three main sections of sonata form?
questions.a: Exposition, development, recapitulation (often plus a coda).

questions.q: In the recapitulation of a minor-key symphony like No. 40, what key does the second theme return in?
questions.a: The home key, G minor.

days.guide: Listen to Chopin's Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2 and describe its expression.

questions.q: What is rubato?
questions.a: Flexible tempo — stretching and pushing the beat for expression.

days.guide: Create a timeline linking periods to world events (e.g., Bach — Enlightenment beginnings; Mozart — American Revolution era; Chopin — revolutions of 1830/1848).

questions.q: Name one historical event during Mozart's lifetime.
questions.a: The American Revolution (1775–1783) or the start of the French Revolution (1789).

days.guide: Give the listening identification quiz.

questions.q: Which period features harpsichord continuo?
questions.a: Baroque.

weeks.assessment_key: Listening quiz key: identify period and composer with one musical clue — Baroque/Bach: continuous motor rhythm, polyphony, terraced dynamics, harpsichord continuo; Classical/Mozart: balanced phrases, clear homophony, contrasting themes in sonata form; Romantic/Chopin: expressive rubato, wide dynamics, lyrical ornamented melody over broken-chord accompaniment. Sonata form map (Mozart 40, mvt. 1): exposition (first theme G minor; transition; second theme B♭ major), development (fragments modulate through keys), recapitulation (both themes return in G minor), coda. Timeline: Baroque c. 1600–1750; Classical c. 1750–1820; Romantic c. 1820–1900.

weeks.prep: Library of Congress and Smithsonian recordings: a spiritual ('Swing Low, Sweet Chariot' or 'Go Down, Moses'), Robert Johnson ('Cross Road Blues'), Louis Armstrong ('West End Blues', 1928), Duke Ellington ('It Don't Mean a Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing)', 1932). Keyboard for blues scale improvisation. Writing prompt for a 400-word response.
misconceptions: Students think jazz is just improvisation. Jazz combines composed forms (blues, 32-bar song form) with improvisation and swing feel.
Students think rock and roll appeared from nowhere. It grew from rhythm and blues, gospel, blues and country.
Students hear swing as faster music. Swing is a rhythmic feel with uneven (long-short) eighth notes and emphasis on 2 and 4.

days.guide: Listen to spirituals and Robert Johnson; identify call and response.

questions.q: What is call and response?
questions.a: A leader sings or plays a phrase and a group or instrument answers — rooted in West African traditions.

days.guide: Listen to Armstrong and Ellington; describe swing.

questions.q: What did Louis Armstrong contribute to jazz?
questions.a: He made the improvised solo central to jazz, with virtuosic trumpet and influential scat singing.

days.guide: Improvise over a 12-bar blues using the blues scale.

questions.q: Spell the C blues scale.
questions.a: C E♭ F F♯ (G♭) G B♭ C.

days.guide: Trace rock, soul and hip-hop origins on a family tree.

questions.q: Where and when did hip-hop begin?
questions.a: The Bronx, New York, in the 1970s (DJ Kool Herc's parties, 1973, are often cited).

days.guide: The student writes a 400-word response on how one genre reflects its era.

questions.q: What are 'blue notes'?
questions.a: Flattened or bent notes (especially the 3rd, 5th and 7th) that give the blues its expressive sound.

weeks.assessment_key: Written response rubric (400 words): 4 = thesis connecting a genre to its era; at least two specific musical features (call and response, blue notes, 12-bar form, swing eighths, improvisation, backbeat) and two historical contexts (slavery and emancipation; Great Migration; Jim Crow; Harlem Renaissance; postwar youth culture; civil rights) with named examples; clear organization; accurate facts. 3 = solid but less specific. 2 = general. 1 = inaccurate or incomplete.

weeks.prep: Smithsonian Folkways recordings of Balinese gamelan (gamelan gong kebyar), a Hindustani raga performance (e.g., Ravi Shankar), mariachi (e.g., Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán) and son jarocho ('La Bamba' traditional versions); a professional music review (newspaper or Pitchfork/NPR).
misconceptions: Students describe unfamiliar music as 'weird'. Use descriptive vocabulary: timbre, texture, tempo, form.
Students think raga is just a scale. A raga includes a set of notes plus characteristic phrases, mood, and often time of day.
Students treat reviews as pure opinion. Good reviews use criteria and evidence.

days.guide: Listen to Balinese gamelan and describe interlocking parts.

questions.q: What is kotekan in Balinese gamelan?
questions.a: Interlocking parts where two players' rhythms fit together to create one fast composite melody.

days.guide: Listen to a raga and describe its structure.

questions.q: What happens in the alap of a Hindustani raga performance?
questions.a: A slow, unmetered opening that explores the raga's notes without drums, over a drone.

days.guide: Study mariachi and son jarocho and their role in California.

questions.q: Name two instruments unique to mariachi.
questions.a: The vihuela and the guitarrón (also violins and trumpets).

questions.q: Where does son jarocho come from?
questions.a: Veracruz, Mexico; it uses jarana, requinto and harp, with zapateado on a wooden platform.

days.guide: Read a professional music review and identify its criteria.

questions.q: What criteria might a reviewer use?
questions.a: Technique, interpretation, sound quality, originality, emotional impact, programming.

days.guide: The student writes a review of a performance.

questions.q: What makes a review persuasive?
questions.a: Specific evidence (moments, sounds) supporting each judgment.

weeks.assessment_key: Music review rubric: 4 = names performance and context; uses at least three criteria (technique, interpretation, timbre/sound, energy, program/structure); supports judgments with specific moments; uses vocabulary correctly; clear verdict; 300–500 words. 3 = criteria with some evidence. 2 = mostly opinion. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Instrument or voice, recordings of the student's semester work, a practice log, a program-notes example, and a feedback sheet for the dress rehearsal.
misconceptions: Students practice only the start of pieces. Rotate practice to begin with the hardest sections.
Students write program notes that are biographies. Program notes guide listeners on what to hear.
Students treat the dress rehearsal casually. Run it exactly like the performance.

days.guide: Select one performance piece and one original.

questions.q: What makes a good showcase program?
questions.a: Contrast in style and tempo, pieces you can play confidently, and an engaging order.

days.guide: Rehearse with a practice log.

questions.q: What's 'chunking'?
questions.a: Practicing a small section until secure before joining it to others.

days.guide: Write program notes.

questions.q: What should program notes include?
questions.a: Title, composer/songwriter, brief context, and what to listen for.

days.guide: Hold a dress rehearsal with feedback.

questions.q: Why do a full run-through without stopping?
questions.a: To build stamina and practice recovering from mistakes.

days.guide: Refine weak passages.

questions.q: How do you fix a passage that keeps breaking down?
questions.a: Slow it down with a metronome, isolate the trouble spot and gradually return to tempo.

weeks.assessment_key: Rehearsal log: daily entries with date, minutes, sections practiced, strategy used (slow practice, chunking, metronome), goal and result; at least 5 entries. Program notes: 100–200 words per piece, title/composer, context, what to listen for.

weeks.prep: A recording device; an audience; the semester theory exam (note names, rhythms, scales, key signatures, intervals, chords, Roman numerals, form); the listening exam (excerpts from Weeks 14–16); a showcase rubric; a portfolio folder.
misconceptions: Students judge a performance by mistakes only. Evaluate musicality, tone and communication too.
Students cram theory. Mixed review of all topics works better.
Students skip the self-evaluation. It builds independence.

days.guide: Perform the showcase for family (live or recorded).

questions.q: What is stage presence?
questions.a: Confidence and communication with the audience through posture, focus and expression.

days.guide: Give the semester theory exam.

questions.q: Which major key has two sharps?
questions.a: D major (F♯, C♯).

days.guide: Give the listening identification exam.

questions.q: What clue identifies a gamelan recording?
questions.a: Bronze metallophones and gongs with interlocking patterns and shimmering tuning.

days.guide: The student evaluates the showcase recording with the rubric.

questions.q: Name one strength and one goal from your recording.
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers cite specific moments.

days.guide: Organize the semester portfolio.

questions.q: What belongs in a music portfolio?
questions.a: Recordings, compositions, lead sheets, beats, written reviews and reflections, labeled and dated.

weeks.assessment_key: Theory exam key (sample): note names on grand staff; 4/4 rhythm values; G and F major scales; key signatures (2 sharps = D major; 3 flats = E♭ major); intervals (C–G P5, C–F P4, C–E M3); triads (D minor = D F A); Roman numerals in C (vi = Am); 12-bar blues; sonata form. Listening exam: identify Baroque/Classical/Romantic, blues/jazz, gamelan, raga, mariachi with one supporting feature each. Showcase rubric: accuracy, expression, tone, stage presence, program notes.

weeks.prep: A phone camera; three media artworks to analyze (e.g., a short film, a music video, a photograph); a composition guide with examples.
misconceptions: Students always center the subject. The rule of thirds often creates more dynamic images.
Students think more photos mean better photography. Intentional composition and careful selection matter.
Students confuse depth of field with focus. Depth of field is how much of the scene front-to-back appears sharp.

days.guide: Define media arts (art made with technology: photography, film, sound, digital design, animation) and analyze three works.

questions.q: What makes something 'media arts'?
questions.a: It's created and shared using technology — cameras, computers, audio and video tools.

days.guide: Learn rule of thirds, leading lines and framing with examples.

questions.q: What are leading lines?
questions.a: Lines in the image (roads, fences, rivers) that guide the viewer's eye to the subject.

days.guide: The student shoots 30 photos applying composition rules.

questions.q: How do you get shallow depth of field on a phone?
questions.a: Use portrait mode or get very close to the subject with a distant background.

days.guide: Select the best five and explain choices.

questions.q: How should you choose your best photos?
questions.a: By clear subject, strong composition, sharp focus and good light.

days.guide: Critique photos with criteria.

questions.q: Give one criterion for critique.
questions.a: Composition, lighting, focus, emotional impact, or storytelling.

weeks.assessment_key: Photo set rubric: five best photos each demonstrating a named technique (rule of thirds, leading lines, framing, depth of field, perspective), with a 2–3 sentence explanation per photo; technical quality (focus, exposure); critique uses criteria. Proficient = all five techniques clearly used and explained.

weeks.prep: A free photo editor (Photopea in a browser or Snapseed); a planning sheet for a 6-photo community essay; permission for photographing people (ask before photographing strangers; get parent okay).
misconceptions: Students over-edit (extreme saturation, heavy filters). Edits should serve the story and stay believable.
Students shoot random scenes. A photo essay has a narrative arc: establishing shot, details, people, action, closing image.
Students skip captions. Captions provide who, what, where and why.

days.guide: Learn exposure, contrast and cropping in a free editor.

questions.q: What does increasing contrast do?
questions.a: Makes darks darker and lights lighter, adding punch.

days.guide: Plan a 6-photo essay about your community.

questions.q: What is an establishing shot?
questions.a: A wide image that shows where the story takes place.

days.guide: Shoot the photo essay.

questions.q: Why ask permission before photographing people?
questions.a: Respect, privacy and consent; it's ethical and sometimes legally required for publication.

days.guide: Edit and sequence images.

questions.q: Why keep editing consistent across the essay?
questions.a: It makes the set feel unified.

days.guide: Present the essay with captions.

questions.q: What should a caption include?
questions.a: Who, what, where, when and why, briefly.

weeks.assessment_key: Photo essay rubric: 6 photos with a clear theme and sequence (establishing, medium, detail, portrait, action, closing), consistent editing, captions (who/what/where/why), ethical practices (permission, no misleading edits). Proficient = coherent story with strong images and captions.

weeks.prep: Canva or Photopea; examples of album covers; font samples (serif, sans-serif, display). Use the student's Semester 1 song.
misconceptions: Students use many fonts. Limit to two (one display/heading, one body) for unity.
Students center everything. Alignment to a clear edge or grid looks more professional.
Students use low-resolution images. Album covers are square, typically 3000 × 3000 pixels for streaming.

days.guide: Learn CRAP principles with examples.

questions.q: What does 'proximity' mean in design?
questions.a: Grouping related items close together so they read as a unit.

days.guide: Compare serif, sans-serif and display fonts.

questions.q: What's the difference between serif and sans-serif fonts?
questions.a: Serif fonts have small strokes at letter ends (Times); sans-serif fonts don't (Helvetica).

days.guide: Design an album cover for the Semester 1 song.

questions.q: Why test the cover at thumbnail size?
questions.a: Most people see it small on a phone; the title must still be readable.

days.guide: Get feedback and revise.

questions.q: What is visual hierarchy?
questions.a: Arranging elements so the most important is seen first, using size, color and position.

days.guide: Submit the album cover with explanation.

questions.q: What are complementary colors?
questions.a: Colors opposite on the color wheel (blue/orange, red/green) that create strong contrast.

weeks.assessment_key: Album cover rubric: square format at high resolution; clear visual hierarchy (artist name and title readable at thumbnail size); applies CRAP (contrast, repetition, alignment, proximity); purposeful color scheme; typography appropriate to the music; original or properly licensed images; written explanation connecting design to the song. Proficient = all criteria met.

weeks.prep: Creative Commons website (creativecommons.org) and search (openverse.org); summaries of sampling cases: Grand Upright Music v. Warner Bros. (1991, Biz Markie), Bridgeport Music v. Dimension Films (2005), VMG Salsoul v. Ciccone (2016, Madonna's 'Vogue'); examples of edited news photos. Build the quiz.
misconceptions: Students think anything online is free to use. Most works are copyrighted automatically when created.
Students think giving credit makes any use legal. Credit doesn't replace permission or a license unless the use is fair use or the license allows it.
Students think fair use has a fixed 'seconds rule'. There's no set number of seconds; fair use is judged on four factors.

days.guide: Learn copyright basics and the four fair-use factors.

questions.q: When does a song you write become copyrighted?
questions.a: Automatically as soon as it's fixed — recorded or written down.

days.guide: Find CC-licensed music and images and attribute them correctly.

questions.q: Write a correct attribution.
questions.a: 'Sunset Beach' by Jane Doe (openverse link), licensed under CC BY 4.0.

days.guide: Analyze music sampling lawsuits.

questions.q: What did Bridgeport Music v. Dimension Films (2005) decide?
questions.a: In the 6th Circuit, any unlicensed sample of a sound recording, however small, could infringe — 'Get a license or do not sample.'

days.guide: Analyze how photos are edited to influence viewers.

questions.q: Give one ethical rule for news photo editing.
questions.a: Don't add or remove content; only minor adjustments like exposure and cropping that don't change meaning.

days.guide: Give the copyright and ethics quiz.

questions.q: What does CC BY-NC mean?
questions.a: You may use it with attribution, but not for commercial purposes.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Copyright is automatic once a work is fixed in tangible form. 2) Term — generally the author's life + 70 years. 3) Four fair-use factors — purpose/character (transformative, educational), nature of the work, amount used, effect on the market. 4) Public domain — no copyright (expired, e.g., U.S. works published in 1930 or earlier as of 2026, or dedicated via CC0). 5) CC BY — use with attribution; SA — share alike; NC — noncommercial; ND — no derivatives. 6) Attribution format TASL — Title, Author, Source, License. 7) Grand Upright (1991) — unlicensed sample ruled infringement. 8) Bridgeport (2005) — even tiny sound-recording samples need a license (6th Circuit: 'Get a license or do not sample'). 9) VMG Salsoul (2016, 9th Circuit) — a de minimis sample was allowed. 10) Misleading photo edits violate journalistic ethics.

weeks.prep: Install Audacity (free). Gather household objects for foley (gloves for bird wings, celery for bone snaps, cornstarch in a pouch for footsteps in snow, rice on a tray for rain). Phone microphone and headphones.
misconceptions: Students record too close or too loud. Keep peaks below about −6 dB to avoid clipping; distance changes tone.
Students think foley must use the real object. Foley uses whatever sounds convincing on screen.
Students apply noise reduction too strongly. Over-processing creates 'underwater' artifacts; use light settings.

days.guide: Learn Audacity: record, select, cut, fade in/out, export.

questions.q: How do you remove a section in Audacity?
questions.a: Select it on the waveform and press Delete (or Edit > Cut).

days.guide: Create foley sounds with household objects and record them.

questions.q: What is foley?
questions.a: Everyday sound effects recorded in sync with picture, named after Jack Foley.

days.guide: Build a 1-minute soundscape of a place.

questions.q: What's the difference between ambience and spot effects?
questions.a: Ambience is the background environment (wind, traffic); spot effects are specific sounds (a door slam).

days.guide: Test mic placement and room acoustics (closet with clothes vs. kitchen).

questions.q: Why does a closet full of clothes make a good vocal booth?
questions.a: Soft materials absorb reflections, reducing echo.

days.guide: Share the soundscape.

questions.q: How does noise reduction work in Audacity?
questions.a: You select a section of pure background noise to 'Get Noise Profile', then apply the effect to the whole track to subtract that noise.

weeks.assessment_key: Soundscape rubric: 1 minute; at least 6 layered sounds (ambience, foley, details); fades in/out; levels balanced; panning to create space; clear sense of place; no clipping; uses noise reduction appropriately. Proficient = place clearly recognizable with clean, balanced audio.

weeks.prep: Podcast examples: Radio Ambulante (Spanish with English transcripts) and Song Exploder (preview for language). Script template with timing. Recruit an interviewee (musician or family member).
misconceptions: Students write scripts that sound like essays. Write for the ear: short sentences, conversational tone.
Students ask yes/no interview questions. Ask open-ended questions (how, why, tell me about).
Students underestimate script length. About 130–150 spoken words per minute; a 6–8 minute script is roughly 900–1,100 words including interview time.

days.guide: Listen to two episodes and outline segments and transitions.

questions.q: What is a cold open?
questions.a: A short, attention-grabbing clip before the intro and theme music.

days.guide: Choose a topic and write a one-sentence pitch.

questions.q: Write a sample pitch.
questions.a: 'This episode traces how Chicano rock in East L.A. shaped bands like Los Lobos, told through an interview with a local musician.'

days.guide: Write a 6–8 minute script.

questions.q: About how many words is a 3-minute host segment?
questions.a: About 400–450 words (130–150 words per minute).

days.guide: Write 8 open-ended interview questions and schedule the interview.

questions.q: Turn 'Do you like jazz?' into an open question.
questions.a: 'How did you first get into jazz, and what drew you to it?'

days.guide: Read the script aloud with a timer and adjust length.

questions.q: Why read aloud?
questions.a: To check timing and catch awkward phrasing.

weeks.assessment_key: Script rubric: cold open (hook), intro (show, host, topic), two segments with transitions, interview placement, outro (summary, credits, call to action); timing marks reaching 6–8 minutes; conversational language; 8 open-ended interview questions; a one-sentence pitch. Proficient = complete and timed within range.

weeks.prep: Audacity, a quiet room with soft surfaces, phone or USB mic, the interviewee, the student's original intro music from Unit 2.
misconceptions: Students skip room tone. Record 30 seconds of silence in the room to patch gaps and for noise reduction.
Students cut out every pause. Natural pauses keep speech human; remove only long gaps and filler.
Students set music as loud as voices. Music beds sit well under speech.

days.guide: Record host segments, re-recording flubbed lines.

questions.q: Why leave a short pause before re-reading a flubbed line?
questions.a: It makes clean edit points.

days.guide: Record the interview and capture 30 seconds of room tone.

questions.q: What is room tone?
questions.a: The natural background sound of a room with no one speaking, used to fill gaps smoothly.

days.guide: Edit the interview to its best 3 minutes.

questions.q: What should you cut?
questions.a: Filler words, long pauses, repetition and off-topic tangents, without changing the meaning.

days.guide: Add intro music, crossfades and balanced levels.

questions.q: What is a crossfade?
questions.a: One sound fades out while another fades in, overlapping for a smooth transition.

days.guide: Export a draft MP3 and collect feedback.

questions.q: Is it ethical to edit an interview so the person seems to say something they didn't?
questions.a: No — edits must preserve the speaker's meaning.

weeks.assessment_key: Draft episode checklist: host segments clean and re-recorded where flubbed; interview edited to best 3 minutes; 30-second room tone captured; intro music, crossfades and balanced levels (speech clear, music lower); exported MP3; feedback from one listener recorded.

weeks.prep: Audacity, the draft and feedback, a professional podcast for comparison, the podcast rubric, CC attribution examples.
misconceptions: Students normalize peaks and think loudness is fixed. Loudness normalization (e.g., about −16 LUFS for podcasts) matches perceived volume across episodes.
Students forget credits for music and sound effects. CC licenses require attribution.
Students reflect only on what went well. Include what you'd change and why.

days.guide: Re-edit using the three most important notes, tightening segments over 2 minutes.

questions.q: How do you decide which feedback to use?
questions.a: Prioritize comments that affect clarity and engagement, especially those mentioned by more than one listener.

days.guide: Write show notes with summary, timestamps and CC attributions.

questions.q: Why include timestamps?
questions.a: Listeners can jump to segments.

days.guide: Normalize the episode in Audacity and export MP3; compare against a professional podcast.

questions.q: What loudness target do many podcast platforms recommend?
questions.a: About −16 LUFS integrated for stereo.

days.guide: Score your episode and a professional one on the same rubric.

questions.q: Why compare to a professional example?
questions.a: To see specific gaps in quality and set targets.

days.guide: Write a 250-word reflection on changes for episode two.

questions.q: Give an example of a specific change.
questions.a: 'Record the host in the closet to reduce echo and cut the intro from 60 to 20 seconds.'

weeks.assessment_key: Podcast rubric (each 1–4): Story (hook, structure, clear focus), Audio quality (clean, consistent loudness ~−16 LUFS, no clipping), Pacing (segments ≤2 min of drag, transitions), Voice (natural delivery), Show notes (50-word summary, timestamps, CC attributions). Proficient 15+/20.

weeks.prep: Clips: Casablanca (1942) airport scene; a modern dialogue scene; the Odessa Steps sequence from Battleship Potemkin (1925; parental note: depicts violence against civilians, no gore by modern standards — preview). Storyboard template with 9 panels. Quiz stills.
misconceptions: Students describe shots by camera distance only. Combine shot size (wide, medium, close-up) with angle (high, low, eye-level, Dutch).
Students think editing just removes mistakes. Editing creates meaning, rhythm and controls time.
Students storyboard art-perfect drawings. Stick figures are fine; clarity of shot type and angle matters.

days.guide: Log each shot of a 3-minute classic scene as wide, medium, close-up or extreme close-up.

questions.q: Why use a close-up?
questions.a: To show emotion and focus attention on a face or detail.

days.guide: Photograph an object at high, low, eye-level and Dutch angles and write the feeling each creates.

questions.q: What does a low-angle shot usually suggest?
questions.a: Power or dominance of the subject.

days.guide: Compare continuity editing in a dialogue scene with the Odessa Steps montage.

questions.q: How does Eisenstein's montage treat time?
questions.a: It expands time, cutting many shots together so the event feels longer and more intense than real time.

questions.q: What is the 180-degree rule?
questions.a: Keep the camera on one side of an imaginary line between characters so screen directions stay consistent.

days.guide: Draw a 9-panel storyboard for a 30-second scene with shot type, angle and sound.

questions.q: Why note sound in a storyboard?
questions.a: Sound shapes meaning and must be planned for recording.

days.guide: Take a quiz identifying shot types and edits, then revise the storyboard.

questions.q: What's a Dutch angle?
questions.a: A tilted camera angle that creates unease or disorientation.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: identify wide/establishing, medium, close-up, extreme close-up; high angle (subject looks small/vulnerable), low angle (powerful), eye level (neutral), Dutch/canted (unease); cut, match cut, cross-cutting, montage, shot/reverse shot, 180-degree rule (keep camera on one side of the action line). Storyboard rubric: 9 panels, shot type/angle/sound noted, clear 30-second story, logical continuity.

weeks.prep: Phone, tripod or steady surface, free editor (DaVinci Resolve or Clipchamp), the storyboard, any actors (family), and a shooting checklist. Charge batteries and clear storage.
misconceptions: Students shoot only one take. Capture each shot twice plus B-roll to have options in editing.
Students ignore audio. Bad sound ruins good video; record close and in quiet locations.
Students color-correct each clip differently. Aim for consistency across a scene.

days.guide: Practice trimming, splitting and ordering clips on the timeline.
